https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Proposed July 2020 amendments to the bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association, distributed to member boards including Troy for the August 18, 2020 meeting. The underlying bylaws carry adoption dates of 11/15/2017 by the Board of Directors and 01/24/2018 and 10/18/2018 by the General Membership, and govern an association whose principal office is 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, Oakland County. The most consequential proposed change adds Article XVI, Section 3, allowing the Board of Directors to set aside bylaw rules governing meetings, elections and the conduct of Association affairs whenever a local, state or national emergency has been declared.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**What it is**
Bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association (the "Association"), shown with proposed July 2020 amendments, in the Troy School District Board of Education packet dated August 18, 2020. Adoption lines on the face of the document: Board of Directors 11/15/2017; General Membership 01/24/2018; General Membership 10/18/2018. Sixteen articles across sixteen numbered pages.

**Offices, purpose, dues (Articles I, II, IV)**
Principal office at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, County of Oakland, Michigan, plus a continuously maintained registered office and agent. Eight purposes (a)-(h) run from advancing education quality in Oakland County to sponsoring programs in partnership with Oakland Schools and advocating for county, state and national legislation. Funding is an annual MASB grant to County Area School Boards Association (CASBA) members, ISD dues not exceeding that grant, and contributions and gifts.

**Membership and member meetings (Articles III, V)**
Eligible members are publicly elected Oakland County board of education members or elected Oakland ISD board members in good standing with the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB). Each Member has one in-person vote; on committee-chair selection, resolutions and bylaw amendments each Member School District casts one (1) vote. Electronic voting is reserved to the Board of Directors for emergency business. An annual meeting - the first Regular Meeting after July 1 - plus not less than three additional regular membership meetings are held yearly; member-meeting notice runs not less than ten nor more than fifty days ahead. Quorum is at least one Member from twenty-five (25%) percent of Member School Districts.

**Board and officers (Articles VI-VIII)**
One Member per district may serve at a time, for a three (3) year term. By May 1st an Election Committee of the three most recently elected Directors from different districts is convened; elections occur at the June meeting, by written ballot if candidates exceed vacancies. Missing three (3) consecutive Board meetings constitutes resignation. Board proceedings are confidential. Officers - President (Chief Executive Officer), Vice-President, Secretary, Treasurer - are elected from the sitting Board and receive no stated salaries.

**Committees (Article IX)**
| Committee | Meeting frequency | Key deadline |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Government Relations | At least 6 times per year | Legislative Priorities to Board by June 15th; chair elected at first meeting after January 31st |
| Resolutions and Bylaws | At least twice per year, amended to once | At least three members appointed by the Board each June |

District voting windows on resolutions and bylaw amendments run at least forty (40) calendar days, and a resolution approved by at least nineteen (19) Member School Districts becomes the Association's official position.

**Financial controls (Article XI)**
Board approval plus signatures of both the President and Treasurer are required for any expenditure exceeding $2,500; expenditures up to $2,500 may be approved by either officer. The Treasurer reports quarterly, presents an annual budget (July 1 to June 30) by June 30th and an annual actual income and expense report by August 30th. Records are reviewed internally by the Board and externally by a third party under agreed-upon procedures, a full audit occurring only if required by law or a third party. An Administrative and Financial Services Agreement with Oakland Schools is permitted.

**Amendments and emergency authority (Article XVI)**
Bylaws are amended by vote of the Member School Districts on written ballots with at least a forty (40) day voting period, one vote per district. Section 2 is amended to allow rules inconsistent with the Articles or Bylaws where a local, state or national emergency has been declared, and a new Section 3 lets the Board set aside bylaw rules on meetings, elections and Association affairs during a declared emergency.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association, shown with proposed amendments circulated in July 2020 and included in the Troy School District Board of Education materials for August 18, 2020. Three adoption lines head the document: adopted by Board of Directors 11/15/2017; adopted by General Membership 01/24/2018; adopted by General Membership 10/18/2018. The text runs sixteen articles across sixteen numbered pages.

ARTICLE I - OFFICES. The principal office of the Association is at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, County of Oakland, Michigan, with authority to maintain other offices within or outside Michigan. A registered office and a registered agent whose office is identical with it must be continuously maintained; the address may be changed by the Board of Directors.

ARTICLE II - PURPOSE. Eight purposes: advancing the quality of public education in Oakland County through cooperative efforts of locally-elected boards; promoting high standards in programs and services; making information on educational issues available to board members; sponsoring meetings and programs in partnership with Oakland Schools; promoting public understanding of the role of school boards; enhancing cooperation among Oakland County boards; representing those boards to political representatives serving the area; and advocating for county, state and national legislation supporting public education.

ARTICLE III - MEMBERSHIP. Any publicly elected Board of Education member of an Oakland County school district, or any elected Oakland ISD Board of Education member (their districts termed "Member School Districts"), in good standing with the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB), is an eligible general member. Each Member has one vote per matter, cast in person; by exception each Member School District has one (1) vote on selecting a committee chair, on resolutions under Article IX, and on amending the Bylaws under Article XVI. District votes are recorded on receipt of the completed resolution or ballot, must arrive before the stated deadline, and results go to all Member Districts by the next general membership meeting. Electronic voting is granted to the Board of Directors only, for emergency business. Membership is not transferable.

ARTICLE IV - DUES. Financing comes from an annual MASB grant to its County Area School Boards Association (CASBA) members, Intermediate School District membership dues not to exceed the MASB CASBA grant, and contributions and gifts.

ARTICLE V - MEETING OF MEMBERS. An annual meeting plus not less than three additional regular membership meetings occur yearly; the annual meeting is the first Regular Meeting after July 1. Special meetings of the Board or Members may be called by voice or email by the President or by two or more Directors with 30 days' notice. The Secretary delivers written notice personally or by email not less than ten nor more than fifty days before a member meeting. Quorum is at least one Member from twenty-five (25%) percent of the Member School Districts.

ARTICLE VI - ELECTION OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS. Only one Member from each Member School District may serve at a time; the term is three (3) years, continuing until a successor is elected and qualified. By May 1st yearly the Board convenes an Election Committee of the three most recently elected Directors from different Member School Districts (the amendment replaces "create" with "convene"), which seeks candidates giving geographical balance across Oakland County; Candidate Application Forms, formerly "Board Nomination" forms, go to all districts for self-nomination. Additional nominations may come from the floor at the Members' June meeting but not at the meeting where the election occurs; the election is held at the June meeting, by written ballot if candidates exceed vacancies. If candidates are fewer than vacancies the Board appoints a member to serve until the next scheduled election. Directors may resign or be removed with or without cause by majority vote of the Members or Directors then in office, excluding the subject Director; a vacancy is filled by Board appointment for the remainder of the vacated term. Failure to attend three (3) consecutive Board meetings constitutes resignation, subject to an excused absence granted by Board action.

ARTICLE VII - BOARD OF DIRECTORS. The Board carries out the purposes in Article II of the Articles of Incorporation. The regular annual Board meeting needs no notice beyond the Bylaws; special meetings may be called by the President or any two Directors on at least two days' written notice delivered personally, by phone, fax or e-mail, or five days' notice by mail. A majority of Directors is a quorum, and the act of a majority of Directors present serving, whether elected or appointed, is the act of the Board. Directors receive no stated salaries, though a fixed sum and expenses of attendance may be allowed by resolution. Section 9 makes the records and business of all Board proceedings confidential absent advance authorization.

ARTICLE VIII - OFFICERS. The Board elects from its current membership a President, Vice-President, Secretary and Treasurer, serving until the next annual meeting and thereafter until successors are chosen or they resign or are removed by majority vote of the Directors. Officers receive no stated salaries. The President is Chief Executive Officer, manages Association activities, executes authorized conveyances and contracts, and presides at Director meetings. The Secretary records all votes and minutes in a book kept for that purpose. The Treasurer has custody of funds and securities, keeps full and accurate accounts, deposits moneys in designated depositories, disburses funds taking proper vouchers, and if required gives a bond for faithful performance. The Board may require bonds of all officers at Association cost.

ARTICLE IX - COMMITTEES. Standing and ad hoc committees may be designated. The Government Relations Committee is standing, shares legislative information with Member School Districts, and meets at least 6 times per year; each district should appoint a representative at its annual organizational meeting, and a Committee Chairperson is elected annually from the appointed Members at the first committee meeting after January 31st, with one (1) vote per district in attendance. Legislative Priorities are revised annually and submitted to the Board of Directors for approval by June 15th, then provided to the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee and Member School Districts. That committee is also standing and manages the resolutions and bylaws process, meeting at least twice per year with the amendment changing "twice" to "once"; at least three members are appointed by the Board annually in June and elect a Chairperson at their first meeting. Revisions may be initiated by a Member School District Board, the Board of Directors, or either standing committee, and the Board reviews all proposals before they go to Member School Districts, which vote within a window of at least forty (40) calendar days. Resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) Member School Districts become the official position of the Association.

ARTICLE X - DISSOLUTION. Assets are distributed as provided in Article VIII of the Articles of Incorporation. No net earnings may inure to any Member, Director or Officer, as prohibited by Section 501(c)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended, the Michigan General Sales Tax Act or the Michigan Use Tax Act.

ARTICLE XI - FIDUCIARY AND FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITIES. Expenditures may not exceed the approved annual budget, and no committee may create financial liability unless authorized by a majority of the Members. Board approval and signatures of both the President and Treasurer are required for any expenditure exceeding $2,500; expenditures up to $2,500 must be approved by either the Board President or the Treasurer, with the Vice President substituting if either is absent or disabled. Reports go to all Board members quarterly or on request; the Treasurer presents an annual budget covering July 1 to June 30 by June 30th and an annual actual income and expense report by August 30th, both presented at the first fall Member Meeting, with records closed annually for IRS filings. Agreed-upon procedures are performed annually by the Board internally and by a third party externally, an audit occurring only if required by law or a third party. Section 4 permits an Administrative and Financial Services Agreement with Oakland Schools, monitored by the Treasurer.

ARTICLE XII - INDEMNIFICATION. Directors and officers are indemnified to the fullest extent authorized by the Michigan Nonprofit Association Act, for third-party claims and claims brought by or in the right of the Association, covering expenses, attorneys' fees, judgments, penalties, fines and settlements where the Indemnitee acted in good faith; claims brought by the Indemnitee are excluded unless authorized by the Board. Determinations are made by majority vote of a quorum of non-party directors, by a committee of not less than two (2) disinterested directors, or by independent legal counsel in a written opinion. Expenses are advanced on an unsecured unlimited general obligation undertaking to repay, and the Association may purchase liability insurance.

ARTICLES XIII-XV. The fiscal year is set by the Board of Directors. The conflicts article requires officers, directors, committee members and employees to avoid conflicts; a contract with an interested director is not void solely for that interest if it is fair and reasonable or if material facts are disclosed and it is approved without counting that director's vote. A conflicted Director must give notice, refrain from voting, is excluded from the quorum on that matter, and the minutes must reflect the disclosure and abstention. Miscellaneous provisions govern conveyances, execution of checks, drafts, bills of exchange, acceptances and notes, borrowing, adjourned meetings, notice by mail, written consent filed with the minutes, participation by conference telephone constituting presence in person, and a corporate seal inscribed with the Association name, "Corporate Seal" and "Michigan."

ARTICLE XVI - AMENDMENTS AND ADDITIONS. Bylaws may be altered or amended by vote of the Member School Districts, with the Board providing a written ballot and at least a forty (40) day voting period, one vote per district. Section 2, on additional rules for Board meetings and Association affairs, is amended to insert "unless a local, state or national emergency has been declared" before the bar on rules inconsistent with the Articles of Incorporation or Bylaws. A new Section 3, "Rules and Regulations During a Declared Emergency," provides that on a declared local, state or national emergency the Board of Directors may set aside rules and regulations within the bylaws, general or specific, regarding the conduct of their meetings and election and the conduct of the affairs of the Association.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Interlocal agreement between Oakland County and the Troy School District distributing a share of the county's federal CARES Act money through the Oakland Together Schools COVID Support Fund, brought to the Board of Education as agenda item 5.G on October 20, 2020. Entered under the Urban Cooperation Act of 1967, 1967 Public Act 7, MCL 124.501 et seq., it reimburses only pandemic costs absent from the district's budget as approved on March 27, 2020, never revenue losses. Treasury guidance presumes eligibility up to $500 per student without itemization; anything above that cap requires detailed records. The agreement runs until January 31, 2021, with Expenditure Submission Forms accepted only through November 30, 2020.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Parties and authority**
Agreement for CARES Act Distribution between Oakland County, a Municipal and Constitutional Corporation, 1200 North Telegraph Road, Pontiac, Michigan 48341, and the Troy School District, 4400 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098. Executed under the Urban Cooperation Act of 1967, 1967 Public Act 7, MCL 124.501 et seq. Board of Education agenda item 5.G, October 20, 2020.

**What is being distributed**
CARES Act funds are money distributed to the County by the United States Department of Treasury under section 601(a) of the Social Security Act, as added by section 5001 of the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act. The portion allocated to school districts is the Oakland Together Schools COVID Support Fund. The Office of the Oakland County Executive (OCE) reviews each Expenditure Submission Form and works with the Board of Commissioners Oversight Committee on eligibility.

**County responsibilities**
- OCE determines eligibility at its discretion under the Coronavirus Relief Fund Guidance for State, Territorial, Local and Tribal Governments, and may request supporting documentation.
- A distribution cap is set for each district based on enrolled students, teachers employed, and students eligible for the federal free and reduced lunch program; the cap is not a guarantee.
- No Expenditure Submission Forms are accepted after November 30, 2020; unclaimed balances are retained and may be redistributed to other eligible districts.

**District responsibilities**
Eligible expenses are limited to costs incurred due to the COVID-19 public health emergency: distance-learning facilitation including technological improvements tied to school closings, acquisition and distribution of medical and protective supplies, disinfection of public areas and facilities, and compliance with COVID-19 public health orders. Funds may only cover expenses not accounted for in the district's most recently approved budget as of March 27, 2020, and may not be used as revenue replacement. Under Treasury guidance the district submits documentation of CARES money already received up to the $500 per-pupil allowable cap and requests the remaining per-pupil amount; requests above the $500 per-pupil administrative cap require records of all excess expenditures with a detailed description of use and compliance. Records must be kept a minimum of 10 (ten) years and produced on request or on audit. Duplicate federal or state funding, and any spending found non-compliant, must be returned to the County.

**Term and termination**
Effective on execution by both Parties with resolutions of their governing bodies, entered in official minutes, and filed by the County Clerk with the Secretary of State. In effect until January 31, 2021 unless cancelled; record-keeping, reporting, audit-response and fund-return duties survive termination. The County may terminate for misuse, with repayment owed; the district may terminate at any time and must immediately return all funds received.

**Legal terms**
Each Party bears its own claims, legal representation and costs; there is no indemnification and no waiver of governmental immunity. Assignment requires prior written consent. No third-party beneficiaries. Governed by Michigan law with venue in the 6th Judicial Circuit Court, the 50th District Court, or the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan, Southern Division. Notices go to the Oakland County Executive at 2100 Pontiac Lake Rd., Waterford, MI 48328 and the Chairperson of the Oakland County Board of Commissioners at 1200 North Telegraph Road, Pontiac, MI 48341, and to the School District Superintendent at 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098.

**Signatures**
Dr. Rich Machesky, Superintendent of Schools, signs for Troy School District under a Board of Education resolution, witnessed by Rick West, Assistant Superintendent. David Woodward, Chairperson of the Oakland County Board of Commissioners, signs for the County.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Agreement for CARES Act Distribution between Oakland County and the Troy School District, carried as item 5.G on the Troy School District Board of Education agenda for October 20, 2020. The County is identified as a Municipal and Constitutional Corporation at 1200 North Telegraph Road, Pontiac, Michigan 48341; the School District at 4400 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098. The agreement is entered pursuant to the Urban Cooperation Act of 1967, 1967 Public Act 7, MCL 124.501 et seq., for the purpose of the County distributing a portion of its CARES Act funds to school districts within Oakland County to assist them in meeting areas of need caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

DEFINITIONS. "CARES Act funds" means money distributed to the County by the United States Department of Treasury pursuant to section 601(a) of the Social Security Act, as added by section 5001 of the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act. "Oakland Together Schools COVID Support Fund" means the portion of those CARES Act funds the County has allocated to school districts within Oakland County. "Expenditure Submission Form" is the form the district must complete and submit to OCE before any disbursement. "OCE" means the Office of the Oakland County Executive, including the Chief Deputy and other Deputy County Executives. "Oversight Committee" means the committee established by the Oakland County Board of Commissioners in the resolution allocating the Oakland Together Schools funds. "Day" means any calendar day beginning at 12:00 a.m. and ending at 11:59 p.m. "Claims" is defined expansively to cover losses, complaints, demands, lawsuits, causes of action, judgments, deficiencies, liabilities, penalties, litigation, costs and expenses including reimbursement for reasonable attorney fees, witness fees, court costs, investigation and litigation expenses and settlement amounts. "County" includes all departments, divisions, the County Board of Commissioners, elected and appointed officials, directors, board members, council members, commissioners, authorities, committees, employees, agents and volunteers. "School District" includes its school board, superintendent, employees, agents, subcontractors, attorneys and volunteers. "School District Employee" reaches officers, directors, members, managers, trustees, volunteers, attorneys, representatives, licensees, concessionaires, contractors, subcontractors, independent contractors and agents who use or access the funds, including former employees during the term, but excludes an individual resident who receives an authorized distribution.

COUNTY RESPONSIBILITIES (Section 2). OCE reviews the district's Expenditure Submission Form to determine eligibility, exercising discretion under the "Coronavirus Relief Fund Guidance for State, Territorial, Local and Tribal Government" or other federal guidance, and may request any supporting documentation it deems necessary. If eligible, the County distributes the eligible amount. The County sets a distribution cap for each district based on three factors: the number of students enrolled in the district, the number of teachers employed by the district, and the number of students eligible for the federal free and reduced lunch program; the cap is expressly not a guarantee or promise of a certain amount. The County has no obligation to distribute funds if OCE finds the district ineligible or if available funds are insufficient to fulfill the submitted form. Under Section 2.5, after November 30, 2020 the County will not accept any further Expenditure Submission Forms, and will retain the balance of funds for which the district was originally eligible but which are not covered by an approved form; the County may then redistribute any or all of that retained amount to other eligible school districts or as otherwise deemed appropriate by OCE. OCE works in collaboration with the Board of Commissioners Oversight Committee in determining eligibility and amounts.

SCHOOL DISTRICT RESPONSIBILITIES (Section 3). The district must complete and submit an Expenditure Submission Form and obtain OCE approval before any distribution. It must follow all United States Treasury Department and County guidance, including Section 601(d) of the Social Security Act and the Coronavirus Relief Fund Guidance. Funds may be spent only on expenses incurred due to the COVID-19 public health emergency, such as expenses to facilitate distance learning including technological improvements in connection with school closings to enable compliance with COVID-19 precautions; expenses for the acquisition and distribution of medical and protective supplies; expenses for disinfection of public areas and other facilities; and expenses to ensure compliance with COVID-19 public health orders. Spending is further restricted to expenses not accounted for in the district's most recently approved budget as of March 27, 2020, and the funds may not be used as revenue replacement. Per Treasury guidance quoted in the agreement - "as an administrative convenience, Treasury will presume that expenses of up to $500 per elementary and secondary school student to be eligible expenditures, such that schools do not need to document the specific use of funds up to that amount" - the district submits documentation of how much CARES Act money it has already received up to the $500 allowable cap and requests the remaining amount per pupil from the County. Any request above the $500 per pupil administrative cap requires the district to submit records of all expenditures in excess of that amount to OCE before reimbursement, with a detailed description of how funds were expended and how the expenditure complied with CARES Act requirements. If the district receives federal or state funding covering the same expenses, it must return that amount to the County. Records sufficient to demonstrate compliance must be kept for a minimum of 10 (ten) years and produced on request by the County or OCE or as required by any future CARES Act audit. Any amount found by OCE or any audit to have been expended in violation of the CARES Act or the agreement must be returned to the County.

DURATION (Section 4). The agreement is effective when executed by both Parties with resolutions passed by their governing bodies where applicable; its approval and terms are entered in the official minutes of each governing body, and an executed copy plus any amendments is filed by the County Clerk with the Secretary of State. It remains in effect until January 31, 2021 unless cancelled or terminated earlier, and the district must comply with record keeping, reporting, audit response and fund return requirements after termination.

ASSURANCES (Section 5). Each Party is responsible for Claims made against it by third parties and for the acts of its employees. Except as provided in Section 3.13, each Party seeks its own legal representation and bears its own costs including judgments and attorney fees. There is no right to indemnification or reimbursement between the Parties. The district is solely responsible for all costs, fines and fees associated with any misuse of the funds or noncompliance by School District Employees. The agreement does not impair, divest, delegate or contravene any constitutional, statutory or other legal right, privilege, power, obligation, duty or immunity, and nothing constitutes a waiver of governmental immunity. Both Parties confirm they have taken all actions and secured all approvals necessary and that their signatories have legal authority to bind them. Each Party must comply with all applicable federal, state and local ordinances, regulations and administrative rules.

TERMINATION (Section 6). The County may terminate or cancel at any time if it determines the district spent funds in violation of the CARES Act or the agreement, with either OCE or the Board of Commissioners authorized to act, and the district then liable to repay the amount spent in violation. The district may terminate at any time if it does not wish to receive funds, in which case it must immediately return all funds already received. Written notice under Section 13 is required from either Party.

REMAINING TERMS. Section 7 bars delegation or assignment without prior written consent; Section 8 creates no third-party beneficiaries; Section 9 requires a written waiver; Section 10 severs illegal or invalid terms; Section 11 gives the Agreement precedence over conflicting documents; Section 12 makes captions non-substantive. Section 13 requires written notices, personally delivered or sent by express delivery service, certified mail, or first class U.S. mail postage prepaid, deemed given on actual receipt, the next business day for express or personal delivery, or three days after mailing; County notices go to the Oakland County Executive, 2100 Pontiac Lake Rd., Waterford, MI, 48328, and the Chairperson of the Oakland County Board of Commissioners, 1200 North Telegraph Road, Pontiac, MI, 48341, and district notices to the School District Superintendent, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. Section 14 applies Michigan law with venue in the 6th Judicial Circuit Court of the State of Michigan, the 50th District Court of the State of Michigan, or the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan, Southern Division. Section 15 lists surviving terms: Definitions (Section 1), Assurances (Section 5), No Third-Party Beneficiaries (Section 8), No Implied Waiver (Section 9), Severability (Section 10), Precedence of Documents (Section 11), Governing Law/Consent to Jurisdiction and Venue (Section 14), Survival of Terms (Section 15), Entire Agreement (Section 16), and the record keeping, reporting, audit compliance and fund return provisions of Section 3. Section 16 makes the agreement the entire understanding regarding the Oakland Together Schools COVID Support funds, superseding all other oral or written agreements on that subject.

EXECUTION. Dr. Rich Machesky, Superintendent of Schools, acknowledges authorization by a resolution of the Troy School District Board of Education, a certified copy of which is attached, to execute the agreement and bind the district; the witness line names Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Troy School District. David Woodward, Chairperson of the Oakland County Board of Commissioners, acknowledges authorization by a resolution of the Oakland County Board of Commissioners to execute on behalf of Oakland County. Execution and date lines are left blank in the packet copy.

**What it is**
Report to the Board of Education from Plante & Moran, PLLC on the audit of Troy School District's basic financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2023. Cover letter and audit report both dated October 3, 2023, signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager. The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the business office.

| Section | Pages |
| --- | --- |
| Results of the Audit | 1-4 |
| Other Recommendations and Observations | 5-6 |
| Informational Items | 7-16 |

**Results of the Audit**
Engagement letter dated May 31, 2023; planning meeting August 4, 2023. The audit was also conducted under Government Auditing Standards, with a separate letter dated October 3, 2023 on internal control over financial reporting and compliance. Significant accounting policies appear in Note 2; no new policies were adopted during 2023. The most sensitive estimates were the District's shares of MPSERS net liabilities under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75: $340,447,659 for pension and $19,240,985 for OPEB at June 30, 2023, from Office of Retirement Services data. No disagreements with management, no significant difficulties, no consultations with other accountants; management corrected all identified misstatements.

**Other Recommendations and Observations**
- GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1: grouped purchases individually below the capitalization threshold but above it in aggregate must be recorded in fixed asset records; effective for the year ending June 30, 2024.
- The Food Service Fund balance continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum of three months' operating expenditures; the spenddown plan with the Michigan Department of Education should continue.
- Troy Career Center (MiWorks) federal and state expenditures are entered manually into an Excel template serving as the subsidiary ledger, including the WIOA program tested in the single audit; automation or more frequent reconciliation is encouraged.
- The Inflation Reduction Act, signed August 16, 2022, allocated $369 billion over the next 10 years toward reducing emissions approximately 40 percent by 2030, and offers tax-exempt entities a direct-payment option for qualifying capital improvements.

**Informational Items - state funding**
For 2022/2023 all schools except hold harmless districts were funded at a target foundation allowance of $9,150 per pupil, an increase of $450 per pupil. For 2023/2024 the target rose $458 per pupil to $9,608, a 5 percent increase; cyber schools remain at $9,150. The blended count stays 90 percent October 2023 and 10 percent February 2023, with a new two-year 50/50 blend under Section 29 for declining enrollment districts. State special education support moves fully to Section 51 rather than Section 20, so foundation dollars no longer supplement the Headlee Amendment obligation. Also noted: Section 31a At-Risk on an opportunity index, Section 31d universal free breakfast and lunch, GSRP eligibility raised to 300 percent of poverty, a riders-per-square-mile transportation formula, and a 5 percent ISD operations increase. Federal pandemic education aid ends September 30, 2024; the next Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference is January 2024.

**MPSERS and fund balance**
At September 30, 2022 the MPSERS net pension liability was approximately $37.9 billion, up approximately 57 percent from $24.2 billion at September 30, 2021; the net OPEB liability was approximately $2.1 billion, up approximately 40 percent from $1.5 billion. The plan returned 27.2 percent for the year ended September 30, 2021 versus a 4.8 percent investment loss for the year ended September 30, 2022. During 2022/2023 General Fund expenditures exceeded revenue by approximately $361,000, reducing fund balance to approximately $32,620,000 at June 30, 2023 - 17.2 percent of expenditures, approximately 8.9 weeks of operation.

**Also covered**
GASB financial reporting model project (final standards targeted March 2024); Revenue and Expense Recognition possibly issued during 2027; sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023; GASB Statement No. 101 effective for the year ending June 30, 2025; Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1; arbitrage; cybersecurity; and real estate strategy through Plante Moran Cresa.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Report to the Board of Education, Troy School District, June 30, 2023, issued by Plante & Moran, PLLC in connection with the audit of the School District's basic financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2023. The transmittal letter, dated October 3, 2023, states that in addition to the audit report the firm is providing the results of the audit, a summary of unrecorded possible adjustments, other recommendations and observations, and informational items, paginated as Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-16). The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness. The Results of the Audit letter is signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager.

RESULTS OF THE AUDIT. Plante & Moran audited the financial statements of Troy School District as of and for the year ended June 30, 2023 and issued its report thereon dated October 3, 2023. As stated in the engagement letter dated May 31, 2023, the auditor's responsibility is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management with Board oversight are fairly presented in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, obtaining reasonable but not absolute assurance. Internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures. The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, under which the firm issued a separate letter dated October 3, 2023 regarding internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements. The audit followed the planned scope and timing communicated at the planning meeting on August 4, 2023.

Significant audit findings. Significant accounting policies are described in Note 2; no new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies was not changed during 2023. No transactions lacked authoritative guidance or consensus, and none were recognized in a different period than when they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the School District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75: $340,447,659 for the pension plan and $19,240,985 for the OPEB plan as of June 30, 2023, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures were characterized as neutral, consistent, and clear. The auditors encountered no significant difficulties, reported no disagreements with management, and stated that management corrected all accumulated known and likely misstatements other than trivial ones. Representations were requested in the management representation letter dated October 3, 2023, and there were no consultations with other independent accountants. The firm read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to its attention suggesting the other information was materially misstated or inconsistent with the financial statements.

OTHER RECOMMENDATIONS AND OBSERVATIONS. GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1 clarifies that items purchased in a group that are individually below a district's capitalization threshold but exceed it in the aggregate should be reported in fixed asset records; the guidance takes effect in the year ending June 30, 2024, and the District should review its practices and written policies. Food Service Fund - Fund Balance: the fund balance continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures, and the District should continue to monitor the spenddown plan entered into with the Michigan Department of Education. Troy Career Center (MiWorks) Expenditure Reporting: the allocation is tracked manually, with the program director entering all federal and state expenditures into an Excel template that serves as a subsidiary ledger by program, including the WIOA program tested as part of the single audit; the firm encourages a more automated process or more frequent reconciliation. Inflation Reduction Act: signed into law August 16, 2022, the IRA allocated $369 billion over the next 10 years for energy and climate projects intended to reduce emissions by approximately 40 percent by 2030, and includes a direct-payment option in lieu of a nonrefundable tax credit for tax-exempt entities; qualifying capital expenditures may include certain electric vehicles and renewable energy equipment such as solar panels.

INFORMATIONAL ITEMS. Managing the Changing Financial Resources Landscape describes the period since 2020 - pandemic uncertainty, a significant infusion of federal resources, and a stable and growing state budget platform. The May 2023 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference predicted sufficient resources for current programs with substantial resources for new initiatives, and the 2023/2024 School Aid Bill was completed and signed into law. For 2022/2023, following the May 2022 conference, all schools except a few hold harmless districts were funded at the target foundation allowance of $9,150 per pupil, and all schools including hold harmless districts received an increase of $450 per pupil, the largest per-pupil increase since the start of Proposal A (1994/1995), with added funding for special education, At-Risk, wraparound services such as nurses and counselors, and the Great Start Readiness Program consistent with the School Finance Research Collaborative. For 2023/2024 the target foundation allowance increases by $458 per pupil to $9,608, a 5 percent increase, with hold harmless districts also receiving $458 while cyber schools remain at $9,150. The blended pupil count continues at 90 percent weighting for the October 2023 count and 10 percent for the February 2023 count, with a two-year blend for declining enrollment districts qualifying under Section 29 based on 50 percent of the blended 2022 count and 50 percent of the blended 2023 count. State special education funding moves entirely to Section 51 of the State Aid Act rather than partly from Section 20, so special education is fully categorical and no longer supplements Headlee Amendment payments from foundation allowance amounts. Other provisions: GSRP reimbursed at the target foundation allowance with income limits raised to 300 percent of the poverty level; Section 31a/At-Risk weighted by an opportunity index; Section 31d universal free breakfast and lunch; a riders-per-square-mile transportation formula; one-time funding for student mental health, school safety, and a student loan repayment program; increased retirement system contributions despite discontinuation of the one-time $1 billion contribution made in 2022/2023; and a 5 percent increase in the intermediate school district operations allocation. The May 2023 conference projected 2024, 2025, and 2026, with a substantial 2023 surplus carrying into 2024, a reduced 2024 surplus because of one-time payments, and a return to significant surplus in 2025; inflation and a potential recession are the two key risks, and the next conference occurs in January 2024. Education-focused federal pandemic funding concludes September 30, 2024, the "federal funding cliff," raising questions about the ESSER III/11t allocation, staff retention and recruitment, pupil count trends, learning loss, expanded GSRP preschool, food service redesign, inflation-driven cost increases, technology, and school security and mental health costs.

Michigan School Meals. Beginning in 2023/2024, free breakfast and lunch are available to all Michigan students, state funded for those who do not qualify under the National School Lunch and National School Breakfast programs. Participation is not automatic; districts must apply using the 2024 Coordinated Application in the State's NexSys system, participate in the National School Lunch Program, serve breakfast and lunch at no cost to pre-K through 12th grade students, adopt the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP), collect family income information, and write off all outstanding student negative balances, which the Food Service Fund is not allowed to absorb.

MPSERS net liabilities. The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2022 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $37.9 billion, an increase of approximately 57 percent from $24.2 billion at September 30, 2021, driven largely by net investment losses; the plan's annual investment rate of return was 27.2 percent for the year ended September 30, 2021 compared with an investment loss of 4.8 percent for the year ended September 30, 2022. The retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB liability of approximately $2.1 billion at September 30, 2022, an increase of approximately 40 percent from $1.5 billion at September 30, 2021, for the same investment reasons.

Fund Balance. During the 2022/2023 school year the School District's General Fund expenditures exceeded revenue by approximately $361,000, reducing the General Fund fund balance to approximately $32,620,000 at June 30, 2023. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2022 was approximately 20.30 percent of expenditures and outgoing transfers, which would approximately equal average operating costs for a 10-week period. The School District's fund balance percentage is 17.2 percent and equals approximately 8.9 weeks of operation.

Other informational items. The GASB financial reporting model project began August 2013; the exposure draft "Financial Reporting Model Improvements" was issued June 2020 with a comment period ending February 2021, and the GASB's goal is final standards by March 2024; at its June 2023 meeting the board tentatively decided to remove governmental fund reporting issues from the scope. A related project, the June 2020 preliminary views titled "Revenue and Expense Recognition," could produce a standard during 2027. Sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023 allows millages approved by voters after May 7, 2023 to fund student transportation vehicles and related parts, supplies and equipment, and trucks and vans registered under the Michigan vehicle code, 1949 PA 300, MCL 257.1 to 257.923; sinking funds authorized prior to March 29, 2017, between March 29, 2017 and May 7, 2023, and after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for separately, each with its own balance sheet and statement of revenue, expenditures, and changes in fund balance, and an annual independent sinking fund audit is required. GASB Statement No. 101 on compensated absences is effective for the year ending June 30, 2025. Michigan Department of Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1, to be released during fiscal year 2023/2024, supersedes Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4 and takes effect for sinking fund and bond compliance audits reported for the June 30, 2024 reporting period; the completion date will always be the June 30 immediately following the later of the certificate of substantial completion or 95 percent of bond proceeds being spent, districts will submit an annual transmittal letter instead of bond closeout financial information, and levies renewed after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for in a separate capital projects fund. Arbitrage is addressed, including the computation generally completed at the five-year anniversary of the original bond sale and amounts due back to the Internal Revenue Service. On data security, the report cites the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021 signed into law in October 2021, warns that passwords like "August2023" are easily guessed, and raises questions about phishing awareness and PII and FERPA data storage. On real estate strategy for owned assets, the firm offers an introduction to its affiliated entity, Plante Moran Cresa.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A memorandum dated November 7, 2023 from Rick West of the Troy School District Business Office (4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098) to the Policy Committee transmits Policy Manual updates recommended by Miller Johnson School Policy Services and the Cabinet team, organized by manual section with an explanation for each change. Proposals span the 2000 through 8000 series and add stand-alone policies on electronic signatures, school visitors, and engagement with outside organizations. The most consequential provision requires each school building to maintain at least two functioning epinephrine auto-injectors and at least one functioning opioid antagonist, administered by trained personnel, with 911 called for a suspected opioid overdose.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Origin**
Memorandum from Rick West, Business Office, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098 (phone 248.823.4022, fax 248.823.4013), to the Policy Committee, dated November 7, 2023, re: Policy Manual Recommended Updates. Changes were recommended by Miller Johnson School Policy Services and the Cabinet team. Each item carries an Action block with lines for Cabinet, Policy Committee, and Board of Education; the Cabinet position is filled in on every item while the Policy Committee and Board of Education lines are blank.

**2000 series - students, health and safety**
- Update 15.01 (Policy 2000.01 Admission and Enrollment): adds a Home Schooled Students provision to the Resident Students section, under which the Board will attempt to accommodate home-schooled students wishing to take non-essential elective classes, citing MCL 380.1561 and MCL 388.1766b.
- Update 15.03 (Policy 2000.07 / Administrative Regulation 2007-AR Health and Safety): combines opioid antagonist language with the existing Epi-Pen policy. Each building must maintain at least two functioning epinephrine auto-injectors and at least one functioning opioid antagonist; trained personnel or authorized contractors administer them; parents are notified; the District will call 911 for a believed opioid overdose and encourage treatment through a program licensed under part 62 of the Public Health Code, 1978 PA 368. The stated purpose is compliance with sections 1178 and 1179 of the Revised School Code, with regulations incorporating the Michigan Department of Education's Medication Administration Guidelines. Cabinet: Supports (Adopt language in its entirety).
- Update 15.04 (Policy 2000.07 Health and Safety): clarifies that annual notice and parental opt-out for physical examinations and screenings do not apply to sports physicals.

**3000 and 4000 series**
- Update 15.06 (Policy 3000.03 Instruction): commits the District to provide homebound and hospitalized instruction to qualified students consistent with federal and state law.
- Update 15.07 (Policy 4000.02 Employment Considerations): adds "pregnancy status" to the prohibited bases for employment discrimination and harassment, cross-referencing Policy [8000.07].
- Update 15.09 (Policy 4000.04 Evaluations, Discipline and Discharge, Resignations): requires a rigorous, transparent, and fair evaluation system with annual year-end evaluations, and provides that the Superintendent's evaluation follow state law and/or the employment contract, that Board members receive training in the evaluation framework, and that untrained members be recused.
- Update 15.10 (Policy 4000.05 Other Matters of Employment): states mandatory reporting duties reflecting the Child Protection Law.

**5000 series - business**
- Update 15.11 (Policy 5000.03 Purchasing): requires administrative regulations and effective internal control over state and federal grants and awards. Cabinet: Supports (Adopt language in its entirety).
- Update 15.12 (Policy 5000.07 Risk Management): requires a District-provided form for injury to students, staff, or visitors.
- Update 15.13 (Policy 5000.12 Use of Electronic Signatures, NEW): authorizes acceptance, distribution, and reliance on electronic records and electronic signatures unless prohibited by law.

**6000, 7000 and 8000 series**
- Update 15.14 (Policy 6000.02 / Administrative Regulation 6002-AR Safety and Security): revised for threat situations, adding a Threat Assessment section requiring a Superintendent-developed protocol. Cabinet: Supports (Also maintain current Firearms and Weapons language).
- Update 15.16 (Policy 7000.12 School Visitors, NEW, cited as Policy 7012): authorizes the Superintendent or building principal to bar or expel disruptive persons and request law enforcement assistance.
- Update 15.17 (Policy 7000.13, NEW, cited as Policy 7013, "Engagement with Outside Organizations"): requires review of requests from civic institutions, charitable organizations, and outside groups.
- Update 15.18 (Policy 8000.03 / Administrative Regulation 8003-AR): Section 504 and ADA Title II nondiscrimination, naming the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services as Compliance Officer for employment issues and the Director of Special Education for FAPE and accessibility, and permitting service animals as required or permitted by law.
- Update 15.19 (Policy 8000.07 / Administrative Regulation 8007-AR): responds to the Elliott Larsen Civil Rights Act amendment signed by Governor Whitmer, effective 2024, adding sexual orientation and gender identity/expression.
- Update 15.20 (Policy 8000.09 Digital Communications): adds a Public Use section declaring District social media a limited public forum and listing prohibited content categories.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Memorandum on Policy Manual Recommended Updates from Rick West, on Troy School District Business Office letterhead showing 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, phone 248.823.4022, fax 248.823.4013, addressed to the Policy Committee and dated November 7, 2023. It outlines proposed updates to the District's Policy Manual as recommended by Miller Johnson School Policy Services and the Cabinet team, with explanations for each contemplated change, broken down by section of the manual; two leading sections carry the note that there are no recommended updates. Each recommendation ends with an Action block listing Cabinet, Policy Committee, and Board of Education, with the Cabinet position recorded for every item and the other two lines left blank.

Update 15.01 (Policy 2000.01 Admission and Enrollment). Because clients raised questions about home-schooled students, language is added to the Resident Students section: the Board will attempt to accommodate students who are home schooled and have a desire to take non-essential elective classes in the School District in a manner consistent with the law, with administrative regulations as needed. Citations given are MCL 380.1561 and MCL 388.1766b. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.03 (Policy 2000.07 / Administrative Regulation 2007-AR Health and Safety). Responding to renewed client interest in opioid antagonists, the recommendation combines opioid antagonist language with the existing Epi-Pen policy and regulation in Policy 2007 and 2007-AR. The School District will acquire or purchase and maintain at least two functioning epinephrine auto-injectors (epi-pens) and at least one functioning opioid antagonist for and at each school building it operates. Properly trained School District personnel or authorized contractors will administer an opioid antagonist to any individual on school grounds believed to be having an opioid-related overdose, an epi-pen injection to any individual believed to be having an anaphylactic reaction, or to any student with a prescription on file. The District will notify the parent of any student to whom it administers an epi-pen injection or opioid antagonist on school grounds or at a school-related activity. For a believed opioid-related overdose, the District will encourage parents or legal guardians to seek treatment from a substance use disorder services program licensed under part 62 of the Public Health Code, 1978 PA 368, and will call 911. The stated purpose is compliance with sections 1178 and 1179 of the Revised School Code; the policy creates no rights or remedies, and the Superintendent will promulgate administrative regulations incorporating by reference the Michigan Department of Education's Medication Administration Guidelines. Cabinet: Supports (Adopt language in its entirety).

Update 15.04 (Policy 2000.07 Health and Safety). To resolve confusion about the Physical Examinations and Screenings policy, a proviso is added: annual notice will be given to parents of any health or physical examinations or screenings, parents may opt their students out of all such examinations and screenings, and the policy is not intended to apply to physical examinations required for sports participation. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.06 (Policy 3000.03 Instruction). A specific policy on homebound instruction: the School District will provide homebound and hospitalized instruction to qualified students consistent with federal and state law and other applicable guidance, with administrative regulations as needed. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.07 (Policy 4000.02 Employment Considerations). Two recent federal legislative changes clarified the prohibition on discriminating against employees or prospective employees on the basis of pregnancy, so the Discrimination and Harassment policy in the Personnel section is supplemented. The revised language bars discrimination or harassment in employment on the basis of race, color, national origin, religion, sex, marital status, pregnancy status, genetic information, disability, age, or any other illegal grounds, and cross-references Policy [8000.07]. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.09 (Policy 4000.04). Added to the Evaluations, Discipline and Discharge, Resignations policy. The District will use a rigorous, transparent, and fair evaluation system complying with Michigan law and including annual year-end evaluations for all teachers and administrators unless otherwise permitted by law. The system is intended to improve performance and encourage professional growth, and also to result in separation from employment of those who, after notice and an opportunity to improve, continue to be ineffective. Evaluation of the Superintendent is to be conducted consistent with state law and/or the employment contract; Board members must receive training in the evaluation framework for the Superintendent before participating in an annual performance evaluation, and any Board member who does not obtain the training in advance shall be recused. Cabinet: Supports (Adopt language in its entirety).

Update 15.10 (Policy 4000.05 Other Matters of Employment). A mandatory reporting statement capturing the spirit of the Child Protection Law: each professional staff member and all other employees who are mandatory reporters and/or who have reasonable cause to suspect child abuse or neglect shall report immediately every case, ascertained or suspected, of abuse or neglect resulting in physical or mental injury to a student by other than accidental means. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.11 (Policy 5000.03 Purchasing). The Superintendent will promulgate legally compliant administrative regulations concerning expenditures of funds received through state and federal grants and awards, and shall establish and maintain effective internal control over grants and awards providing reasonable assurance that programs and funds are managed in compliance with applicable statutes, regulations, and award terms and conditions. Cabinet: Supports (Adopt language in its entirety).

Update 15.12 (Policy 5000.07 Risk Management). The Board seeks to minimize risk in all operations through planning that accounts for the safety of students, employees, and the public, protection of District property, and avoidance of financial loss or liability. The Superintendent is responsible for a risk management program including means for identifying, eliminating, reducing, or transferring risk, and may provide for purchase of insurance. In the event of injury to students, staff, or any visitor to school grounds, a School District provided form shall be completed by the appropriate staff member. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.13 (Policy 5000.12 Use of Electronic Signatures, NEW). A stand-alone policy inserted at the end of the 5000 series. Unless a provision of law specifically prohibits use of an electronic record for the specified purpose, the Board authorizes acceptance and distribution or transmission of electronic records and electronic signatures to and from District staff and other persons and between staff members, and authorizes staff to create, send, receive, store, process, use, and rely upon them. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.14 (Policy 6000.02 / Administrative Regulation 6002-AR). Policy 6000.02, Safety and Security, and its administrative regulation are significantly revised to address threat situations. Facilities and grounds will be kept safe, secure, clean, and attractive, and the Superintendent will implement a maintenance program providing for regular inspection and periodic maintenance of all facilities, compliant with applicable safety, health, and environmental requirements. The District will undertake reasonable cooperative efforts with law enforcement agencies, and the Superintendent and building administrators determine when law enforcement presence is necessary. Under Threat Assessment, the Superintendent will develop a threat assessment protocol for situations posing a threat to the health, safety, and welfare of the school community, aimed at preventive or corrective measures, protecting potential victims, and assisting the student being assessed. Cabinet: Supports (Also maintain current Firearms and Weapons language).

Update 15.16 (Policy 7000.12 School Visitors, NEW). A stand-alone policy in the 7000 series, cited in the text as Policy 7012 and entitled "School Visitors." Visitor guidelines keep the educational program undisturbed and prevent intrusion of disruptive persons. The Superintendent or building principal may prohibit entry of any person or expel any person when there is reason to believe the person's presence would be detrimental to the good order of the school, and if the individual refuses to leave or creates a disturbance the principal may request whatever assistance is required from the local law enforcement agency. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.17 (Policy 7000.13, NEW). A stand-alone policy in the 7000 series, cited as Policy 7013 and entitled "Engagement with Outside Organizations." Any request from civic institutions, charitable organizations, or outside groups involving contests, exhibits, sales of products to and by students, promotional materials sent home with students, graduation prizes, fund raising, and free teaching materials must be carefully reviewed to ensure such activities promote student interests without advancing the special interests of any particular group. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.18 (Policy 8000.03 / Administrative Regulation 8003-AR). Addressing recurring service animal questions covered by the Americans with Disabilities Act and existing Policy 8000.03. In accordance with Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and Title II of the ADA, no otherwise qualified individual with a disability shall, solely by reason of disability, be excluded from participation in, denied the benefits of, or subjected to discrimination; the District does not discriminate in admission, access, participation, or treatment of students with disabilities, nor against any job applicant or employee with a disability. The District has developed guidelines for providing a free appropriate public education (FAPE) under Section 504 and the ADA. The Superintendent appoints the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services as Compliance Officer for employment issues and the Director of Special Education as Compliance Officer for FAPE and other accessibility issues, and will develop a complaint procedure. Service animals will be permitted to the extent required or permitted by law, with administrative regulations governing non-service animal requests. Cabinet: Supports (Adopt language in its entirety).

Update 15.19 (Policy 8000.07 / Administrative Regulation 8007-AR). The Michigan Legislature passed and Governor Whitmer signed an amendment to the Elliott Larsen Civil Rights Act expanding protections for LGBTQ individuals; although it does not take effect until 2024, modification of Policy 8007, Discrimination and Harassment, is recommended now, with "pregnancy status" already addressed in the Series 4000 updates. The revised policy bars discrimination and harassment on the basis of race, color, national origin, religion, sex (including sexual orientation and gender identity/expression), marital status, pregnancy status, genetic information, disability, age, or any other basis prohibited by law, and designates the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services to supervise implementation. Cabinet: Supports (Adopt language in its entirety).

Update 15.20 (Policy 8000.09). In response to issues associated with public interaction on district social media, Policy 8000.09, Digital Communications, is revised to include a new "Public Use" section. Digital communication occurring on District premises or using District equipment is governed by the Acceptable Use Policy and this policy, which also applies off District premises and on non-District equipment; communication between staff and students, and between staff and parents, community members, and other adults, should be professional and of the same content, tone, and demeanor as in-school communication. District social media, to the extent open to the public, collectively constitutes a limited public forum, and all comments and postings are subject to monitoring and, where permitted, removal. Public posts must address District business, and the District may remove content that is off-topic, abusive, illegal, obscene or sexually explicit, campaigning for or against political campaigns, candidates, or ballot measures, compromising to safety or security, containing personal identifying or sensitive personal information such as doxing, commercial such as solicitation or advertisement, or copyrighted, trademarked, or otherwise legally protected. Users who repeatedly or egregiously violate the guidelines may be banned from posting or commenting, and the Public Use portion must be displayed to users or made available by hyperlink.

The 2026 Strategic Plan, approved by board resolution, succeeded the World Class 2020 vision introduced in 2015-16; the district participates in the BELE Network and hired a Supervisor of Equity, Inclusion, and Community Relationships in 2020-2021.

## Identity, governance and document mechanics
Oakland Schools is an autonomous, tax-supported public school district and one of 56 intermediate school districts in Michigan, established in 1962 and governed under Michigan General School Law. The budget book -- agenda item 5.D., "FY23 Proposed Budget Complete Doc," meeting date May 17, 2022 -- carries the cover "Enterprise Wide Executive Summary & Budget Assumptions - Original Budget - March 2022 - Fiscal Year 2022-23," is footed "FY23 Proposed Budget" and stamped 03.24.22. Embedded system reports are OSBG0014A "Proposed Budget Comparison" (by function) and OSBG0014 (by location and by object), run 03/24/2022 by user STYMAD - Dawn Styma. Budgetary authority rests in Board Policies 3050, 3100 (contingency appropriation; amendments at least three times each fiscal year), 3150 (fund balance targets, with the General Education unassigned range reaching 7.5% to 12.5% in FY 2022-23) and 3170 (line-item transfers within a fund; inter-fund transfers need prior Board approval); subsidy reporting is required by Policy 3230. Statutes cited include the General Property Tax Act, Public Act 206 of 1893 (MCL 211.24e); the Uniform Budgeting and Accounting Act, Public Act 2 of 1968; and the Revised School Code, Public Act 451 of 1976 (MCL 380.624 and MCL 380.684, the latter as amended by Public Act 45 of 2007), with Bulletin 1022 as mandatory guide. The proposed budget must go to each constituent district no later than May 1 and be adopted no later than June 30.

## Enterprise-wide sources and uses
Total FY2022-23 funding is $391.2 million: property taxes $216.6 million; other local and investment revenue $36.9 million; state source revenue $21.6 million; other financing sources and indirect revenue $9.1 million; estimated new grant award funding $84.2 million; estimated grant carryover funding $22.8 million. Total expenditures are $393.2 million: salary, wage and benefits $80.4 million; purchased services, supplies, dues and fees $20.5 million; electric and natural gas utilities $.9 million; capital outlay $6.6 million; transfers to LEAs and other funds $174.4 million; grant related expenditures $107.0 million; payment on existing debt $3.4 million. Both figures are net of eligible inter-company eliminated Risk Related Activity Fund amounts.

## Property taxes and the tax environment
Property tax revenue is budgeted to increase 4.0%, or $5.5 million, on Oakland County Equalization Division projections of taxable value growth of more than 6.25%, offset by an assumed Headlee rollback -- the eighth year in a row. By fund: General Education $12,374,900 to $12,869,900; Special Education $157,398,800 to $163,694,800; Career Focused Education $38,503,900 to $40,044,100; total $208,277,600 to $216,608,800, a change of $8,331,200 or 4.00%. Tax base composition is 70% principal residence and 30% non-principal residence. Tax revenues are up 27% since 2014 yet $8.7 million below pre-recession levels as of FY2021-22; the Great Recession produced a 24.5% cumulative loss in county taxable valuations over four declining years and $438.5 million of cumulative district revenue erosion through fiscal year 2022. Tax abatements peaked in fiscal years 2012 and 2013. Michigan Tax Tribunal judgments have cost $12.9 million over the past eleven years; the FY2022-23 MTT reserve is .25% of tax revenues, about $536,300 in expense.

## General Education Fund (Fund 100)
Beginning fund equity is $5,259,000 (non-spendable prepaids $14,300; assigned $435,000; unassigned $4,809,700). Revenue of $22,932,400 comprises local sources $15,732,000, state sources $6,406,100 and other financing sources $794,300; property taxes are 56% of total revenue. Expenditures of $23,544,000 break out as General Administration $2,037,400, Finance and Operations $9,070,000, Instructional Services $9,442,600 and Plant and Fixed Charges $2,994,000, producing a planned operating deficit of $(611,600) and ending equity of $4,647,400 (unassigned $4,633,100; the narrative separately states an unassigned balance of $4,547,800). Notable revenue lines: Section 81 ISD Operations $4,058,400 to $4,139,600 (the Governor's budget included a 5% increase; 2% is budgeted); Section 147c MPSERS UAAL Rate Stabilization $1,841,600 to $2,030,000; Section 147a Normal Cost Offset $55,400; State Payment in Lieu of Taxes $152,100; Illuminate $190,600 to $555,000 as the base-product subsidy returns from 100% to 50%; workshop fees $100,000 to $175,000; CTN $384,600 to $334,400. Department 046 Technology Services Audio/Visual Support is combined into 030 Technical Support Services and department 022 Communications Video Production into 049 Communication Services, both zeroed in FY23. Fund 100 expense by function includes Improve of Instruction $7,238,400, Support Svcs Tech $5,631,500 and Exec Administration $1,663,000. Forecast assumptions include capital outlay of $1,238,000 for 2023-24 through 2026-27 and $238,000 in 2027-28, purchased services growth of 2%, supplies and dues growth of 1.0%, medical CPI of 3.5%, and unassigned balances of $4.3 million (18.2%), $4.1 million (16.8%), $3.8 million (15.1%), $3.3 million (13.0%) and $3.7 million (14.9%).

## Special Education Fund (Fund 200) and PA-18
Revenues total $171,956,400 (property tax $163,694,800; investment $52,500; fee based $100,000; state $5,869,200; state payment in lieu of taxes $1,934,400; other financing sources $305,500) against expenditures of $171,894,000, an operating excess of $62,400. Ending fund balance is $11,520,000, holding $10,419,600 restricted for future center facility renovations, $27,000 non-spendable and $1,073,400 restricted for special education, equal to 5.00% of expenditures net of LEA transfers. The PA-18 base distribution to local districts is $148,300,000, budgeted to increase about $7.9 million or 5.6%, and is forecast to reach $175,141,500 by 2027-28; LEA support transfers are $2,700,000 and the additional distribution line goes to zero from $7,403,700. Revenue is $46,269,300 (local $40,411,100, state $5,730,900, other financing $127,300) and expenditures $46,259,100, a surplus of $10,200; ending equity is $5,825,500 (restricted $5,814,900, non-spendable $10,600). Forecast commitments include $3.6 million annually for Support to LEAs Regional Programs, $1.8 million for transportation reimbursement, $543,700 for STEM mobile classroom operating costs, transfers out to debt service of $2.3 million per year, and annual debt service payments of $2.5 million through 2036. Restricted fund balance is forecast at $6.3 million (13.2%) rising to $8.1 million (15.4%).

## Cost allocation
The general allocation splits 50% General Education / 25% Special Education / 25% Career Focused Education; activity-based FTE allocation is 24/24/52; space utilization 50/24/26; transportation miles 73/25/2; Technology Services Licensing 70/15/15; Financial Services property taxes 6/75.5/18.5. The Special Education Fund carries a 25% maximum allocation cap on each eligible function-based cost pool. Allocated departments total $11,406,200 (Fund 100), $6,555,300 (Fund 200) and $8,282,600 (Fund 600), a grand total of $26,244,100 or 11.61%.

## Personnel, retirement and insurance
A 2% across-the-board increase applies, with non-union step growth of 1.28% and union wage base growth of .98%. FICA is 7.65%, with social security of 6.2% on wages up to $147,000 for calendar year 2022. Eight MPSERS rates run October 1, 2021 through September 30, 2022, with payroll rates of 28.23%, 25.31%, 24.45%, 20.96%, 21.82%, 20.96%, 27.37% and 27.16% plus a 15.05% UAAL stabilization rate; the blended rate exclusive of UAAL is 28.26%, projected to increase 1.0% annually. Hard caps rise to $20,658.54 (family), $15,841.22 (individual plus one) and $7,574.78 (single) on 3.7% medical CPI, with employees contributing approximately 14% on average. Salaries and wages with FICA total $46,836,800 to $51,131,200 (9.2%); MPSERS retirement $20,092,500 to $20,758,300; healthcare insurance $6,355,400 to $6,486,200; other insurances $2,296,500 to $1,987,700; utilities $905,700 to $937,500 (Constellation Energy Services); purchased services, supplies and dues less utilities $21,334,700 to $20,477,900. The district belongs to the SET-SEG Self-Insurers Workers' Compensation Fund and moved dental and vision to premium-based plans effective January 1, 2022. New positions include a 1.0 FTE Recruiting Manager, a .33 FTE part-time Controller, 2.0 FTE in Technology Services (Business Support Specialist and Associate Business Analyst), 2.0 FTE Campus Bookkeepers and a .10 FTE Psychologist increase, offset by a .33 FTE Administration decrease; total staffing moves 653.96, 660.31, 665.41, a change of 5.10.

## Programs, subsidies and collaborations
Cooperative service subsidies total $1,211,750: Xello $302,700; Illuminate DnA $363,800; Atlas Rubicon $184,500; Nepris $155,000; Discovery Education Streaming $149,500; PowerSchool BusinessPlus per pupil $17,400; CDX Automotive $15,000; Meltwater $14,850; Student Achievement Media $5,000; TV Eyes $2,400; Sprout Social $1,600. Literacy Essentials Oakland (LEO) is a five-year early literacy project launched in 2019-20 with up to $5 million from Oakland Schools. The HR/Finance Consortium, named Michigan Partnership for Essential Education Resources (MiPEER), covers twenty-two districts converting to PowerSchool BusinessPlus. Fee-based programs: VLAC K-8 at 500 FTE and $6,450 resident / $6,650 non-resident tuition; VLAC 9-12 at 100 FTE and $6,700 / $6,900; Accelerated College Experience (ACE) at 200 students and $4,900, offering up to 60 transferrable college credits with Oakland Community College. Medicaid Billing Services is expected to generate approximately $11.4 million of revenue for LEAs. Also cited: a $13.6 million Special Education center program renovation; 121 schools in the Michigan Green Schools Program; the county's loss of over 145,000 jobs to COVID-19 with roughly 60% recovered by the first quarter of 2021; Emerging Sectors investment of over $5.4 billion with almost 55,000 jobs created and over 40,300 retained as of December 2020; and the Oakland80 goal of 80% of adults holding a post-secondary credential by 2030. Oakland Schools received no ESSER, Governor's Emergency Education Relief or Coronavirus Relief Fund money, funding COVID costs from tax revenues and state aid, and supported the Oxford School District crisis with mental health consultants, psychologists and social workers.

Funds presented include 105, 205 and 605 funded projects, 270 Shared Services and Tuition Programs, 271 ONE, 273 Medicaid, 277 HR/Finance Consortium, 290 School Activities, 311 (2016 Refunding Bonds), 313 and 314 (2010 QSCB), 404 CFE Campus Renovations, 406 Administration Building Renovations, 409 Career Connections Facility, 710 Production Printing Enterprise and 810 Risk Related Activity. Debt service principal rises $420,000 to $1,395,000 with interest of $1,996,700, total $3,391,700. Grant revenue falls to $106,979,900 (local $1,335,600; state $39,379,700; federal $66,264,600). The 5-Year Capital Outlay Plan, presented for first reading on March 24, 2022, shows grand totals of $9,229,600 for 2024, $8,874,800 for 2025, $3,876,000 for 2026 and $6,669,800 for 2027, with a grand totals memo-only column of $38,279,400; the largest items are HVAC of $4,052,300 in 2025 (including $3,932,800 at the SE campus) and $2,491,700 in 2027, and roof repair and replacement of $1,118,100 in 2027.

## What it is

Oakland Schools (the Oakland County intermediate school district) original proposed budget for fiscal year 2023-24, dated March 2023 with underlying amendment-report data as of 3/14/2023. It covers all governmental, proprietary and internal service funds, adds five-year operating forecasts for the three major funds, and includes the 5-Year Capital Outlay Plan scheduled for Board first reading on March 21, 2023. ISDs must submit the proposed budget to each constituent district's board by May 1 and adopt by June 30.

## Enterprise-wide totals (FY 2023-24)

| Funding source | Amount | Expenditure category | Amount |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Property taxes | $230.2M | Salary, wage and benefits | $81.5M |

| State sources | $21.6M | Electric and natural gas utilities | $1.0M |
| Other financing and indirect | $11.7M | Capital outlay | $20.8M |
