| | | Grant-related expenditures | $138.9M |
| | | Payment on existing debt | $3.4M |
| **Total funding** | **$440.7M** | **Total expenditures** | **$455.8M** |

Amounts are net of eligible inter-company eliminated Risk Related Activity Fund revenues and expenses.

## Three major funds

| Fund | FY24 revenue | FY24 expenditures | Result | Ending fund balance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| General Education (100) | $24,344,200 | $24,540,300 | $(196,100) | $6,557,800 (unassigned $4,327,000) |
| Special Education (200) | $183,221,900 | $183,137,500 | $84,400 | $11,524,700 (restricted-SE $1,068,600) |
| Career Focused Education (600) | $49,234,000 | $49,381,200 | $(147,200) | $6,952,400 (restricted $6,912,400) |

Property taxes supply 56% of GEF revenue, 95% of SEF revenue and 86% of CFEF revenue. Fund-level tax budgets rise 5.0%: GEF $13,026,600 to $13,677,900; SEF $165,688,800 to $173,973,200; CFEF $40,527,100 to $42,553,500.

## Key assumptions

- Property taxes +5.0%, a conservative figure against Oakland County Equalization projections of more than 6.0% taxable-value growth; the tax base is 70% principal residence, 30% non-principal residence. No Headlee rollback expected after eight consecutive years of rollbacks.
- Investment revenue budgeted down about 40% district-wide, from $4,911,800 to $2,886,800.
- Compensation: 2.5% across-the-board increase for non-union staff, 1.0% for union staff per the collective bargaining agreement, plus step increases; blended MPSERS retirement rate of 30.2% ($30.20 per $100 of wages).
- Health care hard caps assume 3.7% medical CPI growth: family $20,180.43 rising to a projected $20,927.11; individual plus one $15,474.60 to $16,047.16; single $7,399.47 to $7,673.25.
- Staffing falls 4.00 FTE (Technology Field Services) to 643.00 total; no new positions.
- Michigan Tax Tribunal reserve set at .25% of tax revenue, roughly $575,500; $12.9 million has been refunded over eleven years.

## Other funds

Shared Services & Tuition Programs (270) budgets $18,078,300 revenue against $19,167,500 expenditures. The ONE fiber network fund (271) spends $2,343,900, including $1,000,000 of infrastructure and $904,100 for Literacy Essentials Oakland. Medicaid (273) passes $12,465,100 through, with $11.7 million returned to LEAs. Three debt service funds carry $3,386,900 of principal and interest. Capital Projects Fund 404 spends $16,928,900 on technical campus renovations; Fund 406 spends $1,295,600 at the Administration Building. The Production Print Enterprise Fund ends at negative $1,115,500 net position; the Risk Related Activity Fund ends at $2,559,200.

## Capital plan

The FY23-FY28 capital plan totals $69,694,300 in needs against $36,600,000 of transfers, with $17,928,900 scheduled in 2023-24 — driven by safety and security work and parking-lot repaving at the four technical campuses.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
## Identity

Oakland Schools FY24 Proposed Budget - Enterprise-Wide Executive Summary & Budget Assumptions, Original Budget, March 2023, Fiscal Year 2023-24. Page footers read 03.21.23; embedded Annual Budgeting Amendment Reports are as of 3/14/2023. Oakland Schools is one of 56 Michigan intermediate school districts established in 1962, at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford, MI 48328-2736 (nondiscrimination contacts: Assistant Superintendent of Human Resources 248.209.2429, Title IX Coordinator 248.209.2590, Executive Director of Legal Affairs 248.209.2062). It reached the Troy School District board packet dated May 16, 2023 under the ISD requirement to submit a proposed budget to each constituent board by May 1; adoption must occur by June 30.

## Enterprise totals

Proposed FY 2023-24 funding is $440.7 million: property taxes $230.2M, other local and investment revenue $38.3M, state sources $21.6M, other financing and indirect revenue $11.7M, estimated grant awards $138.9M. Proposed expenditures are $455.8 million: salary, wage and benefits $81.5M; purchased services, supplies and dues/fees $21.7M; electric and natural gas utilities $1.0M; capital outlay $20.8M; transfers to LEAs and other funds $188.5M; grant-related expenditures $138.9M; debt payments $3.4M. Both are net of eliminated Risk Related Activity Fund amounts.

## Revenue assumptions

Property taxes rise 5.0%, or $10,962,100, from $219,242,500 to $230,204,600: General Education Fund $13,026,600 to $13,677,900; Special Education Fund $165,688,800 to $173,973,200; Career Focused Education Fund $40,527,100 to $42,553,500. Oakland County taxable values are expected to grow more than 6.0%, but 5.0% is used pending actuals. The base is 70% principal residence, 30% non-principal residence. After eight straight years of Headlee rollbacks, none is expected. Forecast growth is 3.7% (2024-25), 3.0% (2025-26) and 2.5% (2026-27 through 2028-29).

Investment revenue is cut about 40%, from $4,911,800 to $2,886,800: GEF $775,000 to $465,000; SEF $2,340,000 to $1,404,000; CFEF $580,000 to $348,000; Fund 270 $47,000 to $28,200; ONE Fund 271 $290,000 to $174,000; Medicaid Fund 273 $169,000 to $101,400; HR/Finance 277 $16,000 to $9,600; debt service $188,500 to $54,800; capital projects $498,300 to $297,000; Production Print $8,000 to $4,800. Other local revenue falls 2.7%, $36,379,700 to $35,386,700 (Community Telecommunications Network up $467,200 to $600,000; Career Connections rent of $120,000 and a one-time $100,000 Oakland County meal reimbursement both ending). State revenue is nearly flat, $21,559,100 to $21,649,100: Section 81 ISD Operations +2.5% (Governor's budget had 5%), Section 51a +8% (Governor's had 16%), Section 147c MPSERS UAAL Rate Stabilization up as a pass-through, Section 61a.1 CTE down 28% to $1,750,000. Indirect revenue falls to $1,159,500; other financing sources fall 45.0% to $10,545,500. Grant awards are estimated at $138,889,500 (state $68,573,600, federal $69,860,100, local $455,800), down 2.7%.

## Personnel and benefits

No new positions; a 4.0 FTE cut in Technology Field Services follows changes in intergovernmental agreements. Total FTE moves 660.31 (2021-22) to 647.00 (2022-23) to 643.00 (2023-24), with Shared & Field Services / MiPEER dropping 121.00 to 117.00; Business and Operations totals 71.16 FTE and Programs and Services 427.53 (Technical Campuses 177.45, Special Populations 83.00). Non-union staff get 2.5% across the board, union staff 1.0% per contract, plus steps (non-union step growth 1.63%; 1.68% in the SEF forecast). Salaries and wages with FICA rise 8.9% to $51,487,400; MPSERS costs rise 8.8% to $21,530,300. Eight retirement rates apply; the common Basic/MIP with Health Care Premium Subsidy is 28.23% through September 30, 2023 and a projected 31.34% from October 1, 2023, with UAAL stabilization moving 16.65% to 16.89%. The budgeted blended rate is 30.2%, or $30.20 per $100 of wages. Healthcare insurance rises 6.1% to $6,445,500 and other insurances 5.4% to $1,991,700, with employees paying about 13% on average. Hard caps for plan years after 1/1/23: family $20,180.43, individual plus one $15,474.60, single $7,399.47; projected after 1/1/24 at $20,927.11, $16,047.16 and $7,673.25 on 3.7% medical CPI growth. FICA is 7.65%, with the 6.2% Social Security portion applied to wages up to $160,200 for 2023. Workers' compensation runs through the SET-SEG Self-Insurers Workers' Compensation Fund pool.

## Other expenditure assumptions

Utilities rise 12.3% to $1,018,600 (electricity and natural gas bought on the open market from Constellation Energy Services). Purchased services, supplies, materials and dues and fees excluding utilities rise 7.6% to $21,722,500, with GEF up nearly 23% to $6,181,700 for countywide wellbeing initiatives. Capital outlay jumps 288.0%, $5,365,600 to $20,820,200, as capital project funds move $3,840,700 to $18,214,500 for campus safety and security and the ONE Fund adds $1,010,000 of fiber infrastructure. Other financing uses fall 2.3% to $188,484,000. Debt service totals $3,386,900 ($1,460,000 principal, $1,926,900 interest). The Michigan Tax Tribunal reserve is .25% of tax revenue, about $575,500; $12.9 million has been repaid over eleven years.

## General Education Fund (100)

Revenue of $24,344,200 (local $17,063,400, state $6,589,600, other financing $691,200) against expenditures of $24,540,300 yields a planned $(196,100) deficit, an intentional spend-down for collaborative programs and capital projects. Spending splits into General Administration $2,051,700, Finance and Operations $9,420,800, Instructional Services $11,110,000 and Plant & Fixed Charges $1,957,800; FY 2022 actuals were $21,899,613 revenue and $21,537,370 expenditures. Ending equity is $6,557,800 (prepaids $30,800, assigned $2,200,000, unassigned $4,327,000). Section 81 goes $4,269,400 to $4,376,100. School Culture and Climate jumps $952,200 to $2,681,800 (+181.64%); Application Services reaches $2,201,500 and Technology Licensing $1,949,400; LEA and other transfers drop $6,238,400 to $638,400 after a $5.2 million FY23 safety and security transfer. FY23 included $2,050,000 from the Career Connections building sale. Grant Fund 105 budgets $67,654,100 both ways (state $62,848,400, federal $4,628,900), including $25,434,400 to other public schools and $27,333,300 to not-for-profits. The forecast projects unassigned balance of $5.2M (19.9%) in 2024-25, $5.1M (19.9%), $4.6M (17.7%), $4.9M (19.0%) and $4.9M (18.5%) through 2028-29, with capital outlay of $1,238,000 a year through 2026-27 then $238,000.

## Special Education Fund (200)

Revenue of $183,221,900 (property taxes $173,973,200, or 95%; state $7,494,700; indirect $250,000) against expenditures of $183,137,500 yields an $84,400 surplus. Spending: program supervision and direction $2,528,800; program operations $11,017,200; plant and fixed charges $7,824,700; PA-18 base distribution $159,316,800; LEA transfers and program subsidies $2,450,000; School for Deaf/Blind $133,500. The PA-18 base rises $11.0 million, or 7.43%, from $148,300,000; the $2,450,000 covers group home and medical student support, incarcerated youth, startup assistance, extraordinary contingency, assistive technology and Section 24 payments to districts running juvenile detention programs. FY 2022-23 also carried an $8,737,600 additional distribution, $3.7 million of which went out in December 2022; none is budgeted for FY24 pending the FY23 audit. State detail: Section 51a $3,735,400, ISD Membership 51a.2 $62,200, MSB/D deduct 51a.1 $(321,200), State Payment in Lieu of Taxes $1,779,600, Section 147c $1,948,300. Ending equity is $11,524,700: non-spendable $36,500, restricted-special education $1,068,600 and $10,419,600 restricted for future center facility renovations. Policy sets a 5%-10% restricted target; the Board budgets 5%. Special Populations serves about 23,116 students with IEPs through Compliance Support, Capacity Building, Student Services for Low Incidence, the Materials Center/Braille & Large Print Library and Specialized Student Support. Grant Fund 205 budgets $69,201,900 (state $5,678,200, federal $63,523,700), including $56,433,100 to other public schools. Forecast LEA base distributions: $164,915,600, $169,844,300, $173,960,800, $178,178,100 and $182,495,700 through 2028-29.

## Career Focused Education Fund (600)

Revenue of $49,234,000 (property taxes $42,553,500, or 86%; state $5,853,400; other financing $128,100) against expenditures of $49,381,200 yields a $(147,200) deficit. Spending: campus and other program operations $26,828,500; LEA transfers and program subsidies $5,439,500; plant and fixed charges $17,113,200. Ending equity is $6,952,400 (restricted $6,912,400). Section 61a.1 falls 28.23% to $1,750,000; Section 147c rises to $3,150,000; State Payment in Lieu of Taxes is $435,300. Nineteen state CTE program codes run from 501 Agriculture to 597 Computer Systems Networking & Telecommunications across four technical campuses serving roughly 2,700 students from all 28 districts. Campus totals: Northwest $5,395,900, Southeast $5,608,700, Northeast $6,101,600, Southwest $5,780,500 - total campus operations $22,886,700. Four School Resource Officers from the Oakland County Sheriff's Department are added, one grant-funded by the Michigan State Police at the Southwest campus and three locally funded, lifting security lines (Northeast $101,100 to $257,300; Southeast $65,800 to $233,400; Northwest $50,000 to $205,400). Facility lines rise on an anticipated 20% natural gas increase for half the year. Transfers out include $4,400,000 to Capital Projects Fund 404, $3,300,000 to debt service and $104,000 to Fund 406. Regional programs hold at $3.6 million a year, including $3,088,000 of K-12 Career Readiness LEA support, $392,000 early college/dual enrollment tuition and $118,500 for certifications and competitions, plus $1,800,000 of transportation reimbursement and $541,000 (later $543,700) for STEMi. Grant Fund 605 budgets $2,033,500. Restricted balance is forecast at $5.6M (10.7%) in 2024-25 rising to $9.2M (16.5%) by 2028-29.

## Other funds

Shared Services & Tuition Programs Fund 270: revenue $18,078,300, expenditures $19,167,500, ending committed $3,183,600 ($3,265,200 total); shared services revenue $11,169,800; tuition programs are VLAC K-8 (500 FTE, $6,450 resident / $6,650 non-resident), VLAC 9-12 (100 FTE, $6,700 / $6,900), Accelerated College Experience (160 students, $4,900), Graduation Alliance and a KCK, Inc. foreign exchange program for about 50 students. Oakland Network for Education Fund 271, a fiber network with 29 consortium members: revenue $1,252,000, expenditures $2,343,900 (infrastructure $1,000,000, Literacy Essentials Oakland $904,100), ending committed $12,062,600. Medicaid Fund 273: $12,465,100 in and out, distributing $10,725,100 of Medicaid fees, $541,500 of outreach fees and $469,600 of Caring 4 Students payments, retaining no committed balance. HR/Finance Consortium Fund 277: revenue $1,271,900, expenditures $1,293,000, ending committed $366,100; a net $4,875,000 came from the CPDI Fund between FY 2012-13 and FY 2015-16 and the ONE Fund's $.7 million startup grant is fully repaid in 2023-24. School Activities Fund 290: $180,000 in and out, balance $263,000. Debt Service Fund 311 (2016 Refunding Bonds partially refunding the 2007 CFE Campus Renovation Bonds, schedule through 2036) pays $1,460,000 principal and $1,001,900 interest, ending restricted $7,310,800. Fund 313 (2010 Qualified School Construction Bond) transfers $770,000 to Fund 314 and ends at $464,400. Fund 314, the QSCB Construction Reserve maturing 2027, takes a $754,700 federal interest subsidy, pays $925,000 term bond interest and ends restricted $11,341,200. Capital Projects Fund 404 (CFE Technical Campus Renovations Phase II) budgets $4,535,000 revenue and $16,928,900 expenditures - building alterations $8,938,400, improvements other than buildings $6,478,100, technology FF&E $654,400, facilities FF&E $548,000, STEMi $200,000 - ending committed $7,582,500. Fund 406 (Administration Building Renovations, allocated 50% GEF / 24% SEF / 26% CFEF): revenue $562,000, expenditures $1,295,600, ending $10,584,900. Production Print Enterprise Fund 710: operating revenue $1,808,300, expenses $1,990,700, ending net position negative $1,115,500. Risk Related Activity Fund 810: revenue $9,514,300, expenses $9,455,000, $59,300 operating profit, ending net position $2,559,200, with claim fluctuation reserves of $1,000,000 cyber liability, $720,000 professional liability, $276,800 dental and $100,000 health care; compensated absence accruals total $3,427,100 and are fully funded.

## Policy, allocation and capital plan

Policies 3050 (preparation), 3100 (annual budget and amendments), 3150 (fund balance) and 3170 (transfer authority) govern the process, with at least three amendments a year. Targets are 7.5%-12.5% of operating expenditures for GEF unassigned and CFEF restricted, and 5%-10% for SEF restricted net of transfers to districts. Governing statutes are the General Property Tax Act (PA 206 of 1893, MCL 211.24e), the Uniform Budgeting and Accounting Act (PA 2 of 1968) and the Revised School Code (PA 451 of 1976, MCL 380.624 and 380.684), with accounting per Bulletin 1022. Costs allocate 50% GEF / 25% SEF / 25% CFEF generally; 70/15/15 for technology licensing net of revenue; 24/24/52 FTE-based for Financial Services, Enterprise Technical Services, Procurement & Contracting and Human Resources; 50/24/26 by space utilization; 73/25/2 by transportation miles; and 6/75.5/18.5 for property tax administration. Allocated departments total $26,824,200 (GEF $11,730,700, SEF $6,648,600, CFEF $8,444,900), 10.43% of the three funds. Subsidies reported under Policy 3230 total $1,308,800: Illuminate DnA $392,500, Xello $342,000, Nepris $230,000, Discovery Education Streaming $170,000, Atlas Rubicon $144,400, CDX Automotive $15,000, STAMP $14,900. Up to $5 million goes to Literacy Essentials Oakland (LEO 2.0), a five-year project launched in 2019-20; the 22-district MiPEER HR/Finance consortium runs PowerSchool BusinessPlus (formerly SunGard Public Sector, acquired 2017). Mental health work adds two consultants under Section 31n, PREPaRE training with the National Association of School Psychologists and five certified trainers, and support to Oxford plus Ferndale, Oak Park, Huron Valley, Pontiac and Royal Oak. Medicaid billing generates about $11.7 million for LEAs; 91 county schools participate in Michigan Green Schools; COR Advantage purchasing saved 53% per license, over $69,520 countywide in 2022-2023. Oakland County unemployment was 2.5% in December 2022, down from 19.7% in the second quarter of 2020 when nearly 150,000 jobs were lost; 94% of jobs are private sector, and Oakland80 targets 80% of adults with a post-secondary credential by 2030. The 5-Year Capital Plan totals $69,694,300 of needs for FY23-FY28 against $36,600,000 of transfers - $5,499,500 (2022-23), $17,928,900 (2023-24), $16,298,700 (2024-25), $6,976,300 (2025-26), $10,464,800 (2026-27), $12,526,100 (2027-28) - leaving Fund 404 $(6,141,500) short, Fund 406 with $9,053,200 and PP&G $(587,600) at 6/30/2028.

Floodplain Certification may be obtained within 7 calendar days of Seller's acceptance, with 2 days from the date of the Certification to notify Seller if the property is in a Special Flood Hazard Area; failure to notify waives the termination right. The due-diligence paragraph allows inspection of structural integrity, mechanical systems, environmental status, health and safety conditions, surveys, and infestation, and recommends research into square footage, building and use restrictions, easements, ordinances, regulations, school district, and property tax status. Purchaser is solely responsible for damage caused by inspections. By closing, the Purchaser is deemed to accept the property in AS IS condition. Where a municipality requires a pre-sale inspection, Seller pays for the inspection and required repairs.

**Broker, legal, and administrative terms (Paragraphs 19, 20, 27-40)**
On Purchaser default the Seller may enforce, declare the sale void, and retain the earnest money as liquidated damages; on Seller default the Purchaser may enforce, declare the sale void, and recover the deposit. Attached documents may include FHA/VA, Unplatted Land, Contingency Sales, Swimming Pool, Private Road, Condominium, Additional General Conditions, Well and Septic, Financing, and Vacant Land addenda, none of which are checked. Legal action related to the property's condition or the agreement must be brought within the shorter of the time provided by law or one year after Closing. Seller agrees not to allow showings after offer acceptance. FIRPTA requirements and an addendum apply if the sale price exceeds $300,000.00. The parties are advised to consult an attorney; no verbal agreements are enforceable and time is of the essence. Brookstone Realtors LLC, its brokers, offices, directors, employees, and agents are released from claims regarding property condition or performance. A final walk-through is permitted within 48 hours prior to closing. Under Paragraph 37, $595.00 will be collected from the Buyer at closing as a Broker Review and Compliance fee, a portion of which may be shared with the Designated Agent. The offer is valid until 11:59 p.m. on July 30th, 2022. Miscellaneous provisions cover amendment only by executed writing, headings, grammar and syntax, Michigan governing law, a wire-fraud warning directing parties to verbally confirm ABA routing or SWIFT codes before wiring funds, and severability. Electronic and facsimile delivery and electronic signatures are authorized, with electronic signatures required to be accompanied by a certificate. The Additional Terms and Conditions block is blank.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of September 20, 2022, this policy update recommendation walks section by section through the district's policy manual and proposes amendments in the 1000 Bylaws, 2000 Students, 3000 Curriculum and Instruction, 4000 Personnel, 5000 Business, and 8000 General Policies series, with no changes recommended for the 6000 Facilities and Operations series. The most consequential item is a comprehensive rewrite of the 3000 series covering curriculum development, parent and family engagement, textbook and instructional material selection, and media center materials, prompted by escalating public scrutiny of curriculum decisions and framed around MCL 380.1278 and MCL 380.1421/22.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Purpose**
A section-by-section set of recommended policy manual amendments presented to the Troy School District Board of Education on September 20, 2022.

**Bylaws - 1000 Series**
Policy 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board: the sub-policy "Removal from Office" addresses removal of Board officers from officer positions rather than removal from the Board itself, so it should be retitled "Removal from Officer Positions" to eliminate ambiguity.

**Students - 2000 Series**
Policy 2000.01, Children of Non-Resident Employees: a loophole allowed a person to obtain employment, enroll a child, then voluntarily leave employment while the pupil kept enrollment without tuition. Revised language, consistent with the State Aid Act and Pupil Accounting Manual, permits tuition-free enrollment of a non-resident employee's child in the K-12 program, continuing through graduation or receipt of a certificate of completion so long as the employee remains employed, and also continuing where the employee no longer works for the district due to layoff or elimination of the position. "Employee" means an individual with regularly scheduled hours while school is in session and excludes seasonal, coaching, and third party contracted employees including substitute teachers; eligibility starts at the next school term or semester.

Policy 2000.06, Personal Electronic Devices: use is limited to scheduled lunch, before and after the regular school day, and teacher-directed educational purposes; otherwise devices must be powered off and out of sight in backpacks, purses, or lockers. New language bars broadcasting or recording audio, images, or video of any student, staff member, or other person without permission, excepting curricular and extracurricular activities such as athletic events and arts performances.

Policy 2000.07, Wellness: policy and administrative regulation 2000.07-AR are updated to match current federal regulatory guidance on student wellness and nutrition.

**Curriculum and Instruction - 3000 Series**
The entire section was reviewed in light of escalating attacks on schools and boards over curriculum. 3000.01 Curriculum Development is revised for Revised School Code compliance, citing MCL 380.1278 and requiring Board approval of core academic curriculum changes to the extent Michigan law requires. 3000.02 is renamed "Parent and Family Engagement (PFE)" with Title I obligations restated. 3000.03 Instruction drops an extraneous word, leaving "research based and peer reviewed instructional methodologies." 3000.04 is retitled "Textbooks, Technology, and Other Essential Curricular Materials" and wholly replaced, citing MCL 380.1421/22 and delegating approval and purchase of non-textbook instructional materials to the Superintendent. 3000.05 becomes "Selection of Media Center/Library Materials."

**Personnel - 4000 Series**
Under Policy 4000.03, the Alcohol and Drug Free Workplace sub-policy gains express authority for the Superintendent to require a medical examination on reasonable suspicion, and the Medical Examinations sub-policy adds that trigger to its list. Examination costs are borne by the School District, the employee signs a release, and the physician's report goes to the Superintendent and into a separate confidential personnel file.

**Business - 5000 Series**
New sub-policy "Real Property and Structures" under Policy 5000.03 (Purchasing) supplies acquisition authority to match existing disposition authority and expressly authorizes the Superintendent to execute closing documents. Policy 5000.05 (Surplus Property) renames "Land, Buildings, Facilities, and Real Estate" to "Real Property and Structures." Policy 5000.11 (Online Fundraising) deletes the list of sites naming DonorsChoose.org, Kickstarter.com, GoFundMe.com, and CrowdRise.com.

**General Policies - 8000 Series**
Policy 8000.07 and regulation 8000.07-AR are revised to separate Title IX matters from other discrimination and harassment matters, following the 2020 U.S. Department of Education guidelines that updated the regulations for the first time since 1997. Draft Title IX regulations issued in June 2022 are not final and are not integrated, with finalization not expected until approximately late 2023. The policy prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, color, national origin, religion, sex including sexual orientation and gender identity, marital status, genetic information, disability, age, or any other basis prohibited by law, and designates the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services and Title IX Coordinator to supervise implementation.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Document and setting**
A recommended policy update memorandum prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of September 20, 2022, organized by policy manual series and stating for each proposed change the reason and the recommended language.

**Bylaws - 1000 Series**
Policy 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board: Removal from Office. The policy addresses removal of Board officers from their Board officer positions, not removal from the Board itself, so the sub-policy heading should become "Removal from Officer Positions" to eliminate ambiguity.

**Students - 2000 Series**
Policy 2000.01, Admission and Enrollment: Children of Non-Resident Employees. Consistent with specific language in the State Aid Act and the Pupil Accounting Manual, the memo recommends updating the sub-policy after discovery of a small loophole in which a person could obtain employment, have their child enrolled under the sub-policy, then voluntarily leave employment while the pupil maintained enrollment without paying tuition. Recommended language: a child of a non-resident employee may enroll without tuition provided the student is enrolling in the K-12 program; once enrolled the student may continue through graduation or receipt of a certificate of completion as long as the employee remains employed with the School District, and may also continue if the employee no longer works for the District due to layoff or elimination of the position. The policy does not bar long-term suspension or expulsion for a violation of the Student Code of Conduct. An "employee" is an individual with regularly scheduled hours while school is in session, excluding seasonal, coaching, and third party contracted employees including substitute teachers, and becomes eligible at the start of the next school term or semester.

Policy 2000.06, Behavior: Personal Electronic Devices. Responding to client interest in language barring students from using cell phones or similar devices to record or photograph others at school without permission, subject to common sense exceptions such as a sporting event or arts performance, the memo adds underlined text to the sub-policy identified as "Distribution and Posting of Materials." The District reserves the right to prohibit possession or use of personal electronic devices on School District property or at School District-related functions; a "personal electronic device" is a privately owned device used for audio, video, or text communications; use is permitted only during the student's scheduled lunch time, before and after the regular school day, and as directed by a teacher or other professional staff member for educational purposes; devices must otherwise be powered off and out of sight in backpacks, purses, or lockers; broadcasting or recording audio, images, or video of any student, staff member, or other person without that person's permission is barred, excepting curricular or extracurricular activities for which personal recording is generally permitted; and the Superintendent may develop regulations.

Policy 2000.07, Health and Safety: Wellness. Citing significantly increased federal agency attention to student wellness and nutrition, changes to the policy and to administrative regulation 2000.07-AR bring the district into compliance with the latest regulatory guidance and interpretations. The Board recognizes student wellness as integral to learning, growth, and development; the District will promote proper nutrition, nutrition education, and regular physical activity; the Board has adopted a Wellness Policy as required by law, periodically reviewed; and the Superintendent will develop administrative regulations.

**Curriculum and Instruction - 3000 Series**
Given the current political environment and escalating attacks on schools and boards over curriculum development, approval, and associated choices, the team reviewed and revised the entire 3000 section.

Policy 3000.01, Curriculum Development. Revised for compliance with the Revised School Code and to clarify the board's responsibilities under Michigan law. The Board directs the Superintendent to develop, implement, and evaluate the core academic curriculum, which must be consistent with the Board's policy on Student Learning and Achievement, meet or exceed all State of Michigan requirements for instructional programs, and be standards based and founded on legally-compliant, research based grade level learning and achievement standards leading to a School District diploma. It must also cover career and technical education students and address students of all abilities, students with disabilities, and gifted students. Changes to the core academic curriculum must be approved by the Board to the extent required by Michigan law, citing MCL 380.1278.

Policy 3000.02, Parental Involvement, renamed "Parent and Family Engagement (PFE)." The Superintendent will develop regulations in consultation with parents and families covering cooperation to develop students' intellectual and vocational skills in a safe and positive environment, review of curriculum, textbooks, and teaching materials, observation of instructional activities other than testing and assessments, and disclosure or use of student information for sales or marketing. Under Title I the District informs parents and families of the program and its objectives, trains them and Title I staff, consults regularly, involves them in program design, operation, and evaluation, and provides for full participation of those who lack literacy skills or whose native language is not English. Services funded with state and local money in Title I schools must be comparable to those in non-Title I schools.

Policy 3000.03, Instruction, written in one line of the memo as Policy 3003.03. An extraneous word is removed, leaving that to the maximum extent feasible instruction will be delivered using research based and peer reviewed instructional methodologies.

Policy 3000.04, retitled Textbooks, Technology, and Other Essential Curricular Materials. Because the former Textbooks and Other Instructional Materials policy has become the focus of many community groups, the language is comprehensively updated and wholly replaced. Textbooks or their modern equivalent are fundamental to delivery of the core academic curriculum, and the Superintendent may use well-qualified administrators and teachers to assist in selecting textbooks recommended to the Board for approval to the extent required by Michigan law, citing MCL 380.1421/22. Other instructional materials do not require Board approval; the Board delegates authority to approve and purchase them to the Superintendent, and they must be compatible with the Board-approved core academic curriculum.

Policy 3000.05, retitled "Selection of Media Center/Library Materials." Amid increasing scrutiny from community members, the Board intends students be provided access to a wide variety of educational materials in various media, with the Superintendent authorized to make or approve purchases for the media center and classroom libraries and to receive recommendations from professional staff members, parents, and students.

**Personnel - 4000 Series**
Policy 4000.03, Conditions of Employment: Alcohol and Drug Free Workplace. Though the district's authority to send a suspected employee for a medical examination was never legally in doubt, clients asked for explicit language. The Board maintains a workplace free of alcohol and illegal drugs and of prescription drugs for which the employee lacks a current valid prescription; an employee or volunteer who manufactures, distributes, dispenses, possesses, or uses alcohol or any drug in the workplace, or is present in the workplace under the influence, is subject to discipline up to and including discharge; and the Superintendent may require a medical examination on reasonable suspicion that the employee is under the influence of drugs, alcohol, or illegal substances while performing job duties or on school grounds.

Policy 4000.03, Conditions of Employment: Medical Examinations. The Superintendent or designee may require an examination when required or permitted by federal or state law or by the employee's contract of employment; when information suggests a health condition may be negatively affecting the employee's ability to perform essential job functions with or without accommodations, or that the employee is a direct threat to their own or others' safety; when medical documentation for a health leave remains insufficient after an opportunity to supplement; or on reasonable suspicion of being under the influence. All costs are borne by the School District, the employee signs a release authorizing the physician to report directly to the Superintendent, and a copy is kept in a separate confidential personnel file.

**Business - 5000 Series**
Policy 5000.03, Purchasing: Real Property and Structures, a new sub-policy. Baseline policies referenced disposition of land, buildings, facilities, and real estate but never expressly provided matching acquisition authority, and title agencies routinely require a board resolution plus a document granting an individual, most commonly the Board President or Superintendent, authority to execute closing documents. Under the new language the Superintendent may identify real property and structures suitable for purchase and recommend procedures to the Board; Board approval is required for both the process and the ultimate purchase or acquisition; and the Superintendent is authorized to execute any and all closing documents. It is separate and distinct from Policy 5000.05.

Policy 5000.05, Surplus Property. The sub-policy "Land, Buildings, Facilities, and Real Estate" is renamed "Real Property and Structures," with the original terms struck. The Superintendent may identify property no longer required for School District purposes and recommend procedures to the Board; Board approval is required for the process and the ultimate sale or disposition; and the Superintendent may execute closing documents.

Policy 5000.11, Online Fundraising. The list of potential fundraising sites naming DonorsChoose.org, Kickstarter.com, GoFundMe.com, and CrowdRise.com is deleted as superfluous. The retained language bars employees from creating, posting, or sponsoring an online fundraiser seeking public funds for school purposes or using the District's name, logo, or likeness without prior written consent from the Superintendent, and makes property so secured District property rather than the employee's.

**Facilities and Operations - 6000 Series and School and Community Relations - 7000 Series**
No recommended updates are listed for the 6000 series, and the 7000 series heading appears with no recommendations under it.

**General Policies - 8000 Series**
Policy 8000.07, Discrimination and Harassment. No topic has garnered as much attention in the past few years as Title IX; in 2020 the U.S. Department of Education issued new guidelines for implementation and enforcement, updating the regulations for the first time since 1997, and 2021-22 was the first meaningful opportunity for most districts to live with them during a normal school year, a road that was at times bumpy. Revisions to policy and administrative regulation 8000.07 and 8000.07-AR provide operational clarity while drawing a clear distinction between Title IX issues and other matters of discrimination and harassment. New draft Title IX regulations issued by the U.S. Department of Education in June 2022 are not yet final and are not integrated into these updates, with finalization not expected until approximately late 2023. The policy commits the Board to a learning and working environment in which all individuals are treated with dignity and respect, free from illegal discrimination and harassment based on a legally prohibited characteristic, with no tolerance for discrimination or harassment on the basis of race, color, national origin, religion, sex including sexual orientation and gender identity, marital status, genetic information, disability, age, or any other basis prohibited by law, and designates the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services and Title IX Coordinator to supervise implementation of the policy and its implementing regulations.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association, circulated with proposed 2021 amendments printed in red, govern the Association's offices, membership, dues, meetings, election of directors, officers, committees, fiduciary duties, indemnification and amendment procedure. The text records adoption by the Board of Directors on 11/15/2017, adoption by the General Membership on 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018, and amendments adopted by the General Membership on 9/16/2020. The most consequential proposed change is a new Article VI, Section 1 fixing the Board of Directors at an odd number of no fewer than 7 nor more than 9 Directors, with the Board given discretion to set the number and to shrink it by attrition.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Identification**
Bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association (the "Association"), a Michigan nonprofit. Adopted by Board of Directors 11/15/2017; adopted by General Membership 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018; amendments adopted by General Membership 9/16/2020. Proposed 2021 amendments appear in red within the text.

**Articles I-II: Offices and Purpose**
Principal office at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, County of Oakland. A registered office and registered agent are continuously maintained. Stated purposes include advancing public education quality in Oakland County through cooperative effort of locally elected boards, conducting meetings and programs in partnership with Oakland Schools, and advocating for county, state and national legislation supporting public education.

**Articles III-V: Membership, Dues, Member Meetings**
Members are publicly elected board members of Oakland County school districts or the Oakland ISD Board of Education whose district is in good standing with the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB). One vote per Member, in person; exceptions give each Member School District one (1) vote on committee-chair selection, resolutions (Article IX) and bylaws amendments (Article XVI). Electronic voting is reserved to the Board of Directors for emergency business, reaffirmed at the next Board meeting. Membership is not transferable. Financing comes from an annual MASB grant to County Area School Boards Association (CASBA) members, ISD dues not exceeding that grant, plus contributions and gifts. An annual meeting plus not less than three additional regular membership meetings are held yearly; the annual meeting is the first regular meeting after July 1. Special meetings require 30 days' notice; written notice of meetings is delivered not less than ten nor more than fifty days ahead. Quorum is at least one Member from twenty-five (25%) percent of Member School Districts.

**Articles VI-VIII: Directors and Officers**
Proposed new Section 1 sets an odd number of Directors, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9; decreases occur by attrition (possibly an eight-member Board for up to one year), increases by election. Terms are three (3) years. By May 1 the Board convenes an Election Committee of the three most recently elected Directors; elections occur at the June meeting; no floor nominations. Failure to attend three (3) consecutive Board meetings constitutes resignation unless excused on written request within thirty (30) days. Officers are President, Vice-President, Secretary and Treasurer, elected from the Board; Directors and officers receive no stated salaries. Board records and proceedings are confidential absent advance authorization.

**Articles IX-XVI: Committees, Finances, Indemnification**
Committee quorum is twenty-five (25%) percent of appointed representatives; chairs are elected annually at the first meeting after January 31 with seven (7) calendar days' written notice. The Government Relations Committee meets at least 6 times per year and submits Legislative Priorities to the Board by June 15. The Resolutions and Bylaws Committee meets at least once per year; Member School District voting windows run at least forty (40) calendar days; resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) Member School Districts become official Association positions. Expenditures over $2,500 require Board approval plus President and Treasurer signatures; up to $2,500 either officer may approve. The Treasurer presents an annual budget (July 1 to June 30) by June 30 and an actual income and expense report by August 30. Article XII provides indemnification under the Michigan Nonprofit Association Act. Article XVI amendments require a written ballot to each Member School District with at least a forty (40) day voting period.

**Appendix 1**
"Definition of Cause for Removing a Board Member or Officer," adopted by the OCSBA Board of Directors September 16, 2020, framed around the duties of care, loyalty and obedience.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Identity and adoption history**
"Bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association" with proposed 2021 amendments printed in red. Header records: Adopted by Board of Directors 11/15/2017; Adopted by General Membership 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018; Amendments Adopted by General Membership 9/16/2020. Articles I through XVI plus Appendix 1.

**Articles I-II: Offices and Purpose**
The principal office is at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, County of Oakland; other offices within or without Michigan may be established by the Board of Directors, and a registered office and registered agent are continuously maintained. Purposes (a) through (h): advance the quality of public education in Oakland County through cooperative efforts of locally elected boards of education; promote high standards in educational programs and services for all students; inform school board members on educational issues; sponsor meetings and programs in partnership with Oakland Schools; promote public understanding of the role of school boards; enhance cooperation among Oakland County boards; represent Oakland County school board views to political representatives; and advocate for legislation supporting public education services by locally elected boards.

**Article III - Membership**
Eligible Members are publicly elected Board of Education members of school districts located in Oakland County, or elected Oakland ISD Board of Education members ("Member School Districts"), whose district is a member in good standing of the Michigan Association of School Boards ("MASB"). Each Member has one vote, cast in person. Exception: each Member School District has one (1) vote on selecting a committee chair, on resolutions (Article IX) and on amending the Bylaws (Article XVI); district votes are recorded on receipt of the completed resolution or ballot indicating the vote of the district's Trustees, must arrive before the stated deadline, and results go to all Member Districts no later than the next general membership meeting. Electronic voting is granted to the Board of Directors only for emergency business, reaffirmed at the next Board meeting. Membership is not transferable or assignable.

**Articles IV-V - Dues and Member Meetings**
Financing comes from an annual MASB grant to its County Area School Boards Association (CASBA) members, Intermediate School District membership dues not exceeding the MASB CASBA grant, and contributions and gifts. An annual meeting plus not less than three additional regular membership meetings are held each year; the annual meeting is the first regular meeting after July 1. Special meetings may be called by voice or email by the President or by two or more Directors with 30 days' notice, and written notice is delivered personally or by email by the Secretary not less than ten nor more than fifty days before a meeting. Quorum is at least one Member from twenty-five (25%) percent of the Member School Districts.

**Article VI - Election of Board of Directors (renumbered by the 2021 amendments)**
New Section 1, Number of Directors: an odd number, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9; the Board has discretion over the number and shall consider a change whenever an election produces fewer candidates than open seats and before seeking candidates to fill a vacancy under Section 6; the Secretary promptly communicates any change to all Members; decreases occur by attrition, which may result in an eight member Board for up to one year until the next election, and increases by election. Eligibility: only one Member from each Member School District may serve at a time. Term: three (3) years, continuing until a successor is elected and qualified. Board Election: by May 1 yearly the Board convenes an Election Committee of the three most recently elected Directors, which seeks candidates providing geographical balance throughout Oakland County; Board Candidate Application Forms go to all Member School Districts; nominations cannot be made from the floor; election takes place at the June meeting; more candidates than vacancies means a written ballot, fewer means the Board fills the vacancy at its next meeting. Resignation/Removal: removal by the Members or the Board, with cause as defined in Appendix I, by majority affirmative vote excluding the Director subject to the action. Vacancy: the Board first considers decreasing the number of Directors under Section 1; if the number is retained, the President notifies the Members, each district receives a Board Candidate Application Form, and the Board appoints for the remainder of the vacated term until the next scheduled election. Attendance: failure to attend three (3) consecutive Board meetings constitutes a resignation, though a Director may be granted an excused absence on written request to the Board President within thirty (30) days of the missed meeting.

**Articles VII-VIII - Board and Officers**
The Board carries out the purposes specified in Article II of the Articles of Incorporation. Special meetings may be called by the President or any two Directors, with at least two days' notice personally, by phone, fax or email, or five days' notice by mail. Quorum is a majority of the Board, and Directors receive no stated salaries. Action without a meeting requires written consent signed by all Directors, and Board proceedings are confidential absent advance authorization. Officers, elected from the current Board, are a President, Vice-President, Secretary and Treasurer, serving until the next annual meeting and removable with cause by majority vote. The President is Chief Executive Officer; the Secretary records all votes and minutes; the Treasurer holds custody of funds and securities and may be required to furnish a bond at the Association's cost.

**Article IX - Committees**
Committee quorum is twenty-five (25%) percent of appointed representatives, each present representative having one vote; alternates count for quorum or vote only when the primary representative is absent. Each standing and ad hoc committee elects a Chairperson annually as the first order of business at its first meeting after January 31, with written notice at least seven (7) calendar days prior; chairs set schedules and agendas, maintain attendance records, distribute minutes and report to the Board through the President, and may be removed without cause. The Government Relations Committee is a standing committee meeting at least 6 times per year, with a representative appointed by each Member School District at its annual organizational meeting, one (1) vote per district in attendance, and Legislative Priorities submitted to the Board for approval by June 15. The Resolutions and Bylaws Committee is a standing committee meeting at least once per year; revisions may be initiated by a Member School District Board, the Board of Directors, the Government Relations Committee or the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee; the district voting window is at least forty (40) calendar days; and resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) Member School Districts become the official position of the Association.

**Articles X-XVI**
On dissolution, assets are distributed as provided in Article VIII of the Articles of Incorporation, with no inurement to any Member, Director or Officer as prohibited by Section 501(c)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 as amended, the Michigan General Sales Tax Act or the Michigan Use Tax Act. Article XI: expenditures may not exceed the approved annual budget; Board approval plus signature by both the President and Treasurer are required for any expenditure exceeding $2,500, while expenditures up to $2,500 require approval by either the President or the Treasurer, and the Vice-President may approve if both are absent or disabled. Financial reports go to Board members quarterly or on request; the Treasurer presents an annual budget (July 1 to June 30) by June 30 and an annual actual income and expense report by August 30, both presented at the first fall Member Meeting. Agreed-upon procedures are performed annually; an external audit replaces them only if required by law or a third party. The Board may enter an Administrative and Financial Services Agreement with Oakland Schools, monitored by the Treasurer. Article XII indemnifies directors and officers to the fullest extent authorized by the Michigan Nonprofit Association Act ("the Act"), with indemnification approved by a disinterested quorum vote, a committee of not less than two (2) disinterested Directors, or independent legal counsel in a written opinion. Article XIII leaves the fiscal year to the Board. Article XIV requires avoidance of conflicts, and a conflicted Director is not counted toward quorum. Article XV covers contracts and borrowing by Board resolution, action by written consent, Section 7 Remote Participation in Meeting by Telephone (two-way communication constituting presence in person), and a corporate seal inscribed with the Association name, "Corporate Seal" and "Michigan". Article XVI, retitled "AMENDMENTS, RULES AND REGULATIONS," provides for amendment by vote of the Member School Districts on a written ballot with at least a forty (40) day voting period and one vote per district, and permits the Board to set aside rules during a declared local, state or national emergency.

**Appendix 1 - Definition of Cause for Removing a Board Member or Officer**
Adopted by the OCSBA Board of Directors September 16, 2020. The preface sets out three primary legal duties: duty of care (prudent use of all assets, including facility, people and good will), duty of loyalty (advancing the mission, disclosing conflicts of interest, deciding in the nonprofit's best interest), and duty of obedience (obeying applicable laws and regulations, following its own bylaws, adhering to stated corporate purposes). Cause includes willful failure to follow OCSBA bylaws; willful neglect of duties; failure to disclose a conflict of interest or using the Association for personal gain; using the OCSBA Board position or OCSBA's logo in a political endorsement; frequently missed Board or committee meetings; creating an unhealthy or dysfunctional boardroom through inappropriate behavior or disrespect; ethical concerns such as discrimination, harassment or criminal behaviors; and acts of malfeasance, misfeasance or nonfeasance. Removal should be done only when absolutely necessary, with the reasons left to the Association's other Directors and Members.
