https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Oakland County School Boards Association's 2021 Proposed Resolutions and Amendments packet, marking deletions and additions, puts new items before Member School Districts and reprints the continuing resolutions adopted by OCSBA's Member School Districts on September 14, 2019. The 2021 items are a proposed amendment to the School Finance Research Collaborative resolution originally adopted 9/24/2019, a proposed Broadband Access and Devices resolution tied to MASB Resolution A-10.30, and a Teacher Shortages resolution drawn from the MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Format**
"2021 Proposed Resolutions & Amendments," with a key indicating struck text as Deletion and capitalized text as ADDITION. Each item pairs a Legislative Priority with a proposed resolution or amendment, a bracketed cross-reference to the corresponding Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) resolution, and a rationale.

**School Finance Research Collaborative (SFRC) - proposed amendment**
Legislative Priority (Rev. 2021): review and implement SFRC recommendations, including the recommended additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure and transportation, while holding higher funded districts harmless. The proposed amendment, to the original resolution adopted 9/24/2019, restates OCSBA support and adds in capitals that WHILE IMPLEMENTING THE SFRC RECOMMENDATIONS, HIGHER FUNDED DISTRICTS MUST BE HELD HARMLESS. Cross-referenced to MASB resolution G 11.01 and A-10.25 - 2021 amendment. Rationale: continued support for raising all districts to SFRC funding levels toward equitable funding, opposition to legislation lowering any district's current funding, and alignment with a MASB proposed 2021 amendment.

**Broadband Access and Devices - proposed resolution**
Legislative Priority: expand access to quality internet and proper devices for all students and staff. Proposed resolution: broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan; support for additional federal and state funding to expand affordable and reliable broadband access; support for federal and state programs for the purchase of internet capable devices and software. Cross-referenced to MASB Resolution A-10.30 - 2021 amendment. Rationale cites pandemic-highlighted inequities in access to reliable broadband and devices.

**Teacher Shortages - proposed resolution**
Legislative Priority: implement state-based programs to address teacher shortages and retain teachers. Proposed resolution supports statewide initiatives while maintaining quality teacher preparation programs, listing possible incentives to enter and complete a teaching college program, incentives for teachers to remain in the classroom, and easing the process to obtain Michigan certification for teachers certified in other states. Cross-referenced to the MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority.

**Continuing resolutions adopted September 14, 2019**

| Resolution | MASB / NSBA reference |
|---|---|
| Mental Health | G 9.01; G 9.05; G 9.50 |
| Local Control | A 10.10; A 10.55; A 12.70 |
| Evidence-Based Decision Making | G 11.01 |
| Unfunded Mandates | A 10.20 |
| School Finance Research Collaborative | G 11.01 (2021 amendment proposed) |
| School Aid A-E | A 10.25 and subparts; A 10.05; A 10.55 |
| Accountability and Transparency | A 6.65 (c), (d), (f) |
| Universal Preschool | A 6.15 (c) |
| Special Education / IDEA | A 5.01; NSBA Advocacy: IDEA |

The School Aid resolution has five parts: oppose using School Aid Fund dollars for any purpose other than K-12 education; support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students; protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes; specify in Michigan's Constitution that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education and oppose private school voucher or tax credit programs; and enact the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 so districts can meet the June 30 budget deadline. A Lame Duck resolution addresses accelerated passage of legislation after the November election. When aligned with its own priorities OCSBA also supports the NSBA, MASB and Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) legislative agendas. Links given: https://www.masb.org/resolutions.aspx and https://www.nsba.org/Advocacy.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Packet identity and conventions**
"2021 PROPOSED RESOLUTIONS & AMENDMENTS" of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), with a key for amendments showing struck text as Deletion and capitalized text as ADDITION. The packet is organized as Legislative Priority statements followed by the proposed resolution or amendment text, a bracketed cross-reference to Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) resolution numbers, and a rationale; the continuing resolutions previously adopted by Member School Districts are reprinted at the end.

**School Finance Research Collaborative (SFRC) - proposed amendment**
Legislative Priority (Rev. 2021), printed in the source with the heading typo "SCHOL FINANCE RESEARCH COLLABORATIVE": review and implement recommendations of the SFRC including the recommended additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure, and transportation; while implementing the SFRC recommendations, higher funded districts must be held harmless. The proposed amendment notes the original resolution was adopted 9/24/2019 and reads: "SCHOOL FINANCE RESEARCH COLLABORATIVE (SFRC): OCSBA supports review and implementation of the recommendations of the SFRC, including the recommended additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure, and transportation. WHILE IMPLEMENTING THE SFRC RECOMMENDATIONS, HIGHER FUNDED DISTRICTS MUST BE HELD HARMLESS." Cross-reference: MASB resolution G 11.01 and A-10.25 - 2021 amendment. Rationale: "We continue to support increasing all districts to the funding levels recommended by the SFRC, with a goal of achieving equitable funding for all districts. We oppose legislation that would lower any district's current funding in the process. This proposed amendment is aligned with a MASB proposed 2021 amendment." For a comparatively high-revenue district such as Troy, the hold-harmless addition is the operative clause.

**Broadband Access and Devices - proposed resolution**
Legislative Priority: expand access to quality internet and proper devices for all students and staff. Proposed resolution text: broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan; OCSBA supports additional federal and state funding opportunities to expand affordable and reliable broadband access; and supports federal and state programs for the purchase of internet capable devices and software. Cross-reference: MASB Resolution A-10.30 - 2021 amendment. Rationale: broadband is an important component of school infrastructure, the pandemic highlighted inequities in access to reliable broadband and devices, and the amendment is aligned with a proposed 2021 MASB Amendment.

**Teacher Shortages - proposed resolution**
Legislative Priority: implement state-based programs to address teacher shortages and to retain teachers. Proposed resolution: OCSBA supports statewide initiatives to address teacher shortages and retain teachers while maintaining quality teacher preparation programs; initiatives might include, but should not be limited to, incentives to enter and complete a teaching college program, incentives for teachers to remain in the classroom, and easing the process to obtain Michigan certification for teachers that are certified in other states. Cross-reference: MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority.

**Continuing resolutions adopted by OCSBA's Member School Districts on September 14, 2019**
MENTAL HEALTH: OCSBA supports increased mental health services and professionals in schools and providing adequate state resources to allow schools both to educate and to keep students and staff safe [MASB Resolutions G 9.01; G 9.05; G 9.50]. Two sub-points: help staff identify potential mental health issues for students; and encourage the Michigan Department of Education (MDE) to develop a model policy for staff regarding identifying mental health issues and appropriate staff response.
LOCAL CONTROL: support local control of community-governed public schools with elected school boards [MASB Resolution A 10.10; A 10.55; A 12.70].
EVIDENCE-BASED DECISION MAKING: OCSBA supports evidence-based education policy that will maximize opportunities for the highest achievement of each student [MASB Resolution G 11.01].
UNFUNDED MANDATES: OCSBA opposes any state or federal legislation that results in increased costs for school districts without full funding, and encourages the Michigan Legislature to oppose any federal laws or programs that are not fully funded and thus cost the state valuable resources [MASB Resolution A 10.20].
SCHOOL FINANCE RESEARCH COLLABORATIVE (SFRC): the continuing form of the resolution, supporting review and implementation of SFRC recommendations including additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure and transportation [MASB Resolution G 11.01], flagged "* 2021 - AMENDMENT PROPOSED *".

**School Aid resolution, parts A through E**
A. Oppose using School Aid Fund dollars for any other purpose than K-12 education [MASB Resolution A 10.25]. B. Support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (g) and (j); A 10.55]. C. Protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (c); A 10.55]. D. Specify that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education in Michigan's Constitution and oppose any attempts to create private school voucher or tax credit programs [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (a) and A 10.05]. E. OCSBA supports enacting the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 so that school districts have factual information to meet their constitutional/statutory requirement to approve a budget by June 30 [MASB Resolution A 10.25 (h)].

**Remaining continuing resolutions**
ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY: OCSBA supports transparency and accountability for ALL school aid funds, naming community governed public school districts, charter schools, cyber schools, community colleges and public universities [MASB Resolution A 6.65 (c), (d), (f)].
LAME DUCK: OCSBA supports lame duck parameters that will address introduction and accelerated passage of legislation after the November election.
UNIVERSAL PRESCHOOL: OCSBA supports additional new dollars to fund universal preschool for all four year old children [MASB Resolution A 6.15 (c)].
SPECIAL EDUCATION: OCSBA supports full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), noting that although federal legislation initially promised to provide 40 percent of the excess cost to educate students with disabilities, appropriations have fallen short, leaving states and local school districts to make up the difference [MASB Resolution A 5.01; NSBA Advocacy: IDEA].

**Aligned external agendas and references**
When aligned with OCSBA Legislative Priorities, OCSBA also supports the National School Boards Association (NSBA) Legislative Agenda, the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Legislative Agenda, and the Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) Legislative Agenda. Links provided: MASB Resolutions at https://www.masb.org/resolutions.aspx and NSBA Advocacy: IDEA at https://www.nsba.org/Advocacy. The packet is the ballot material a member board such as Troy School District's Board of Education would act on before these proposals can become official positions of the Association.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Three-page tabular crosswalk titled "Summary of 2021 Proposed Bylaws Amendments" for the Oakland County School Boards Association, listing for each change the page, article, section, the proposed language with current text in black and additions or deletions in red, and a rationale. Rows cover Articles III, VI, IX, XV and XVI. The central change adds a new Article VI, Section 1 setting the Board of Directors at an odd number between 7 and 9, noting that the current bylaws do not specify a number and that the Board currently has 9 Directors serving a 29 District, 201 Member Association.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Format**
"SUMMARY OF 2021 PROPOSED BYLAWS AMENDMENTS," paginated 1 of 3 through 3 of 3, in a table with columns for Page, Article, Section, Proposed Change (current language in black, added language and/or deletion in red) and Rationale.

**Article III, Membership, Section 2, Voting Rights - Exceptions (page 2)**
The exception giving each Member School District one (1) vote on selecting a committee chair, on resolutions (Article IX) and on bylaws amendments (Article XVI) is edited to strike the committee-chair clause. Rationale: move committee chair language to Article IX Committees, Election of Committee Chairs.

**Article VI, new Section 1, Number of Directors (pages 3-5)**
Adds an odd number of Directors, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9, with Board discretion over the number, reconsideration whenever an election produces fewer candidates than open seats, Secretary notice of any change, decreases by attrition that may leave an eight member Board for up to one year, and increases by election. Subsequent sections are renumbered. Rationale: the current bylaws do not specify the number of Directors (currently 9 Directors for the 29 District / 201 Member Association) and provide no process to alter it; the new language gives flexibility given multiple openings and/or a lack of candidates.

**Article VI, Section 3 to 4, Board Election (page 4)**
Retains the May 1 Election Committee of the three most recently elected Directors, geographical balance across Oakland County, Board Candidate Application Forms, no floor nominations, and election at the June meeting. The closing sentence changes to following the vacancy procedure in Section 6. Rationale: align language with Section 1.

**Article VI, Section 4 to 5, Resignation/Removal (page 4)**
Removal with cause "as defined in Appendix 1." Rationale: renumber and add reference to Appendix 1.

**Article VI, Section 5 to 6, Vacancy (page 4)**
On a vacancy the Board first considers decreasing the number of Directors under Section 1; otherwise the President notifies Members, districts receive a Board Candidate Application Form, and the Board appoints for the remainder of the vacated term. Rationale: board seats have become increasingly difficult to fill; the language allows the BOD to decrease to a 7 member BOD serving 29 Districts and 201 members and removes the requirement to fill the seat; an appointee serves up to one year, then must be elected.

**Article VI, Section 6 to 7, Attendance (page 5)**
Failure to attend three (3) consecutive Board meetings constitutes a resignation, with excused absences requested in writing within thirty (30) days. Rationale: renumber, plus a clerical correction adding "may," inadvertently omitted in 2020.

**Article IX, Committees, new Sections 2 and 3 (pages 8-9)**
Adds Quorum and Voting Rights (twenty-five (25%) percent of appointed representatives; one vote each; alternates counted only when the primary representative is absent) and Committee Chairs (annual election as first order of business at the first meeting after January 31; seven (7) calendar days' written notice; duties for schedules, agendas, attendance records, minutes and reporting to the Board through the President; removal without cause). Rationale: provide structure for any future standing or ad hoc committee; quorum and voting rights were never defined; some committees may have more than one representative per district (e.g., DEI); clarify alternates' rights; chair responsibilities and replacement were undefined.

**Article XV Section 7 and Article XVI (page 16)**
Section 7 is retitled Remote Participation in Meeting by Telephone, the rationale noting participation could be by telephone or another means of electronic communication such as Zoom or WebEx using two way audio, with video not required. The Article XVI header becomes "AMENDMENTS, RULES AND REGULATIONS" to accurately reflect the sections contained within.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Document identity**
"SUMMARY OF 2021 PROPOSED BYLAWS AMENDMENTS," a three-page table (marked 1 of 3, 2 of 3, 3 of 3) prepared by the Oakland County School Boards Association to accompany the full marked-up bylaws. Columns: Page, Article, Section, Proposed Change with the note "[Current Language in BLACK. Added Language &/or Deletion in RED]," and Rationale. Rows address Article III, several parts of Article VI, Article IX, Article XV and Article XVI.

**Page 2, Article III Membership, Section 2 Voting Rights, Exceptions**
Proposed change: "Exceptions: Each Member School District shall have one (1) vote on any proposal to select a committee chair or vote on resolutions (as outlined in Article IX) or to amend these Bylaws (as outlined in Article XVI)." with the committee-chair language struck. Rationale: move committee chair language to Article IX Committees, Election of Committee Chairs.

**Pages 3-5, Article VI Election of Board of Directors, Section 1**
Instruction: ADD New Section 1 Language and Renumber The Subsequent Sections. New text: "Section 1: Number of Directors. The Board of Directors shall consist of an odd number of Directors, with no fewer than 7 nor more than 9 members. The Board of Directors shall have discretion to determine the number of Directors to best meet the needs of the Association. The Board shall consider such a change whenever an election produces less candidates than open seats, and prior to seeking candidates to fill a vacancy under Section 6. The Secretary shall promptly communicate any change to the number of Directors to all Members. Any decrease in the number of Directors shall be accomplished by attrition, which may result in an eight member Board for up to one year, until the next election. An increase in the number of Directors shall be accomplished by election as outlined in Section 4." Rationale: the current bylaws do not specify the number of Directors (currently 9 Directors for the 29 District / 201 Member Association), nor is there a process or provision to alter the number of Directors; the new language will give flexibility in the event of multiple openings on the Board of Directors and/or a lack of candidates for the Board of Directors.

**Page 4, Article VI, Section 3 renumbered to Section 4, Board Election**
Text: by May 1 yearly the Board shall convene an Election Committee comprised of the three most recently elected Members of the Board of Directors; the Election Committee shall seek candidates who will create a Board with a geographical balance from throughout Oakland County; Board Candidate Application Forms will also be sent to all Member School Districts to be delivered to their board members; candidates must submit a completed application to the Election Committee prior to the deadline specified on the form; nominations cannot be made from the floor during the meeting at which the election occurs; election of candidates from Member School Districts shall take place at the June meeting; if there are more candidates than vacancies the Member vote shall be by written ballot; if there are fewer candidates than vacancies the Board of Directors shall fill the vacancy at its next meeting and the appointee shall serve until the next scheduled election. The final clause is amended from "At the next election, the Election Committee will seek candidates to fill the remainder of the three year term" to directing that the procedure to fill a vacancy as outlined in Section 6 be followed. Rationale: language requires updating to align with Section 1.

**Page 4 (continued), Article VI, Section 4 renumbered to Section 5, Resignation/Removal**
Text: any Director may resign by written notice to the Association; any Director may be removed by the Members or the Board at any meeting of the Members or the Board, with cause as defined in Appendix 1, by the affirmative vote of a majority of the Members or the Directors then in office (excluding the Director who is the subject of such action). Rationale: renumber and ADD reference to Appendix 1.

**Page 4 (further), Article VI, Section 5 renumbered to Section 6, Vacancy**
Text: if a vacancy shall occur among the Board of Directors as a result of death, resignation, removal, or otherwise, the Board will first consider whether it is appropriate to decrease the number of Directors as outlined in Section 1; if the Board determines that the needs of the Association are best met by retaining the current number of Directors, the President will notify the Members of the vacancy, each Member School District shall be sent a Board Candidate Application Form, and the Board of Directors shall appoint a member to fill the vacancy at its next meeting; the appointee shall serve for the remainder of the vacated term until the next scheduled election. Rationale: Board seats have become increasingly difficult to fill; the added language allows the BOD flexibility to decrease to a 7 member BOD to serve the 29 Districts and 201 members; should the Board decide to decrease to 7 members by attrition, the new language removes the current requirement to fill the seat; an appointee will serve up to one year, then have to be elected by the Members to retain their seat.

**Page 5, Article VI, Section 6 renumbered to Section 7, Attendance**
Text: failure to attend three (3) consecutive Board meetings shall constitute a resignation; however, a Director may be granted an excused absence by action of the Board; such a request shall be made in writing to the Board President within thirty (30) days of the missed meeting. Rationale: renumber section, and a clerical correction to add "may," which was inadvertently omitted in 2020.

**Pages 8-9, Article IX Committees, Sections 2 and 3**
Instruction: ADD New Language And Renumber The Subsequent Sections. New Section 2, Quorum and Voting Rights: unless otherwise stated within the Article, the presence of twenty-five (25%) percent of the appointed representatives to a Committee will constitute a quorum and each appointed representative present in the meeting shall have one vote; Member School Districts may designate an alternate representative to any committee comprised of representatives of Member School Districts, but any appointed alternate shall only be counted for quorum and/or vote when the primary appointed representative for their District is absent. New Section 3, Committee Chairs: each standing and ad hoc committee shall elect a Chairperson annually from the appointed representatives, the election being the first order of business at the Committee's first meeting after January 31, with written notice of the election date, time and place provided to all appointed representatives not less than seven (7) calendar days prior to the meeting at which the vote will occur; each Committee Chair is responsible for establishing and distributing the meeting schedule and agendas, maintaining committee attendance records, distributing meeting minutes to the appointed representatives after each meeting, and regularly reporting to the Board of Directors through the President; any Committee Chair may resign by written notice to the Association President, and any Committee Chair may be removed by the Committee Members or the Board at any meeting of the Committee Members or the Board, without cause, by the affirmative vote of a majority of the appointed representative(s) present or the Board of Directors then in office, excluding the Committee Chair who is the subject of such action. Rationale, four bullets: this will apply to and provide structure for any future standing or ad hoc committee; quorum and voting rights were never defined for committee meetings and some committees may have more than one designated representative per Member School District (e.g., DEI); clarify voting rights for District alternates to maintain equal voting rights for all districts; and committee chair responsibilities have not been previously defined, with no current process to replace a Committee Chair.

**Page 16, Article XV Miscellaneous Provisions, Section 7**
Section 7 is retitled from "Participation in Meeting by Telephone" to "Remote Participation in Meeting by Telephone." Text: by oral or written permission of a majority of the Board of Directors, a Member of the Board of Directors or of a committee designated by the Board may participate in a meeting by means of conference telephone, or similar communications equipment by means of which all persons participating in the meeting can hear each other ("two way communication"); participation in a meeting pursuant to this Section constitutes presence in person at the meeting. Rationale: update to refer to "remote" participation, which could be by telephone or another means of electronic communication (e.g., Zoom or WebEx), using two way audio communication; video is not required.

**Page 16 (continued), Article XVI Amendments**
Section listed as N/A. The article header "ARTICLE XVI AMENDMENTS, AND ADDITIONS RULES AND REGULATIONS" is amended by striking "AND ADDITIONS" and adding "RULES AND REGULATIONS." Rationale: change the Article header to accurately reflect the sections contained within.

**Net effect**
The package is administrative rather than substantive on most points, but two changes carry practical weight for member districts: the Board of Directors may shrink from 9 to as few as 7 by attrition without being obliged to fill vacant seats, and committee governance gains a defined quorum, voting rule for alternates, and a chair election and removal process. Under the amendment procedure the summary describes, each Member School District casts one vote, which is why the packet appears on a local board agenda.

Covers all governmental and proprietary funds plus grant and state-funded projects; fiduciary (custodial) funds are not presented. Budgets take effect July 1, 2021.

**Key assumptions**
Taxable values in Oakland County are expected to rise more than 3.75%, but the budget assumes another Headlee rollback — the seventh year in a row. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Identification.** Oakland Schools — one of 56 Michigan intermediate school districts established in 1962, an autonomous tax-supported district serving 28 constituent local districts in Oakland County — issued the FY22 Proposed Budget Complete Document for the May 18, 2021 board meeting. Every page carries the footer "FY 22 Proposed Budget" and the date stamp 3.16.21. Mission: "Oakland Schools: Learning today. Transforming tomorrow." Budgets are adopted effective July 1, 2021 and cover all governmental fund types, proprietary fund types and a summary of grant and state-funded projects; fiduciary (custodial) funds are not presented.

**Enterprise-wide totals.** Proposed total funding of $359.6 million comprises property taxes $207.6 million, other local and investment revenue $32.2 million, state source revenue $18.8 million, other financing sources and indirect revenue $8.9 million, expected new grant award funding $78.6 million and estimated grant carryover funding $13.5 million. Proposed total expenditures of $364.3 million comprise salary, wage and benefits $76.4 million; purchased services, supplies, dues/fees $20.3 million; electric and natural gas utilities $.9 million; capital outlay $5.6 million; transfers to LEAs and other funds $166.0 million; grant related expenditures $92.1 million; and payment on existing debt $3.0 million. Both figures are net of eliminated Risk Related Activity Fund amounts.

**Property taxes.** Revenue is budgeted to increase 2.7%, or $5.5 million, to $207,634,700 — General Education Fund $12,337,500, Special Education Fund $156,909,100, Career Focused Education Fund $38,388,100, each +2.70%. Oakland County taxable values are expected to increase more than 3.75%, but the budget anticipates another Headlee rollback, which would be the seventh year in a row. Tax revenues have increased 23% since the end of the recession in 2014 and remain $14.8 million below pre-recession levels; the Great Recession's 24.5% cumulative loss in taxable value produced $430.2 million of cumulative district revenue erosion through fiscal year 2021. The tax base is 70% principal residence and 30% non-principal residence. Michigan Tax Tribunal judgments have returned $12.8 million in property taxes over the past ten years; the FY 2021-22 MTT reserve is .25% of tax revenues, about $519,000 in expense.

**General Education Fund (100).** Revenue $21,286,500 — property taxes $12.3 million (58% of total), other local $2.5 million, state source $5.8 million, other financing sources $.7 million; total local sources $14,785,800 and state sources $5,790,900 (Section 81 general aid $3,902,300; Section 147c UAAL rate stabilization $1,614,700; Section 147a $119,600; State Payment in Lieu of Taxes $145,000). Expenditures $23,506,900: General Administration $1,815,600, Finance and Operations $9,002,300, Instructional Services $10,228,700, Plant & Fixed Charges $2,460,300. The planned operating deficit of $(2,220,400) is described as an intentional spend-down to fund collaborative and supplemental instructional programs. Ending fund equity $2,540,800 — $74,800 non-spendable prepaids and $2,466,000 unassigned, or 10.5% of budgeted expenditures, down from 16.8%. Department 085 Instruction & Pedagogy rises to $3,662,800 on supplemental learning programs; COVID-19 response is budgeted at $1.3 million. Five-year forecast total revenues reach $24,084,400 by 2026-27 with unassigned balance of $3,405,800 (14.2%).

**Special Education Fund (200).** Revenue $164,267,600 — property taxes $156.9 million (95% of total), local sources $157,088,700, state sources $6,948,900 (Special Ed Sec 51A $3,207,200; State Payment in Lieu of Taxes $1,843,700; Section 147c $1,520,000; Sec 51.a.2 $115,500; Sec 51f $265,500; School for Deaf/Blind 54 $197,900), indirect revenue $230,000. Expenditures $164,258,900, producing an $8,700 surplus. Ending equity $11,430,400: $13,800 non-spendable, $997,000 restricted (5.0% of budgeted expenditures), $10,419,600 restricted for future center facility renovations. The PA-18 base distribution is $140,386,800, up $3.8 million or 2.8%, plus $3,933,200 for group home and medical student support, incarcerated youth, startup assistance, extraordinary contingency, assistive technology and Section 24 payments. The FY 2020 audited fund balance exceeded the 5% target, prompting a supplemental PA-18 distribution of $5.6 million in FY 2021 that does not recur. District distributions include Bloomfield Hills $10,707,800, Rochester $10,386,300, Walled Lake $10,174,300, Farmington $9,725,900, Birmingham $9,110,200, Waterford $8,564,500, Troy $7,330,500, Southfield $6,541,500, Hazel Park $6,372,100, Lake Orion $6,146,300, Clarkston $5,407,100, Huron Valley $5,502,900, Royal Oak $4,575,500, Pontiac $4,002,000, Public School Academies $1,558,800 and $2,000,000 "to be distributed." The Hazel Park center facility renovation project is complete, dropping that line to zero. Services support approximately 21,185 students with an IEP. Forecast LEA base distributions reach $163,758,000 by 2026-27.

**Career Focused Education Fund (600).** Revenue $43,755,500 — property taxes $38.4 million (88% of total), state sources $4,874,500 including Section 61a.1 at $1,422,000 (a 20% reduction reflecting pandemic effects on CTE completers), Section 147c $2,549,000, Section 147a $188,800 and State Payment in Lieu of Taxes $451,100. Expenditures $45,200,400: campus and other program operations $26,514,100, LEA transfers and program subsidies $5,843,000, plant and fixed charges $12,843,300; operating deficit $(1,444,900). Ending equity $3,997,800 — $25,200 non-spendable and $3,972,600 restricted, 8.8% of expenditures. Four Oakland Schools Technical Campuses serve approximately 2,700 students from all 28 districts: NW $5,552,300, SE $5,803,800, NE $6,095,900, SW $5,880,200. Nineteen state CTE program codes are submitted under Public Act 451 of 1976, MCL 380.684, as amended by Public Act 45 of 2007, including Cosmetology (NE only), Cyber Security and Public Safety (SE only), and Medium & Heavy Truck Technician (SW only). LEA transportation support is $1,800,000 annually and K-12 Career Readiness LEA support $3,088,000; STEM mobile classroom operating costs are $412,000 per year.

**Personnel and benefits.** Total staffing moves from 633.59 FTE in 2019-20 to 653.96 in 2020-21 to 654.96 in 2021-22, a change of 1.00 — a new 1.0 FTE Transportation Manager split 73% GEF, 25% SEF, 2% CFEF, previously a part-time retiree position. No across-the-board pay increases; non-union salary/wage step growth 1.63%, union wage growth .43%. The state-mandated retirement structure has eight rates; the most common, Basic/MIP with Health Care Premium Subsidy, is 28.21% through September 30, 2021 and a projected 28.23% from October 1, 2021, the blended budgeting rate. The MPSERS UAAL stabilization rate rises from 14.51% to 15.05%. FICA is 7.65%, with Social Security at 6.2% on wages to $142,800 for calendar year 2021. Health care "hard cap" limits for plan years beginning after 1/1/21 are family $19,210.66, individual plus one $14,730.96, single $7,043.89, projected to $19,844.61, $15,217.08 and $7,276.34 assuming 3.3% medical CPI growth; employees contribute approximately 13% on average. Dental and vision are self-funded; workers' compensation runs through the SET-SEG Self-Insurers pool.

**Subsidies and initiatives.** Financial subsidies for cooperative services total $1,551,950: Illuminate DnA $718,300, Xello career cruising software $257,000, Nepris $192,500, Atlas Rubicon $170,000, Discovery Education Streaming $156,000, PowerSchool BusinessPlus per-pupil subsidy $27,400, CDX Automotive $15,000, Meltwater $6,750, Student Achievement Media $5,000, TV Eyes $2,400, Sprout Social $1,600. Oakland Schools is providing up to $5 million for Literacy Essentials Oakland, a five-year project launched in 2019-20, and an estimated $2 million for learning-loss programs — the Oakland Youth Innovation Lab, Design Studio, tutoring, and OSTC supplemental instruction. Other flagged commitments include a $13.6 million special education center program renovation and the STEMi mobile STEM classroom. Oakland Schools received no ESSER, Governor's Emergency Education Relief or Coronavirus Relief Fund money and will not receive ESSER II; COVID expenditures are funded with tax revenues and state aid. Fee-based programs: VLAC K-8 projected at 295 FTE at $6,450 resident / $6,650 non-resident; VLAC 9-12 at 30 FTE, $6,700 / $6,900; the Accelerated College Experience at an estimated 180 students, $4,900 per pupil — none increased from 2020-21.

**Cost allocation.** Costs are spread across the three major funds using a general allocation of 50% GEF / 25% SEF / 25% CFEF, an FTE-based activity method at 24/24/52, space utilization at 50/24/26, transportation miles at 73/25/2, and a property-tax millage split of 6% / 75.5% / 18.5%. **Capital and debt.** The 5-Year Capital Outlay Plan received first reading March 16, 2021; FY21–FY26 projected needs total $34,351,500 against $15,950,000 of net transfers, leaving an estimated 6/30/2026 surplus of $3,428,300; the FY2022 need is $5,036,500. Debt service expenditures are $975,000 principal redemption and $2,045,400 interest, $3,020,400 total.

**Governance and statute.** Board policies 3050 (budget preparation), 3100 (annual operating budget and amendments), 3150 (fund balance) and 3170 (budget transfer authority) govern the process; changes flow through budget amendments at least three times each fiscal year, and inter-fund transfers require prior Board approval. The GEF and Career Focused Education Fund unassigned/restricted balance targets rise .5% each year from 5%–10% in FY 2017-18 to 7.5%–12.5% in fiscal year 2022-23. Compliance obligations cited: the General Property Tax Act, PA 206 of 1893 (MCL 211.24e); the Uniform Budgeting and Accounting Act, PA 2 of 1968; the Revised School Code, PA 451 of 1976 (MCL 380.624 and MCL 380.684); and the Michigan School Accounting Manual, Bulletin 1022. The proposed budget must go to each constituent district board by May 1 and be adopted no later than June 30. County context includes the Oakland80 goal of 80% of adults holding a post-secondary credential by 2030 and emerging-sector investment of over $5.4 billion with almost 55,000 jobs created and over 40,300 retained as of December 2020.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**What it is**
A memorandum from the law firm Collins & Blaha, P.C., dated January 26, 2021, addressed to the International Academy (IA) Governing Body c/o Dr. Richard M. Machesky, Superintendent, Troy School District, authored by Gary J. Collins, Esq. and John C. Kava, Esq., on the subject "Requested Consortium Agreement Amendments." It was included in the Troy Board of Education packet for February 23, 2021.

**Background**
Bloomfield Hills Schools sent a proposed International Academy Consortium Agreement Amendment to the Governing Body on November 24, 2020. Bloomfield's Board of Education did not approve the Consortium Agreement that the other IA districts approved in the summer of 2020, but Bloomfield has continued to participate in the IA Consortium. Bloomfield had earlier raised concerns about the 2020 Agreement's governance structure and other provisions, including employment of the principal. Counsel report that the latest proposal omits most of those earlier issues and focuses on clean-up and clarification, and that the amendments can be agreed upon so the Consortium can move forward with all current member districts.

**The six substantive amendments described**
1. Clarify in the definition of "Academy" that the Consortium operates at more than one campus.
2. Amend Article III, Section 3(A) on admission of new participants so that, in addition to Governing Body approval, the Superintendent of the Fiscal Agent for the campus the new participant will attend must vote in the affirmative; the approval must also specify the number of Shares allotted.
3. Amend Article IV, Section 1(B)(1) to list overhead costs the Governing Body may allocate to each campus, including IB license fees, legal fees and expenses, and the cost of employing the Principal and other administrators shared by all three campuses, including salaries, benefits, and insurance premiums.
4. Amend Article IV, Section 1(C) to remove the reference to a Superintendent's "designee," so that Superintendents themselves must act.
5. Amend Article IV, Section 1(G)(3) so that discipline resulting in a suspension longer than ten days must be referred to the student's district of residence, which provides due process.
6. Update the Appendices, including the list of Consortium participants and the billing and payment provisions of Appendix B, which counsel say business managers should review.

**Exhibit A — redlined First Amendment**
The draft First Amendment to the Amended and Restated International Academy Consortium Agreement names Bloomfield Hills Schools, Troy School District, and Huron Valley Schools as Fiscal Agents, and Appendix D assigns IA OKMA Campus to Bloomfield Hills Schools, IA West to Huron Valley School District, and IA East to Troy School District. It restates paragraphs in Articles II, III, IV and VI, requires all blanks and Appendices A, B and C to be completed before execution, and provides that the First Amendment controls in the event of conflict with the Agreement.

**Exhibit B — model resolution**
A blank resolution for each Participating District's board, reciting that a majority of IA Participating School Districts approved an amended governance structure and Consortium Agreement effective July 1, 2020, that Section X, Paragraph 5 permits amendment by written instrument executed by a majority of the Participating districts, approving the amended Agreement and authorizing the District's Superintendent to execute it, with an Open Meetings Act (Act 267, Public Acts of 1976) certification.

A memorandum on the letterhead of COLLINS & BLAHA, P.C., dated January 26, 2021, from Gary J. Collins, Esq. and John C. Kava, Esq. to the International Academy Governing Body, c/o Dr. Richard M. Machesky, Superintendent, Troy School District, captioned "Re: Requested Consortium Agreement Amendments." The memo, with two attached exhibits, was carried in the Troy School District Board of Education packet for the February 23, 2021 meeting. Document control numbers appearing in the filing include 4819-1377-8905 v. 1 (the memorandum and Exhibit B cover), 4850-6138-0821 v. 1 and 21974\390020\261132652.v2 (Exhibit A), and 4830-5626-7993 v. 1 (Exhibit B resolution).

BACKGROUND. Bloomfield Hills Schools ("Bloomfield") sent a proposed International Academy Consortium Agreement Amendment to the Governing Body on November 24, 2020. Counsel reviewed the proposal and discussed it with Bloomfield's legal counsel, and it is counsel's understanding that Governing Body members had the opportunity to speak with the Participating School Districts' superintendents to explain the request. The memorandum is framed as an update that the Governing Body can share with the Consortium Participating Districts; Exhibit A is a redlined version of the proposed amendment and Exhibit B is a draft resolution each Participating School District may use for board approval. Bloomfield's Board of Education did not approve the Consortium Agreement that the other IA school districts approved in the summer of 2020, but Bloomfield has continued to participate in the IA Consortium. Bloomfield had previously raised concerns with the governance structure of the 2020 Consortium Agreement and several other provisions, including employment of the principal. Counsel state that the latest proposal does not include many of those previously raised issues and instead focuses on clean-up and clarification, and that the amendments are items the IA Consortium members can agree upon so the Consortium can move forward with all districts currently in it.

THE SIX SUBSTANTIVE AMENDMENTS SUMMARIZED IN THE MEMO. (1) Clarify in the definition of "Academy" that the Consortium operates at more than one campus. (2) Amend the admission-of-new-participants paragraph, Article III, Section 3(A), so that in addition to Governing Body approval, the Superintendent of the Fiscal Agent for the campus at which the new participant will be located must vote in the affirmative for the Governing Body's action to be effective, and so that approval specifies the number of Shares allotted to the new participant. (3) Amend Article IV, Section 1(B)(1), on the Governing Body's powers, to include a more detailed list of overhead costs the Governing Body can allocate to each campus, including IB license fees, legal fees and expenses, and costs to employ the Principal and other administrators shared by all three campuses, including salaries, benefits, and insurance premiums. (4) Amend Article IV, Section 1(C) to remove the reference to the Superintendent's "designee," the substance being that Superintendents must be the individuals to act rather than designees who do not regularly attend meetings. (5) Amend Article IV, Section 1(G)(3) to state clearly that disciplinary action resulting in a suspension longer than ten days must be referred to the student's district of residence, which shall provide due process. (6) A statement that the Appendices must be updated, including the list of IA Consortium participants and the operation of payments and billing under Appendix B, with counsel advising that business managers review Appendix B.

EXHIBIT A — FIRST AMENDMENT TO AMENDED AND RESTATED INTERNATIONAL ACADEMY CONSORTIUM AGREEMENT. The redlined instrument is drafted to be entered into as of a blank Effective Date in 2020 and attached to the Amended and Restated Agreement, between and among the Boards of Education of the school districts listed in Appendix A. Recitals note the Amended and Restated Agreement was ratified by a blank number of school districts and that additional districts desire to ratify with the First Amendment's modifications. Amended and restated provisions include: Article II Definitions Paragraph A, "ACADEMY" — the International Academy operated by the Consortium at one or more Campuses; Article II Definitions Paragraph G, "FISCAL AGENT" — Bloomfield Hills Schools District, Troy School District, and Huron Valley Schools serve as Fiscal Agents for all Consortium Programming and services at their respective Campuses per Appendix D; Article III, Section 3(A) Admission of New Participants — a Michigan school district may be admitted by Governing Body action, but the Superintendent of the Fiscal Agent for the Campus the new Participating District intends to send its students must vote affirmatively for that action to be effective, the decision must then be ratified by a majority of the Participating Districts, and the approval must specify the number of Shares and the Campus, with the new district contributing to operating, capital outlay and start-up costs on a pro-rata basis depending on Shares and admission date; Article III, Section 3(B) Limited Effects of Withdrawal — no resignation or withdrawal by a Participant or Fiscal Agent annuls the Agreement, terminates the Consortium, or relieves the withdrawing party of its obligations unless all Participants agree otherwise.

Article IV, Section 1(B)(1), fifth paragraph, limits the Governing Body's powers to: (i) allocation of Consortium overhead expenses to each Campus Program, including dues and fees payable to the International Baccalaureate organization including the cost of the IB license, administrative expenses incurred on behalf of all three Campus Programs, other expenses incurred on behalf of more than one Campus Program including legal fees and expenses for legal advice or representation, and costs of employing the Academy's Principal, Coordinator(s) or other administrators shared by all three Campuses including salaries, benefits and liability/professional insurance premiums; (ii) monitoring and ensuring compliance with IB standards and certification requirements; (iii) management of the process of electing at-large members to the Governing Body; (iv) oversight of the withdrawal and dissolution processes; and (v) any other express power granted in the Agreement, with all other powers exercised by the Fiscal Agents. Article IV, Section 1(C) names Bloomfield Hills Schools, Troy School District, and Huron Valley Schools as the Consortium's Fiscal Agents, each Fiscal Agent's board adopting a resolution appointing its Superintendent as District representative; Bloomfield Hills Schools serves the OKMA Campus, Troy School District the Troy East Campus, and Huron Valley Schools the West Campus.

Article IV, Section 1(G)(3) Discipline provides that each Campus shall have a Student Code of Conduct set by its Fiscal Agent; students are subject to the Campus's code while in attendance; the building principal or other designated administrator of that Campus may discipline students; where a disciplinary action results in suspension from school for more than ten (10) days the building principal shall advise the student's district of residence, which shall provide due process and take appropriate action; and the Fiscal Agent for the Campus retains authority to exclude a student from its Campus, after which the student's School District of residence determines the admittance, suspension, or expulsion process. Article VI, Section 2 provides that the Academy Principal shall be employed by one of the Fiscal Agents, shall be the Academy Principal for all Consortium Campuses, and shall be evaluated by the employing Fiscal Agent, which may seek evaluation input from the other Fiscal Agents; the job description is approved and may be modified by the employing Fiscal Agent with input from the others.

Housekeeping items in Exhibit A: signature lines must be updated to refer only to school districts that authorized the amendment by board resolution before execution; Appendix A's "[UPDATE MEMBER DISTRICTS]" reference must be replaced with the actual list of Participating Districts; Appendix B must state that the Consortium and each Campus operate under the Uniform Budgeting and Accounting Act, Public Act No. 2 of 1968, the State School Aid Act and other state financial laws, and counsel flag that the billing and payment schedule cross-reference is defective — Appendix B cites Article IV, Section 3, which concerns Transfer of Shares, while counsel believe the proper citations may be Article II, Section 2(A)(2) and Article V, Section 1(E), the latter applying only to the OKMA Campus, and further note it is unclear what start-up costs mean for a Consortium that has been running for years; Appendix C-3 blanks must be filled in and the Letters of Agreement referenced in Appendix C, Article VI, Section 1(D) must actually be attached. Appendix D sets the Campus/Fiscal Agent pairs: IA OKMA Campus — Bloomfield Hills Schools; IA West — Huron Valley School District; IA East — Troy School District. Section B ratifies and reaffirms the Agreement except as modified, with the First Amendment controlling in the event of conflict.

EXHIBIT B — MODEL BOARD RESOLUTION. A fill-in-the-blank "Resolution Regarding International Academy Agreement" for a named school district and county in the State of Michigan, to be adopted at a regular meeting in 2021, with blanks for the presiding officer, members present and absent, and the mover and supporter. Recitals state that the District is a Participating District in the International Academy and a party to the Consortium Agreement; that a majority of IA Participating School Districts approved an amended governance structure and Consortium Agreement effective July 1, 2020; that the Governing Body received a proposed amendment from a Participating School District, reviewed it, consulted legal counsel, and circulated it with a memo; that Section X, Paragraph 5 of the Consortium Agreement permits amendment only by written instrument executed by a majority of the Participating districts; and that the Board deems approval in the District's best interests. The resolution approves the proposed Amended Consortium Agreement attached as Exhibit A, authorizes the District's Superintendent to execute it, and rescinds conflicting resolutions. A secretary's certification follows, attesting compliance with the Open Meetings Act, being Act 267, Public Acts of 1976.

Observations at the seven-month mark of fiscal 2020-21: the winter property tax settlement has pushed local revenue collection well ahead of the calendar in both the General Fund and the debt service funds, producing a large positive General Fund operating result to date and an even larger debt service surplus because no bond principal is due until spring. State aid remains the slowest revenue category. On the spending side, Operations/Maintenance and Instructional Staff are the fastest-moving support-service categories, while Pupil Transportation continues to run far behind budget. Among special revenue funds, the Facilities Rental Fund is essentially without revenue for the year, the Community Service Fund and Troy Preschool Fund carry substantial unbudgeted federal and state receipts, and the Troy Career Center Fund's revenues and expenditures are reported as identical.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Recognition item 2.B. on the Troy School District Board of Education agenda for October 19, 2021, commending seventy-four Troy students named 2022 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists. The narrative notes that more than one million students nationwide from some 21,000 high schools entered the National Merit Scholarship Program, yet only 16,000 seniors are selected as semifinalists. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Agenda item**
Item 2.B. under Recognition, dated 10.19.21, on the Troy School District Board of Education agenda: "2022 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists." The recommendation is to adopt the accompanying resolution, with blank lines for the moving and supporting members and for recording the YES and NO tallies.

**Scale of the program**
More than one million students nationwide, from some 21,000 high schools, entered the National Merit Scholarship Program; only 16,000 of those seniors are selected to be semifinalists. Troy School District had seventy-four semifinalists, described in the item as "a remarkable number of semifinalists, and a tribute to the staff and parents of the Troy School District."

**Qualification criteria as stated in the resolution**
Student achievement is honored through the National Merit Scholarship semifinalist and finalist recognition programs. Three items are proposed: a notice-period change to the special meetings provision of Section 1002/1000.02 for compliance with Michigan's Open Meetings Act, 15.261, et seq.; a rewritten Student Bullying subpolicy under Policy 2006/2000.06 to comply with MCL 380.1310b; and a new "Animals on District Property" policy in the 8000 section prompted by increased requests for therapy and service animals.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Memorandum details**
From the Business Office at 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098; phone 248.823.4022, fax 248.823.4013. TO: Dr. Rich Machesky, Superintendent of Schools. FROM: Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services. CC: Judy Holmes. RE: Policy Update Considerations for Board of Education. DATE: Thursday, November 4, 2021. Administration and the Policy Committee recommend the listed policy additions and changes be approved by the Board of Education.

**Section 1002/1000.02 - Special Meetings**
Recommended for compliance with Michigan's Open Meetings Act, 15.261, et seq. The revised provision reads that special meetings of the Board may be called by the President or any three (3) Board members by providing "not less than 2418 hours' notice" to all Board members; the extracted text runs the struck-through existing figure and the underlined replacement figure together at that point. The notice to Board members and the public shall be consistent in manner and form with the requirements of the OMA.

**Student Bullying subpolicy - Policy 2006/2000.06**
Revised to comply with MCL 380.1310b. The Board prohibits bullying "at school" as defined in the policy, as well as off-campus conduct that could likely lead to a material or substantial disruption of the school learning environment. The policy protects all students regardless of the subject matter or motivation for the behavior, prohibits retaliation and false accusations, and keeps the identity of a reporter confidential. Key structural elements:

| Element | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Responsible School Official | The principal of each school building implements the policy for that building |
| Publication | Superintendent revises the Student Code of Conduct and posts the policy on the District website |
| Reporting | Superintendent reports annually to the Board all verified incidents of bullying and consequences imposed |
| Administrative regulations | Procedures for reporting, prompt investigation by the building principal or designee, parent/guardian notification of both claimed victim and alleged perpetrator, confidentiality of reporters, documentation of incidents, and the annual Board report |

Definitions cover "bullying" (written, verbal, physical, or electronic acts, including cyberbullying, that substantially interfere with educational opportunities, place a student in reasonable fear of physical harm or cause substantial emotional distress, have a substantial detrimental effect on physical or mental health, or substantially disrupt school operations), with physical, verbal, and psychological examples; "at school" (classroom, school premises, school bus or other school-related vehicle, and school-sponsored activities on or off premises, including off-premises use of a telecommunications access device or service provider owned or controlled by the District); and "cyberbullying" with four enumerated clauses (i) through (iv). Further sections address Accountability and Retaliation, and state that intentionally false reports may result in disciplinary action.

**New policy - Animals on District Property (8000 section)**
Proposed in response to increased requests for use of therapy and service animals. The draft recognizes that animals are present on District property for many reasons, are commonly utilized by teachers during classroom presentations, and are often housed in classrooms and other campus locations; and that employees, students, parents, vendors, and other members of the public may be accompanied at school by a service or therapy animal in accordance with Federal and State law and the policy. The policy applies to all animals on District property, including service animals, and directs the Superintendent to promulgate consistent administrative regulations.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Troy School District Business Office memorandum, agenda item 5.D. for the November 16, 2021 Board of Education meeting, transmitting policy update considerations.

**Header.** Business Office, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098; Phone 248.823.4022; Fax 248.823.4013. TO: Dr. Rich Machesky, Superintendent of Schools. FROM: Rick West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services. CC: Judy Holmes. RE: Policy Update Considerations for Board of Education. DATE: Thursday, November 4, 2021. Opening line: "Administration and the Policy Committee recommend the following policy additions/changes be approved by the Board of Education."

**Section 1002/1000.02, Special Meetings.** Recommended "to ensure compliance with Michigan's Open Meetings Act, 15.261, et seq." The provision as presented reads: "Special meetings of the Board may be called by the President or any three (3) Board members by providing not less than 2418 hours' notice to all Board members. The notice to Board members and the public shall be consistent in manner and form with the requirements of the OMA." The memo marks its revisions by underlining; extraction has flattened the strikethrough and underline formatting, leaving the old and new notice-period figures printed adjacent to one another as "2418 hours."

**Student Bullying subpolicy, typically found under Policy 2006/2000.06.** Presented as underlined changes to comply with MCL 380.1310b.

Preamble: The Board recognizes that bullying and cyberbullying significantly interfere with the learning process. Through this Policy, the Board prohibits bullying "at school," as defined below, as well as off-campus conduct that could likely lead to a material or substantial disruption of the school learning environment for one or more students. The Policy is intended to protect all students from bullying, regardless of the subject matter or motivation for the behavior. It also prohibits retaliation or false accusations against a target of bullying, a witness, or another person with reliable information about an act of bullying. The identity of an individual who reports an act of bullying shall remain confidential. The Superintendent will promulgate administrative regulations to implement the policy.

Implementation. Responsible School Official: the principal of each school building is responsible for implementing this Policy for the school to which he or she is assigned. Publication: the Superintendent shall revise the District's Student Code of Conduct, consistent with this Policy, to specifically prohibit bullying and cyberbullying, and is directed to post this Policy on the District's website. Reporting: the Superintendent shall report to the Board of Education, on an annual basis, all verified incidents of bullying, and the resulting consequences that were imposed.

Administrative Regulations. The Superintendent shall promulgate regulations including: a procedure for an individual to report an act of bullying; a procedure for the prompt investigation of a report of an act of bullying by the building principal or his/her designee; a procedure for providing notification to the parent or guardian of both the claimed victim of an act of bullying and the parent or guardian of the alleged perpetrator; a procedure to protect the confidentiality of a person making a report of bullying; a procedure for documenting any prohibited bullying incident that is reported; and the procedure for the Superintendent's annual report to the Board of all verified incidents of bullying and the consequences imposed.

Definitions. "Bullying" means any written, verbal or physical act, or any electronic communication, including but not limited to cyberbullying, that is intended or that a reasonable person would know is likely to harm one or more District students, either directly or indirectly, by substantially interfering with educational opportunities, benefits or programs; adversely affecting a student's ability to participate in or benefit from educational programs or activities by placing a student in reasonable fear of physical harm or by causing substantial emotional distress; having an actual and substantial detrimental effect on a student's physical or mental health; or causing substantial disruption in, or substantial interference with, the orderly operation of the school. Examples listed are Physical (hitting, kicking, spitting, pushing, pulling; taking and/or damaging a person's belongings; extorting money; blocking or impeding student movement; unwelcome physical contact; punching, shoving, poking, choking, pulling hair, beating, biting, throwing objects), Verbal (taunting, malicious teasing, insulting, hurtful name-calling, making threats, gossiping), and Psychological (spreading rumors, manipulating social relationships, coercion, engaging in social exclusion/shunning, extortion or intimidation).

"At school" means in a classroom, anywhere else on school premises, on a school bus or other school-related vehicle, and at a school-sponsored activity or event, whether or not held on school premises; it includes the off-premises use of a telecommunications access device or telecommunications service provider if the device or service provider is owned by or under the control of the District.

"Cyberbullying" means any electronic communication that is intended or that a reasonable person would know is likely to harm one or more pupils either directly or indirectly by: (i) substantially interfering with educational opportunities, benefits or programs; (ii) adversely affecting a student's ability to participate in or benefit from educational programs or activities by placing a student in reasonable fear of physical harm or by causing substantial emotional distress; (iii) having an actual and substantial detrimental effect on a student's physical or mental health; or (iv) causing substantial disruption in, or substantial interference with, the orderly operation of the school.

Accountability. Each student in the School District is accountable for his/her own behavior, based on age-appropriate expectations. The Board believes standards for student behavior must be set cooperatively through interaction among students, parents/guardians, staff, and community members, producing an atmosphere that encourages students to grow in self-discipline. Respect for all students is part of a safe and healthy learning environment, demonstrated through the give-and-take of friendships, group cooperation, social interaction, compromise, and acceptance of differences among other students and staff.

Retaliation. Retaliation against a target of bullying, a witness, another person with reliable information about an act of bullying, or any person who reports, is thought to have reported, files a complaint, or otherwise participates in an investigation or inquiry concerning allegations of bullying is prohibited and will not be tolerated. Such retaliation is a serious violation of Board policy independent of whether a complaint is found to have been substantiated, and suspected reprisal or retaliation should be reported in the same manner as bullying. Making intentionally false reports about bullying for the purpose of getting someone in trouble is similarly prohibited. Retaliation and intentionally false reports may result in disciplinary action. The Superintendent is directed to implement the Policy and is authorized to promulgate such administrative regulations as may be deemed necessary.

**Animals on District Property, proposed for the 8000 section of the policy manual.** Introduced with the observation that requests for use of therapy and service animals have increased. Proposed text: "The Board of Education recognizes that there are many occasions when animals are present on District property and many reasons for those animals' presence. Animals are commonly utilized by teachers during classroom presentations and are often housed in classrooms and other locations on campus. Additionally, employees, students, parents, vendors, and other members of the public may be accompanied at school by a service or therapy animal in accordance with Federal and State law and this policy. This policy applies to all animals on District property, including service animals. The Superintendent will promulgate administrative regulations consistent with this policy."

The memorandum contains no dollar amounts, contract parties, vote records, or millage figures; it is a policy transmittal only.

**Budget versus actual, General Fund**
Original budgeted revenue of $163,603,984 was amended to $170,565,175 against actual revenue of $170,116,893; original budgeted expenditures of $166,301,381 were amended to $173,657,294 against actual expenditures of $172,507,660. Budgeted revenue was increased $7.0 million, with federal revenue increased $5.0 million for ESSER III and Section 11t American Rescue Plan funding, plus $1.2 million of transfers in from the Community Service and Troy School District Preschool funds.

**Capital assets and debt**
Total capital assets were $400,750,723 less accumulated depreciation and amortization of $201,792,959, or $198,957,764 net. Depreciation and amortization expense was $9,725,109. Construction commitments totaled $8,090,089 spent to date with $8,836,206 remaining. General obligation bonds outstanding were $116,165,000 plus $6,970,844 of unamortized premium; total long-term debt was $131,831,910, of which $17,430,446 is due within one year. The bond rating is AA/Stable, affirmed by Standard & Poor's in May 2021.

**Pension and OPEB (MPSERS)**
Net pension liability $210,869,230 and net OPEB liability $13,509,781, both measured as of September 30, 2021. Pension expense was $25,126,063 and OPEB recovery was $7,228,236. Required and actual contributions were $31,043,947 for pension and $7,221,409 for OPEB.

**Enrollment and outlook**
Spring 2022 enrollment was 12,519 students, roughly 600 fewer than the district was funded for in 2020, equating to approximately $6 million less annual operational revenue. The state foundation allowance rises by $450 to $9,880 per pupil for 2022-2023. A $555 million bond proposal goes to voters on November 8, 2022; if passed, the debt millage is expected to increase by 2.0 mills.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A four-item slate of proposed 2023 bylaw amendments for the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), laid out in side-by-side "Currently Reads" and "Would Read" columns with a proposed change and rationale for each. The amendments touch Article VI (Election of Board of Directors), Article IX (Committees, two separate items in Section 4), and Article XI (Fiduciary and Financial Responsibilities). The most substantive change would let the OCSBA Board call a mid-year special election to increase the number of Directors, allowing seats to be restored twice per year rather than only once.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**What it is**
The 2023 OCSBA Bylaw Amendments packet, distributed to member districts ahead of the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of February 14, 2023. Four amendments are presented in a two-column "Currently Reads" / "Would Read" format, each followed by a stated proposed change and rationale. New language is described as shown in blue.

**Amendment 1 - Article VI, Election of Board of Directors, Section 1: Number of Directors**
Existing text: the Board of Directors shall consist of an odd number of Directors, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9 members; the Board has discretion to set the number to best meet the needs of the Association; it shall consider a change whenever an election produces less candidates than open seats and prior to seeking candidates to fill a vacancy under Section 6; the Secretary shall promptly communicate any change to all Members; any decrease is accomplished by attrition, which may result in an eight member Board for up to one year until the next election; an increase is accomplished by election as outlined in Section 4.
Proposed change: add one sentence at the end - "In addition, the Board may call for a mid-year special election to increase the number of Directors."
Rationale: allows the Board to restore seats twice per year if necessary, rather than only once per year as in Section 4.

**Amendment 2 - Article IX, Committees, Section 4: Legislative Priorities**
Existing text: the Government Relations Committee will review/revise their Legislative Priorities annually, and revised Legislative Priorities will be submitted to the Board of Directors for approval by June 15th; once approved, they are provided to the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee and Member School Districts.
Proposed change: remove "by June 15th".
Rationale: the process needs to be moved up so that legislative priorities are adopted by the GRC in the fall (Sept/Oct), sent to the Board of Directors in October and then to Member Districts for voting, with consideration given to ending the voting period by the start of the common calendar's school break.

**Amendment 3 - Article IX, Committees, Section 4: Committee Membership/Leadership**
Existing text: committee members are appointed by the Board of Directors annually, may be reappointed for additional terms, and elect a Committee Chairperson at the first committee meeting after appointment.
Proposed change: add one sentence - "The Government Relations Committee Chairperson shall be a member of the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee."
Rationale: the Government Relations Committee (GRC) chair is not necessarily a member of the Board of Directors, and GRC Chair involvement is important to be sure the GRC's intent is reflected in resolutions.

**Amendment 4 - Article XI, Fiduciary and Financial Responsibilities, Section 2: Financial Reports**
Item (a) is unchanged: reports shall be completed on a timely basis and distributed to all Board members on a quarterly basis or upon request. Item (b) currently requires the Treasurer to present for approval by the Board of Directors an annual budget (July 1 to June 30) by June 30th along with an annual actual income and expense report by August 30th following the end of the fiscal year. It would be split into two numbered obligations: (1) no later than the June Board of Directors meeting, a budget for the upcoming fiscal year (July 1 to June 30); and (2) no later than August 30th, the end of year revenue and expense reports for the immediately preceding fiscal year.
Rationale: the current wording is confusing because the budget and the end of year reports are 2 separate documents.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The 2023 OCSBA Bylaw Amendments packet sets out four proposed changes to the bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association, presented to the Troy School District Board of Education for the meeting of February 14, 2023. The document is formatted as a four-page comparison table, with each amendment shown twice - once under a "Currently Reads" heading and once under a "Would Read" heading - followed by a plain-language statement of the proposed change and the rationale behind it. New language is noted as being shown in blue in the original.

FIRST AMENDMENT: ARTICLE VI, ELECTION OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS, SECTION 1, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS. The existing section provides that the Board of Directors shall consist of an odd number of Directors, with no fewer than 7 nor more than 9 members, and that the Board of Directors shall have the discretion to determine the number of Directors to best meet the needs of the Association. The Board is directed to consider such a change whenever an election produces less candidates than open seats, and prior to seeking candidates to fill a vacancy under Section 6. The Secretary shall promptly communicate any change to the number of Directors to all Members. Any decrease in the number of Directors shall be accomplished by attrition, which may result in an eight member Board for up to one year, until the next election, while an increase in the number of Directors shall be accomplished by election, as outlined in Section 4. The proposed change adds a single sentence at the end of the section: "In addition, the Board may call for a mid-year special election to increase the number of Directors." The rationale given is that this allows the Board to restore seats twice per year if necessary, rather than only once per year as provided in Section 4.

SECOND AMENDMENT: ARTICLE IX, COMMITTEES, SECTION 4, LEGISLATIVE PRIORITIES. As currently written, the section states that the Government Relations Committee will review and revise their Legislative Priorities annually, that revised Legislative Priorities will be submitted to the Board of Directors for approval by June 15th, and that once approved by the Board, Legislative Priorities will be provided to the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee and Member School Districts. The proposed change is to remove the phrase "by June 15th," leaving the requirement that revised priorities be submitted to the Board of Directors for approval without a fixed deadline. The rationale states that the process needs to be moved up so that legislative priorities are adopted by the Government Relations Committee in the fall (September or October), sent to the Board of Directors in October, and then sent to Member Districts for voting, with the suggestion that the voting period end by the start of the common calendar's school break.

THIRD AMENDMENT: ARTICLE IX, COMMITTEES, SECTION 4, COMMITTEE MEMBERSHIP/LEADERSHIP. The current text provides that committee members will be appointed by the Board of Directors annually, that committee members may be reappointed for additional terms, and that the appointed committee members will elect a Committee Chairperson at the first committee meeting after appointment. The proposed change adds one sentence at the end of the paragraph: "The Government Relations Committee Chairperson shall be a member of the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee." The rationale explains that the Government Relations Committee (GRC) chair is not necessarily a member of the Board of Directors, and that GRC Chair involvement is important to be sure that the GRC's intent is reflected in resolutions.

FOURTH AMENDMENT: ARTICLE XI, FIDUCIARY AND FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITIES, SECTION 2, FINANCIAL REPORTS. The section opens with the requirement that the Treasurer shall maintain all financial statements, reports, and budgets, and this framing language is unchanged. Subsection (a) is also unchanged in both columns: reports shall be completed on a timely basis and distributed to all Board members on a quarterly basis or upon request. Subsection (b) currently requires that the Treasurer shall present for approval by the Board of Directors an annual budget covering July 1 to June 30 by June 30th, along with an annual actual income and expense report by August 30th following the end of the fiscal year. Under the proposed revision, subsection (b) would instead read that the Treasurer shall present for approval by the Board of Directors: (1) no later than the June Board of Directors meeting, a budget for the upcoming fiscal year (July 1 to June 30); and (2) no later than August 30th, the end of year revenue and expense reports for the immediately preceding fiscal year. The stated proposed change is to separate and clarify item (b), and the rationale is that the provision is confusing as written because the budget and the end of year reports are 2 separate documents.

Read together, the four amendments address governance flexibility in restoring vacant Director seats, the calendar for adopting and distributing OCSBA legislative priorities, the cross-membership of the Government Relations Committee Chairperson on the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee, and the drafting clarity of the Treasurer's reporting obligations. None of the amendments changes the permissible size range of the Board of Directors, which remains an odd number between 7 and 9 members, and none alters the quarterly financial reporting requirement in Article XI, Section 2(a).
