**What it is**
The 2023 OCSBA Bylaw Amendments, supplied in Word format for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of February 14, 2023. Content matches the PDF version in the same packet: four amendments, each shown in a "Currently Reads" column and a "Would Read" column, followed by the proposed change and rationale. Added language is described as shown in blue.

**Article VI - Election of Board of Directors, Section 1: Number of Directors**
The unchanged body of the section keeps the Board of Directors at an odd number of Directors, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9 members, with Board discretion to set the number; consideration of a change whenever an election produces less candidates than open seats and before seeking candidates to fill a vacancy under Section 6; prompt communication of any change by the Secretary to all Members; decrease by attrition, which may result in an eight member Board for up to one year until the next election; and increase by election as outlined in Section 4.
Proposed change: add one sentence - "In addition, the Board may call for a mid-year special election to increase the number of Directors."
Rationale: allows the Board to restore seats twice per year if necessary, rather than only once per year as in Section 4.

**Article IX - Committees, Section 4: Legislative Priorities**
Current text has the Government Relations Committee review/revise Legislative Priorities annually, with revised priorities submitted to the Board of Directors for approval by June 15th and then provided to the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee and Member School Districts.
Proposed change: remove "by June 15th".
Rationale: the process needs to be moved up so priorities are adopted by the GRC in the fall (Sept/Oct), sent to the Board of Directors in October and then to Member Districts for voting, with consideration of ending the voting period by the start of the common calendar's school break.

**Article IX - Committees, Section 4: Committee Membership/Leadership**
Current text has committee members appointed annually by the Board of Directors, eligible for reappointment, electing a Committee Chairperson at the first committee meeting after appointment.
Proposed change: add one sentence - "The Government Relations Committee Chairperson shall be a member of the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee."
Rationale: the GRC chair is not necessarily a member of the Board of Directors, and GRC Chair involvement is important to be sure the GRC's intent is reflected in resolutions.

Proposed change: separate and clarify item (b), which would read that the Treasurer shall present for approval by the Board of Directors: 1. no later than the June Board of Directors meeting, a budget for the upcoming fiscal year (July 1 to June 30); 2. no later than August 30th, the end of year revenue and expense reports for the immediately preceding fiscal year.
Rationale: the provision is confusing as written because the budget and end of year reports are 2 separate documents.

This is the Word-format copy of the 2023 OCSBA Bylaw Amendments distributed with the Troy School District Board of Education agenda for February 14, 2023. It carries the same four proposed amendments to the bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association as the PDF copy in the same packet, but with cleaner paragraph formatting; each amendment appears first under "Currently Reads" and then under "Would Read," followed by a stated proposed change and rationale, with new language indicated as shown in blue.

ARTICLE VI, ELECTION OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS, SECTION 1, NUMBER OF DIRECTORS. The section as it stands provides that the Board of Directors shall consist of an odd number of Directors, with no fewer than 7 nor more than 9 members, and that the Board of Directors shall have the discretion to determine the number of Directors to best meet the needs of the Association. The Board shall consider such a change whenever an election produces less candidates than open seats, and prior to seeking candidates to fill a vacancy under Section 6. The Secretary shall promptly communicate any change to the number of Directors to all Members. Any decrease in the number of Directors shall be accomplished by attrition, which may result in an eight member Board for up to one year, until the next election. An increase in the number of Directors shall be accomplished by election, as outlined in Section 4. The proposed version keeps all of that language and appends: "In addition, the Board may call for a mid-year special election to increase the number of Directors." The rationale is that this allows the Board to restore seats twice per year if necessary, rather than only once per year as in Section 4.

ARTICLE IX, COMMITTEES, SECTION 4, LEGISLATIVE PRIORITIES. The existing provision states that the Government Relations Committee will review/revise their Legislative Priorities annually; that revised Legislative priorities will be submitted to the Board of Directors for approval by June 15th; and that once approved by the Board, Legislative Priorities will be provided to the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee and Member School Districts. The revised version strikes the deadline, so that revised Legislative priorities will simply be submitted to the Board of Directors for approval. The stated proposed change is to remove "by June 15th," and the rationale is that this process needs to be moved up so that legislative priorities are adopted by the GRC in the fall (Sept/Oct), sent to the Board of Directors in October and then to Member Districts for voting, with the parenthetical suggestion of considering having the voting period end by the start of the common calendar's school break.

ARTICLE IX, COMMITTEES, SECTION 4, COMMITTEE MEMBERSHIP/LEADERSHIP. The existing paragraph provides that committee members will be appointed by the Board of Directors annually, that committee members may be reappointed for additional terms, and that the appointed committee members will elect a Committee Chairperson at the first committee meeting after appointment. The revision appends one sentence: "The Government Relations Committee Chairperson shall be a member of the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee." The rationale explains that the Government Relations Committee (GRC) chair is not necessarily a member of the Board of Directors, and that GRC Chair involvement is important to be sure that the GRC's intent is reflected in resolutions.

ARTICLE XI, FIDUCIARY AND FINANCIAL RESPONSIBILITIES, SECTION 2, FINANCIAL REPORTS. The current text opens with the requirement that the Treasurer shall maintain all financial statements, reports, and budgets, then lists two obligations without letter labels in this Word rendering: reports shall be completed on a timely basis and distributed to all Board members on a quarterly basis or upon request; and the Treasurer shall present for approval by the Board of Directors an annual budget (July 1 to June 30) by June 30th along with an annual actual income and expense report by August 30th following the end of the fiscal year. Under the proposed language the first obligation is unchanged, while the second becomes an explicitly labeled item (b) with two numbered sub-items: "1. No later than the June Board of Directors meeting, a budget for the upcoming fiscal year (July 1 to June 30)" and "2. No later than August 30th, the end of year revenue and expense reports for the immediately preceding fiscal year." The stated proposed change is to separate and clarify item (b), and the rationale is that the provision is confusing as written because the budget and end of year reports are 2 separate documents.

The practical effect of the package is fourfold: the OCSBA Board gains a mid-year mechanism for restoring Director seats without waiting for the next annual election; the legislative-priorities calendar is freed from the June 15th deadline so that the cycle can shift to a fall adoption and a member-district voting window; the Government Relations Committee Chairperson is guaranteed a seat on the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee regardless of Board of Directors membership; and the Treasurer's two distinct annual deliverables - the forward-looking budget and the backward-looking revenue and expense reports - are separated with distinct deadlines of the June Board of Directors meeting and August 30th respectively. The size range of the Board of Directors remains an odd number between 7 and 9 members and the quarterly distribution requirement for financial reports is untouched.

**What it is**
The Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) resolutions packet circulated to member districts for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of February 14, 2023. It sets out two proposed new resolutions, one proposed amendment to a previously adopted resolution, and the full list of continuing resolutions with their adoption and amendment dates and cross-references to Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) resolution numbers.

**Proposed new resolutions for 2023**
- SCHOOL NUTRITION: OCSBA supports the expansion of the Free and Reduced Meals program to include all children, as was done during the pandemic.
- SCHOOL SAFETY: OCSBA supports that there be adequate state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe.

**Proposed amendment to a previously adopted resolution**
- SCHOOL FINANCE RESEARCH COLLABORATIVE (SFRC) [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 9/11/2021]: support for review and implementation of the SFRC recommendations, including the recommended additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure, and transportation, with the proviso that while implementing the SFRC recommendations, higher funded districts must be held harmless. Cited to MASB resolution G 11.01 and A-10.25 - 2021 amendment.

**Continuing resolutions**

| Resolution | Adopted / Amended | MASB citation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mental Health | 9/24/2019 | G 9.01; G 9.05; G 9.50 |
| Local Control | 9/24/2019 | A 10.10; A 10.55; A 12.70 |
| Evidence-Based Decision Making | 9/24/2019 | G 11.01 |
| Unfunded Mandates | 9/24/2019 | A 10.20 |
| School Aid (items A-E) | 9/24/2019 | A 10.25; A 10.55; A 10.05 |
| Accountability and Transparency | 9/24/2019 | A 6.65 (c), (d), (f) |
| Lame Duck | 9/24/2019 | - |
| Universal Preschool | 9/24/2019 | A 6.15 (c) |
| Special Education | 9/24/2019 | A 5.01; NSBA Advocacy: IDEA |
| Broadband Access and Devices | 9/11/2021 | A-10.30 - 2021 amendment |
| Teacher Shortages | 9/11/2021 | MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority |

**School Aid, in detail**
A. Oppose using School Aid Fund dollars for any other purpose than K-12 education. B. Support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students. C. Protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes. D. Specify that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education in Michigan's Constitution and oppose any attempts to create private school voucher or tax credit programs. E. Support enacting the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1, so that school districts have factual information to meet their constitutional/statutory requirement to approve a budget by June 30.

**Other content**
The Mental Health resolution adds two bullets: help staff identify potential mental health issues for students, and encourage MDE to develop a model policy for staff regarding identifying mental health issues and appropriate staff response. The Special Education resolution notes that federal legislation initially promised to provide 40 percent of the excess cost to educate students with disabilities but that appropriations have fallen short. When aligned with OCSBA legislative priorities, OCSBA also supports the National School Boards Association (NSBA) Legislative Agenda, the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Legislative Agenda, and the Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) Legislative Agenda [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]. Links are provided to MASB Resolutions at https://www.masb.org/resolutions.aspx and NSBA Advocacy: IDEA at https://www.nsba.org/Advocacy.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) resolutions packet for 2023 was circulated to member boards, including the Troy School District Board of Education, for its meeting of February 14, 2023. The document is organized into three parts: proposed new resolutions for 2023, a proposed amendment to a previously adopted resolution, and the standing body of continuing resolutions previously adopted by member school districts, each tagged with its adoption and, where applicable, amendment date, and cross-referenced to the corresponding Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) resolution numbers.

PROPOSED NEW RESOLUTIONS. Two are put forward. Under SCHOOL NUTRITION, OCSBA supports the expansion of the Free and Reduced Meals program to include all children, as was done during the pandemic. Under SCHOOL SAFETY, OCSBA supports that there be adequate state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe.

PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO A PREVIOUSLY ADOPTED RESOLUTION. The SCHOOL FINANCE RESEARCH COLLABORATIVE (SFRC) resolution, originally adopted by OCSBA on 9/24/2019 and amended on 9/11/2021, would be amended again. As presented, OCSBA supports review and implementation of the recommendations of the SFRC, including the recommended additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure, and transportation, and states that while implementing the SFRC recommendations, higher funded districts must be held harmless. The citation given is MASB resolution G 11.01 and A-10.25 - 2021 amendment. The hold-harmless language is of direct interest to a comparatively high-revenue district such as Troy.

CONTINUING RESOLUTIONS. MENTAL HEALTH [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] states that OCSBA supports increased mental health services and professionals in schools and provide adequate state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe, citing MASB Resolutions G 9.01, G 9.05 and G 9.50. Two bullets follow: help staff identify potential mental health issues for students; and encourage MDE to develop a model policy for staff regarding identifying mental health issues and appropriate staff response.

LOCAL CONTROL [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] supports local control of community-governed public schools with elected school boards, citing MASB Resolution A 10.10, A 10.55 and A 12.70.

EVIDENCE-BASED DECISION MAKING [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] states that OCSBA supports evidence-based education policy that will maximize opportunities for the highest achievement of each student, citing MASB Resolution G 11.01.

UNFUNDED MANDATES [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] provides that OCSBA opposes any state or federal legislation that results in increased costs for school districts without full funding, and also encourages the Michigan Legislature to oppose any federal laws or programs that are not fully funded thus costing the state valuable resources, citing MASB Resolution A 10.20.

SCHOOL AID [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] contains five lettered planks. A. Oppose using School Aid Fund dollars for any other purpose than K-12 education [MASB Resolution A 10.25]. B. Support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (g) and (j); A 10.55]. C. Protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (c); A 10.55]. D. Specify that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education in Michigan's Constitution and oppose any attempts to create private school voucher or tax credit programs [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (a) and A 10.05]. E. OCSBA supports enacting the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1, so that school districts have factual information to meet their constitutional/statutory requirement to approve a budget by June 30 [MASB Resolution A 10.25 (h)].

ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] states that OCSBA supports transparency and accountability for ALL school aid funds, naming community governed public school districts, charter schools, cyber schools, community colleges and public universities, citing MASB Resolution A 6.65 (c), (d), (f).

LAME DUCK [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] states that OCSBA supports lame duck parameters that will address introduction and accelerated passage of legislation after the November election.

UNIVERSAL PRESCHOOL [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] states that OCSBA supports additional new dollars to fund universal preschool for all four year old children, citing OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019 and MASB Resolution A 6.15 (c).

SPECIAL EDUCATION [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] states that OCSBA supports full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), noting that although federal legislation initially promised to provide 40 percent of the excess cost to educate students with disabilities, the appropriations have fallen short, leaving states and local school districts to make up the difference. It cites MASB Resolution A 5.01 and NSBA Advocacy: IDEA.

BROADBAND ACCESS AND DEVICES [OCSBA Adopted 9/11/2021] states that broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan, that OCSBA supports additional federal and state funding opportunities to expand affordable and reliable broadband access, and that it supports federal and state programs for the purchase of internet capable devices and software, citing MASB Resolution A-10.30 - 2021 amendment.

TEACHER SHORTAGES [OCSBA Adopted 9/11/2021] states support for statewide initiatives to address teacher shortages and retain teachers while maintaining quality teacher preparation programs, listing as possible but not exclusive initiatives incentives to enter and complete a teaching college program, incentives for teachers to remain in the classroom, and easing the process to obtain Michigan certification for teachers that are certified in other states. It cites the MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority.

ALIGNED AGENDAS. A closing section, adopted 9/24/2019, provides that when aligned with OCSBA legislative priorities, OCSBA also supports the National School Boards Association (NSBA) Legislative Agenda, the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Legislative Agenda, and the Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) Legislative Agenda.

LINKS. The packet closes with two references: MASB Resolutions at https://www.masb.org/resolutions.aspx and NSBA Advocacy: IDEA at https://www.nsba.org/Advocacy.

- SCHOOL SAFETY: OCSBA supports that there be adequate state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe.

**Proposed amendment to a previously adopted resolution**
- SCHOOL FINANCE RESEARCH COLLABORATIVE (SFRC) [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 9/11/2021]: support for review and implementation of the SFRC recommendations, including the recommended additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure, and transportation, with the proviso that while implementing the SFRC recommendations, higher funded districts must be held harmless. Cited to MASB resolution G 11.01 and A-10.25 - 2021 amendment.

**Continuing resolutions**

| Local Control | 9/24/2019 | A 10.10; A 10.55; A 12.70 |

| Teacher Shortages | 9/11/2021 | MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority |

**School Aid, in detail**
A. Oppose using School Aid Fund dollars for any other purpose than K-12 education. B. Support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students. C. Protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes. D. Specify that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education in Michigan's Constitution and oppose any attempts to create private school voucher or tax credit programs. E. Support enacting the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1, so that school districts have factual information to meet their constitutional/statutory requirement to approve a budget by June 30.

**Other content**
The Mental Health resolution adds two bullets: help staff identify potential mental health issues for students, and encourage MDE to develop a model policy for staff regarding identifying mental health issues and appropriate staff response. The Special Education resolution notes that federal legislation initially promised to provide 40 percent of the excess cost to educate students with disabilities but that appropriations have fallen short. When aligned with OCSBA legislative priorities, OCSBA also supports the National School Boards Association (NSBA) Legislative Agenda, the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Legislative Agenda, and the Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) Legislative Agenda [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]. Links are provided to MASB Resolutions at https://www.masb.org/resolutions.aspx and NSBA Advocacy: IDEA at https://www.nsba.org/Advocacy.

The Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) resolutions packet for 2023 was circulated to member boards, including the Troy School District Board of Education, for its meeting of February 14, 2023. The document is organized into three parts: proposed new resolutions for 2023, a proposed amendment to a previously adopted resolution, and the standing body of continuing resolutions previously adopted by member school districts, each tagged with its adoption and, where applicable, amendment date, and cross-referenced to the corresponding Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) resolution numbers.

PROPOSED NEW RESOLUTIONS. Two are put forward. Under SCHOOL NUTRITION, OCSBA supports the expansion of the Free and Reduced Meals program to include all children, as was done during the pandemic. Under SCHOOL SAFETY, OCSBA supports that there be adequate state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe.

PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO A PREVIOUSLY ADOPTED RESOLUTION. The SCHOOL FINANCE RESEARCH COLLABORATIVE (SFRC) resolution, originally adopted by OCSBA on 9/24/2019 and amended on 9/11/2021, would be amended again. As presented, OCSBA supports review and implementation of the recommendations of the SFRC, including the recommended additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure, and transportation, and states that while implementing the SFRC recommendations, higher funded districts must be held harmless. The citation given is MASB resolution G 11.01 and A-10.25 - 2021 amendment. The hold-harmless language is of direct interest to a comparatively high-revenue district such as Troy.

CONTINUING RESOLUTIONS. MENTAL HEALTH [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] states that OCSBA supports increased mental health services and professionals in schools and provide adequate state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe, citing MASB Resolutions G 9.01, G 9.05 and G 9.50. Two bullets follow: help staff identify potential mental health issues for students; and encourage MDE to develop a model policy for staff regarding identifying mental health issues and appropriate staff response.

LOCAL CONTROL [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] supports local control of community-governed public schools with elected school boards, citing MASB Resolution A 10.10, A 10.55 and A 12.70.

EVIDENCE-BASED DECISION MAKING [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] states that OCSBA supports evidence-based education policy that will maximize opportunities for the highest achievement of each student, citing MASB Resolution G 11.01.

UNFUNDED MANDATES [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] provides that OCSBA opposes any state or federal legislation that results in increased costs for school districts without full funding, and also encourages the Michigan Legislature to oppose any federal laws or programs that are not fully funded thus costing the state valuable resources, citing MASB Resolution A 10.20.

SCHOOL AID [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] contains five lettered planks. A. Oppose using School Aid Fund dollars for any other purpose than K-12 education [MASB Resolution A 10.25]. B. Support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (g) and (j); A 10.55]. C. Protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (c); A 10.55]. D. Specify that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education in Michigan's Constitution and oppose any attempts to create private school voucher or tax credit programs [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (a) and A 10.05]. E. OCSBA supports enacting the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1, so that school districts have factual information to meet their constitutional/statutory requirement to approve a budget by June 30 [MASB Resolution A 10.25 (h)].

ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] states that OCSBA supports transparency and accountability for ALL school aid funds, naming community governed public school districts, charter schools, cyber schools, community colleges and public universities, citing MASB Resolution A 6.65 (c), (d), (f).

LAME DUCK [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] states that OCSBA supports lame duck parameters that will address introduction and accelerated passage of legislation after the November election.

UNIVERSAL PRESCHOOL [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] states that OCSBA supports additional new dollars to fund universal preschool for all four year old children, citing OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019 and MASB Resolution A 6.15 (c).

SPECIAL EDUCATION [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019] states that OCSBA supports full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), noting that although federal legislation initially promised to provide 40 percent of the excess cost to educate students with disabilities, the appropriations have fallen short, leaving states and local school districts to make up the difference. It cites MASB Resolution A 5.01 and NSBA Advocacy: IDEA.

BROADBAND ACCESS AND DEVICES [OCSBA Adopted 9/11/2021] states that broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan, that OCSBA supports additional federal and state funding opportunities to expand affordable and reliable broadband access, and that it supports federal and state programs for the purchase of internet capable devices and software, citing MASB Resolution A-10.30 - 2021 amendment.

TEACHER SHORTAGES [OCSBA Adopted 9/11/2021] states support for statewide initiatives to address teacher shortages and retain teachers while maintaining quality teacher preparation programs, listing as possible but not exclusive initiatives incentives to enter and complete a teaching college program, incentives for teachers to remain in the classroom, and easing the process to obtain Michigan certification for teachers that are certified in other states. It cites the MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority.

ALIGNED AGENDAS. A closing section, adopted 9/24/2019, provides that when aligned with OCSBA legislative priorities, OCSBA also supports the National School Boards Association (NSBA) Legislative Agenda, the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Legislative Agenda, and the Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) Legislative Agenda.

LINKS. The packet closes with two references: MASB Resolutions at https://www.masb.org/resolutions.aspx and NSBA Advocacy: IDEA at https://www.nsba.org/Advocacy.

Transmittal letter dated March 21, 2023 from Dr. Wanda Cook-Robinson, Superintendent of Oakland Schools, addressed "Dear Board of Education Designate," accompanying the proposed FY 2023-24 Oakland Schools budget documents. Copies went to the District Superintendent and District Business Manager.

**Statutory process**
Under Michigan School Code Section 380.624(2) the proposed FY 2023-24 General Fund budget is submitted to constituent districts' Boards of Education for review by May 1. Not later than June 1, the board of each constituent district shall adopt a resolution of support or non-support of the General Fund budget. Budgets for all Oakland Schools funds are included for transparency, but constituent districts vote only on the General Fund budget.

**Revenue outlook**
Oakland Schools is primarily funded by property tax dollars, with a projected growth factor in property tax revenues of 5.0%. Projections are described as conservative compared to Oakland County taxable value increase projections because actual taxable value figures are not available during budget preparation. For the first time in eight years, a Headlee rollback is not being budgeted; additional information on taxable values and the millage reduction factor will be received by June 1.

**Major budget features**
- Mental health: two mental health consultants were added in 2022-23, with the work continuing in 2023-24 under Section 31n of the Revised School Aid Act; programs include PREPaRE, Behavioral Threat Assessment and Management (BTAM), Suicide Assessment, Life Space Crisis Intervention and Non-Violent Crisis Intervention, with a county-wide summit the first week in August.
- School safety: funding for four school resource officers from the Oakland County Sheriff's Department, with 50% of one SRO funded by a Michigan State Police grant and the rest through the Career and Technical Education millage; approximately $8 million for safety and security updates at the four technical campuses.
- Cybersecurity: multi-factor authentication, an endpoint detection and response platform for local districts, and phishing simulation exercises.
- Shared services: technology services to sixteen constituent districts; business office services on a limited basis to five districts through an intergovernmental agreement.
- MiPEER: formed in FY 2012-13 by Oakland Schools and 22 Oakland County school districts, using BusinessPLUS; a new Time and Attendance solution arrives in 2023-24.
- LEO 2.0: a $5 million research-based literacy initiative, originally launched in 2019-20.
- Subsidies: over $1.3 million for software and instructional tools in CTE and curriculum and assessment.
- Countywide communications channel: $700,000 for an emergency radio channel linking districts to first responders.

**Personnel and benefits**

| Item | Figure |
| --- | --- |
| Nonunion salary increase | 2.5% |
| Union salary increase | 1% |
| Basic/MIP with Health Care Premium Subsidy retirement rate beginning October 1, 2023 | 31.34% |
| Projected blended retirement rate 2023-24 | 30.2% |
| Projected Medical CPI growth | 3.7% |

Hard cap health care limits: Family $20,180.43 for plan years beginning after 1/1/23 and a projected $20,927.11 after 1/1/24; Individual plus one $15,474.60 and $16,047.16; Single $7,399.47 and $7,673.25.

**PA-18 special education**
The base distribution of PA-18 funding to local school districts is budgeted to increase approximately $11.0 million or 7.4%, with $2.5 million budgeted for other LEA distributions covering group home expenditures, reimbursements for educating incarcerated youth, special education program startup, extraordinary expenditures and capital. In FY 2022-23 Oakland Schools distributed additional PA-18 funds totaling $3.7 million above the base distribution.

**Calendar**
Budget presentation to 28 local school district business managers at the Oakland County School Business Officials meeting on April 14, 2023; Designates Meeting April 20 at 6:00 PM; district resolutions due on or before June 1, 2023; Truth in Budgeting hearing June 6 with budget approval considered at the regular meeting that night. Questions to 248.209.2424.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Dated March 21, 2023 and opening "Dear Board of Education Designate," this is the transmittal letter from Dr. Wanda Cook-Robinson, Superintendent of Oakland Schools, that accompanies the proposed FY 2023-24 Oakland Schools budget documents sent to constituent districts, including Troy School District, and placed before the Troy Board of Education on May 16, 2023. Copies are directed to the District Superintendent and the District Business Manager.

STATUTORY FRAMEWORK. Per the Michigan School Code, Section 380.624(2), the proposed FY 2023-24 General Fund budget is to be submitted to its constituent districts' Boards of Education for review by May 1. Not later than June 1, the board of each constituent district shall adopt a resolution of support or non-support of the General Fund budget. For transparency purposes Oakland Schools includes the budgets for all of its funds in the enclosed document, but it is only the General Fund budget upon which constituent districts vote, and LEA Designates are only voting on the General Fund budget.

PROPERTY TAX AND HEADLEE. Oakland Schools is primarily funded by property tax dollars, and the letter states a projected growth factor in Oakland Schools' property tax revenues of 5.0%. Tax revenue projections are described as conservative compared to Oakland County taxable value increase projections, since actual taxable value figures are not available during preparation of the budget. For the first time in eight years, a Headlee rollback is not being budgeted. The letter explains that a Headlee rollback occurs when the annual growth on existing property is greater than the rate of inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index, and notes that additional information will be received by June 1 regarding taxable values and the millage reduction factor.

SOCIAL-EMOTIONAL WELLBEING AND MENTAL HEALTH SUPPORT. Oakland Schools shifted resources toward mental health support by adding two mental health consultants in 2022-23 and continues that work in 2023-24, broadening the support of mental health workers in schools under Section 31n of the Revised School Aid Act. The mental health team is responsible for oversight and provision of intensive mental health and complex behavior support, and for school-wide school safety and crisis preparedness and response initiatives, specifically naming PREPaRE, Behavioral Threat Assessment and Management (BTAM), Suicide Assessment, Life Space Crisis Intervention, and Non-Violent Crisis Intervention. Professional Learning events focused on engaging stakeholders in ensuring supports that address the wellbeing needs of the whole child are scheduled throughout the 2023-24 year, beginning with a county-wide summit the first week in August.

SCHOOL SAFETY. The 2023-24 budget contains funding for four school resource officers (SROs) to be provided by the Oakland County Sheriff's Department. Funding for 50% of one SRO is provided through a grant by the Michigan State Police, while the remaining officers are funded through the Career and Technical Education millage. The District is also planning safety and security updates at the four technical campuses, with approximately $8 million provided in the 2023-24 budget for these projects.

CYBERSECURITY. To maintain the safety, security and integrity of applications and data managed by Oakland Schools, significant investments are being made in cybersecurity, including increasing the use of multi-factor authentication, implementing an endpoint detection and response platform for local districts to detect and thwart security threats, and conducting cybersecurity awareness and phishing simulation exercises. Significant supports are available to constituent districts to assist with cybersecurity awareness and evaluation.

SHARED SERVICES. Oakland Schools provides technology, business office, instruction and truancy services on a cost-recovery basis. Technology services are currently being provided to sixteen constituent districts, and business office services are currently being provided on a limited basis to five districts through an intergovernmental agreement (IGA) with Oakland Schools.

MiPEER CONSORTIUM. In FY 2012-13, Oakland Schools and 22 Oakland County school districts formed the Michigan Partnership for Essential Education Resources (MIPEER) to select a countywide Enterprise Resource Planning system for human resource and financial applications. Since then the Consortium has standardized the Chart of Accounts for the selected solution, BusinessPLUS, and created best practice business processes for finance, human resources, budgeting and procurement. In 2023-24, Consortium members will be able to participate in a new Time and Attendance solution that will integrate with the existing BusinessPLUS product.

LITERACY ESSENTIALS OAKLAND (LEO) 2.0. The LEO project, initially kicked off in 2019-20, has been reimagined and relaunched as LEO 2.0, a $5 million research-based literacy initiative tailored to the needs of local districts, building capacity and focused on job-embedded professional learning. During 2023-24 the LEO 2.0 team will continue working with the countywide coaching network and district Literacy Leadership Teams on building capacity for early literacy success.

SUBSIDIES. Oakland Schools provides over $1.3 million in subsidies for software and other instructional tools in the areas of Career and Technical Education and curriculum and assessment. The subsidies in the 2023-24 budget are detailed within the budget document and are exclusive of pass-through grant funds, other district allocations, and the cost of dedicated staff who support student and finance/HR software and applications.

COUNTYWIDE COMMUNICATIONS CHANNEL. The 2023-24 General Education Fund budget includes costs for a countywide communications channel in the amount of $700,000, intended to connect constituent districts to first responders via an emergency radio channel.

PERSONNEL COSTS. Step increases for eligible employees are included in the 2023-24 budget along with a 2.5% salary increase for nonunion staff and a 1% increase for union staff. All union salary changes including step adjustments are subject to collective bargaining, and the increase cited is in accordance with the current bargaining agreement. On the State-mandated retirement rate, there are 8 rates in effect depending on the hire date of employees and their choices for eventual retirement benefits; the most common employee choice is Basic/MIP with Health Care Premium Subsidy, whose rate is projected to increase to 31.34% beginning October 1, 2023. Oakland Schools analyzed its own employee choices and projected an overall blended retirement rate of 30.2% for 2023-24.

HEALTH CARE HARD CAP. The "Hard Cap" for employee health care costs remains in effect for all labor groups. The dollar limits employers may pay are subject to annual adjustment based on the medical price index, over which the school district has no jurisdiction. Oakland Schools has projected growth in the medical price index of 3.7%. For plan years beginning after 1/1/23 and, on the projected basis, after 1/1/24, the limits are: Family $20,180.43 rising to $20,927.11; Individual plus one $15,474.60 rising to $16,047.16; and Single $7,399.47 rising to $7,673.25.

PA-18 SPECIAL EDUCATION FUNDING. Oakland Schools receives property tax revenue for support of Special Education programs. The base distribution of PA-18 funding to local school districts is budgeted to increase approximately $11.0 million or 7.4%. Additionally, $2.5 million is budgeted for other LEA distributions covering group home expenditures, reimbursements to districts for educating incarcerated youth, special education program startup and extraordinary expenditures, and capital. In FY 2022-23, Oakland Schools distributed additional PA-18 funds totaling $3.7 million above the base distribution.

PLANNING FOR THE FUTURE. Oakland Schools uses a five-year forecast updated with each budget amendment that incorporates projections from Oakland County Equalization for taxable values, and maintains a five-year capital plan updated annually. The organization pre-funds at least three years and up to five years of the capital plan requirements.

CALENDAR AND CONTACT. A presentation of the budget to the 28 local school district business managers was scheduled to occur at their meeting of the Oakland County School Business Officials on April 14, 2023. The Oakland Schools Board of Education would then hold a Designates Meeting on April 20 at 6:00 PM, giving local board designates and district administration an opportunity to review the General Fund budget before submitting their board's resolution to Oakland Schools on or before June 1, 2023. The Oakland Schools Board of Education will hold a Truth in Budgeting hearing on June 6 and will consider the FY 2023-24 proposed budget documents for approval during its regular meeting that night. Questions may be directed to the Superintendent's office at 248.209.2424.

In the auditors' opinion, the School District complied, in all material respects, with the compliance requirements identified in the OMB Compliance Supplement that could have a direct and material effect on each major federal program for the year ended June 30, 2022. **What this is**
Report to the Board of Education from Plante & Moran, PLLC on the audit of Troy School District's basic financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2022, dated October 5, 2022 and signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager. The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the business office. Structure: Results of the Audit (1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (5-6), Informational Items (7-17).

**Audit results**
Engagement letter dated June 1, 2022; planning-matters letter dated July 29, 2022; audit report and management representation letter both dated October 5, 2022. The District adopted GASB Statement No. 87, Leases, as of July 1, 2021. The most sensitive estimates were the District's shares of MPSERS net liabilities under GASB 68 and 75: $210,869,230 for pension and $13,509,781 for OPEB at June 30, 2022, from Office of Retirement Services data. No transactions lacked authoritative guidance, no significant difficulties arose, there were no disagreements with management, and management corrected all immaterial misstatements. A separate 2 CFR Part 200 report on federal programs was also issued October 5, 2022.

**Other recommendations and observations**
GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1 clarifies that grouped purchases individually below the capitalization threshold but above it in the aggregate belong in fixed asset records, effective for the year ending June 30, 2024. The Food Service Fund's fund balance exceeds the USDA maximum of three months of operating expenditures; a spenddown plan must go to the Michigan Department of Education.

**State funding**

| Item | 2021/2022 | 2022/2023 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Target foundation allowance | $8,700 per pupil | $9,150 per pupil |
| Change | at least $171 per pupil increase (former target $8,529) | $450 per pupil increase, 5.2 percent |
| Troy foundation allowance | $9,430 per pupil, up $115 from 2021 | at target, except hold harmless districts |
| MPSERS overall contribution rate | 43 percent, up from 42 percent | 45 percent, up from 43 percent |

Net MPSERS cost to the District approximates 28 percent in both years; the total contribution rate was 11 percent when Proposal A was adopted. State retirement support received: $1,062,198 in Section 147a1, $1,841,462 in 147a2, $13,922,709 in 147c1, and $311,632 in 147e. Other 2022/2023 items: GSRP expansion of 1,300 new openings; Section 31a/At-Risk fully funded; $10,000 tuition support for future teachers and $9,600 stipends per semester for student teachers; $475 million for a school consolidation and infrastructure fund; ISD operations allocation increasing to 5.2 percent. Pupil counts blend 90 percent fall and 10 percent spring. Statewide enrollment, historically slightly under 1.5 million, fell about 10,000 per year pre-pandemic and by more than 50,000 during the pandemic. The May 2022 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference projected surpluses for 2024 and 2025; the next was set for January 2023, and most federal pandemic funding must be used by September 30, 2024.

**Fund balance**
General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $247,000 in 2021/2022, bringing General Fund fund balance to approximately $33,000,000 at June 30, 2022. The District's fund balance percentage is 19.12 percent, roughly 9.9 weeks of operation; the statewide average at June 30, 2021 was approximately 19.30 percent, roughly 10.0 weeks.

**MPSERS plan status**
At September 30, 2021 the plan's net pension liability was approximately $24.2 billion, down approximately 30 percent from $35 billion a year earlier; net OPEB liability was approximately $1.5 billion, down approximately 72 percent from $5.4 billion. The plan returned 27.2 percent for the year ended September 30, 2021, versus 5.0 percent (pension) and 4.9 percent (OPEB) the prior year.

**Upcoming standards and cybersecurity**
GASB's Financial Reporting Model Improvements project (started August 2013, exposure draft June 2020, comments closed February 2021) targets final standards by December 2023, with phased adoption at June 30, 2025 for districts with annual revenue over $75 million and June 30, 2026 for those under. Revenue and Expense Recognition could be issued during 2027. GASB 96 (subscription-based IT arrangements) is effective for June 30, 2023; GASB 101 (compensated absences) for June 30, 2025. The report closes with cybersecurity guidance citing the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021, signed October 2021, weak passwords such as "August2022," and PII/FERPA data handling.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Engagement and signatories**
Report to the Board of Education of Troy School District covering the audit of the basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2022, issued by Plante & Moran, PLLC and signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager. The transmittal letter and the audit communications are dated October 5, 2022, and the firm extends thanks to Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office. The report is organized in three parts: Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-17).

**Responsibilities, scope, and timing**
The engagement letter was dated June 1, 2022, and the planning-matters letter was dated July 29, 2022; the audit was performed according to the planned scope and timing. The audit was conducted under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards and Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, and a separate letter dated October 5, 2022 addressed internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements. As required by 2 CFR Part 200, an audit of federal programs was also completed, with results provided to the Board in a report dated October 5, 2022. A management representation letter was obtained dated October 5, 2022.

**Significant audit findings**
Significant accounting policies are described in Note 2. As described in Note 2, the School District adopted GASB Statement No. 87, Leases, with the accounting change adopted as of July 1, 2021. The auditors noted no transactions entered into during the year for which there is a lack of authoritative guidance or consensus, and no significant transactions recognized in a different period than when they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75: $210,869,230 for pension and $13,509,781 for OPEB as of June 30, 2022, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures were described as neutral, consistent, and clear. No significant difficulties were encountered, no disagreements with management arose, management corrected all immaterial misstatements, and there were no consultations with other independent accountants. The auditors read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to their attention suggesting material misstatement or inconsistency.

**Other recommendations and observations**
GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1 updates guidance on fixed assets, clarifying that items purchased in a group that are individually below a district's capitalization threshold but exceed it in the aggregate should be reported in fixed asset records; the clarified guidance takes effect in the year ending June 30, 2024, and the District should review its practices and written policies. Separately, the Food Service Fund's fund balance exceeds the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures; the District will be required to develop a spenddown plan and submit it to the Michigan Department of Education.

**School funding narrative**
The informational section is headed "School Funding - From Projected Hardships to the Largest Level of Funding Since the Start of Proposal A." It notes that pandemic-era predictions of cuts and prorations did not materialize; that in 2021/2022 the gap between base and target foundation was eliminated; that 2022/2023 brought the largest per pupil increase since the start of Proposal A (1994/1995); and that state contributions rose above constitutional minimums for special education and for retirement system cost reduction.

**2021/2022 state funding**
All schools were moved to the target foundation allowance of $8,700 per pupil, eliminating the equity gap, and all schools including hold harmless districts received an increase of at least $171 per pupil from the former target level of $8,529. Progress was also made on School Finance Research Collaborative recommendations covering special education, At-Risk, wraparound services such as nurses and counselors, and the Great Start Readiness Program (GSRP). Based on these changes, Troy School District's foundation allowance per pupil was $9,430, an increase of $115 from the 2021 funding level.

**2022/2023 state funding**
Key highlights listed include: increasing the target foundation allowance by $450 per pupil to $9,150, a 5.2 percent increase, with hold harmless districts also receiving the $450 increase; continuing the traditional blended pupil count with 90 percent weighting for the October 2022 count and 10 percent weighting for the February 2022 count; continuing increases in special education cost reimbursement, with 2022 and 2023 marking the first time since the start of Proposal A that special education allocations exceeded state constitutional minimum levels; increasing GSRP funding to create 1,300 new openings for students; fully funding Section 31a/At-Risk programs, previously subject to proration; increasing career and technical education funding; increasing student mental health funding; teacher recruitment resources including $10,000 in tuition support for future teachers, $9,600 stipends per semester for student teachers, and "Grow Your Own" programs; expansion of before- and after-school programs focused on at-risk and economically disadvantaged students; dedicated school safety funding for school resource officers, intervention systems, and a school safety commission; increased retirement system contributions; allocation of $475 million of state aid funds for a school consolidation and infrastructure fund, described as the first such state allocation; and an ISD operations allocation increasing to 5.2 percent to mirror the foundation increase.

**Federal resources and outlook**
Federal assistance has come in waves since March 2020, with most funding ending in 2024; ARP ESSER III and Section 11t carry more restrictions than earlier relief. The window for using the majority of those funds closes by September 30, 2024. The most recent Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference, finalized in May 2022, projected a healthy School Aid Fund with a 2022 surplus carrying into 2023 and surpluses expected for 2024 and 2025; the next conference was scheduled for January 2023. Risks identified include inflation and a potential recession, noting that the 5.2 percent foundation increase is higher than any seen under Proposal A but could be consumed by higher operating costs.

**2022 funding implications for the District**
Listed items include the 2021/2022 foundation allowance changes above; the ESSER programs, with ESSER III made available during 2021/2022 in two components, ESSER III formula and ESSER III equalization (also known as 11t, authorized by Section 11t of PA 48 of 2021), federally funded under the American Rescue Plan and scheduled to end during 2024; the pupil membership blend for 2021/2022 returning to 90 percent fall and 10 percent spring after the 2020/2021 "super blend"; summer school and learning assistance funding through ESSER II and state appropriations, with costs and revenue split between the 2021 and 2022 fiscal years; and MPSERS costs for 2021/2022, where the overall contribution rate increased to 43 percent from 42 percent with net cost to the District approximating 28 percent. State support is provided through Sections 147a, 147c, and 147e of the State Aid Act; the District received $1,062,198 in 147a1, $1,841,462 in 147a2, $13,922,709 in 147c1, and $311,632 of 147e funding.

**2023 funding implications for the District**
The school aid package, described as the largest ever, was agreed before the start of the District's 2022/2023 fiscal year, though a budget amendment is likely because the state budget passed after districts had to adopt original budgets. All districts are at the target foundation allowance of $9,150 except a few hold harmless districts. Pupil count uses 90 percent of the fall 2022 count and 10 percent of the spring 2022 count. For 2023 the MPSERS overall contribution rate increases to 45 percent from 43 percent, with net cost to the District continuing at up to approximately 28 percent; by comparison, the total contribution rate was 11 percent when Proposal A was adopted. Beginning in 2021/2022 the State increased funding of its share of special education costs by 3 percent of those costs, continuing in 2022/2023 with a reduction in the amount of foundation allowance credited against the State's required support.

**Pupil count trends**
Statewide enrollment has historically been slightly under 1.5 million students, declining about 10,000 per year before the pandemic and decreasing in excess of 50,000 during the pandemic. Some recovery is estimated but not to pre-pandemic levels.

**Grants management and budgeting**
The report describes increased workload and grants management risk from ESSER, GEER, and CRF programs, touching superintendents and leadership, board members, the business office, staff, procurement, information technology, and facilities, and recommends continued assessment of compliance risks moving into the 2023 fiscal year.

**Fund balance**
During the 2021/2022 school year the School District's General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $247,000, increasing General Fund fund balance to approximately $33,000,000 at June 30, 2022. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2021 was approximately 19.30 percent of expenditures and outgoing transfers, which would equal approximately 10.0 weeks of average operating costs. The School District's fund balance percentage is 19.12 percent and equals approximately 9.9 weeks of operation.

**MPSERS plan net liabilities**
The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2021 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $24.2 billion, a decrease of approximately 30 percent from the reported $35 billion at September 30, 2020, driven largely by net investment gains; the plan's annual investment rate of return was 27.2 percent for the year ended September 30, 2021 compared with 5.0 percent for the year ended September 30, 2020. The retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB liability of approximately $1.5 billion at September 30, 2021, down from $5.4 billion at September 30, 2020, a decrease of approximately 72 percent, attributed to the 27.2 percent return compared with 4.9 percent the prior year. Because markets declined after the valuation date, the net liabilities are expected to increase significantly next year.

**Future GASB standards**
The GASB financial reporting model project began in August 2013, with an exposure draft titled "Financial Reporting Model Improvements" issued June 2020 and a comment period that ended February 2021 (Plante & Moran submitted comments); final standards are targeted for December 2023. Proposed changes include additional MD&A information, a budget-to-actual column showing variances between original and amended budget, terminology changes replacing "revenue" with "inflows of resources" and "expenditures" with "outflows of resources," and replacement of modified accrual with a "short-term financial resources measurement focus" using a 12-month conversion window rather than the current 60-day rule. Phased adoption would apply at the year ending June 30, 2025 for districts with total annual revenue across all funds over $75 million and June 30, 2026 for those under $75 million. A related project, "Revenue and Expense Recognition," released as preliminary views in June 2020, could produce a standard during 2027. GASB Statement No. 96, Subscription-based Information Technology Arrangements, is effective for the District's June 30, 2023 financial statements and mirrors GASB 87 by requiring a right-to-use subscription asset and subscription liability measured at the net present value of extended payment terms, with fund-level expenditures reclassified as debt service payments. GASB Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences, effective for the year ending June 30, 2025, requires a full-accrual liability for leave attributable to services already rendered that accumulates and is more likely than not to be used or paid, measured at each employee's pay rate at the financial statement date, and removes the gross additions/reductions and liquidating-fund disclosure requirements.

**Cybersecurity**
Education remains a top target for ransomware; the "K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021" was signed into law in October 2021. The report warns that easily guessed passwords such as "August2022" and phishing emails make the human element the weakest link, asks whether staff are aware of phishing risks, where district data resides, and whether PII or FERPA-protected data is stored on file-sharing sites, flash drives, or personal email, and suggests an external vulnerability assessment.

**What this is**

Oakland Schools (one of 56 Michigan intermediate school districts established in 1962; 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford, MI 48328-2736) proposed original budget for fiscal year 2024-25, pages footered 04.02.2024. It contains the Enterprise-Wide Executive Summary & Budget Assumptions, budgets and five-year forecasts for the General Education, Special Education and Career Focused Education Funds, budgets for the special revenue, debt service, capital projects, enterprise and internal service funds, and the 5-Year Capital Outlay Plan given first reading April 2, 2024. State law requires an ISD board to submit its proposed budget to each constituent district board for review and comment by May 1 and to adopt by June 30; the item carries a May 21, 2024 board meeting date.

**Enterprise-wide totals (net of eliminated Risk Related Activity Fund amounts)**

| Funding - $470.0M total | Amount | Expenditures - $480.9M total | Amount |

**Property taxes and PA-18**

The tax base is 70% principal residence / 30% non-principal residence; no Headlee rollback occurred in 2023-24 and none is expected for 2024-25. Michigan Tax Tribunal reserve is set at .25% of tax revenues, about $623,700; the district has repaid over $13.0 million in property taxes on MTT judgments over eleven years. The PA-18 base distribution to local districts is budgeted at $173,556,600, up about $14.2 million or 8.9%; the FY2023-24 budget also carried a $10,687,000 supplemental distribution, of which $3.8 million was distributed in December 2023.

Districts vote only on the General Fund budget, and each constituent board must adopt a resolution of support or non-support no later than June 1. The letter also reports that Oakland Schools' 2020-21 COVID-19 actions saved constituent districts approximately $1.9 million.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Origin**
Letter dated April 5, 2021 from Dr. Wanda Cook-Robinson, Superintendent, Oakland Schools, addressed to "Board of Education Designate," with copies to the District Superintendent and District Business Manager. It accompanies the proposed FY 2021-22 Oakland Schools budget documents and appears in the Troy School District packet for the May 18, 2021 meeting.

**Statutory review process**
Per Michigan School Code, Section 380.624(2), the proposed FY 2021-22 General Fund budget is submitted to constituent district boards for review by May 1; not later than June 1 each constituent board must adopt a resolution of support or non-support. Oakland Schools supplies budgets for all of its funds for transparency, but LEA Designates vote only on the General Fund budget.

**Revenue outlook**
Oakland Schools is primarily funded by property tax dollars. Projected growth factor in property tax revenues is 2.7%, described as conservative relative to Oakland County taxable value increase projections because a Headlee rollback of the operating millage is considered probable for FY 2021-22 (triggered when annual growth on existing property exceeds inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index). Additional information on taxable values and the millage reduction factor was expected by June 1.

**COVID-19 response**
2020-21 actions -- subsidies for Illuminate DnA and the Oakland Human Resource Consortium, elimination of ONE Network Fees, reduction in Shared Services IGA fees, carryover of CTE Regional Allocation funding, and payment of 100% of CTE transportation costs -- saved constituent districts approximately $1.9 million. Budgets cut in 2020-21 for travel, conference fees, printing and certain purchased services are reinstated in 2021-22. An estimated $2 million is provided in 2021-22 for tutoring, OSTC Supplemental Instruction, the Oakland Youth Innovation Lab and the Design Studio. Oakland Schools received no ESSER Fund, Governor's Emergency Education Relief Fund or MDE-distributed Coronavirus Relief Fund money and will not receive ESSER II; its COVID-19 expenditures are funded with tax revenues and state aid ISD funding.

**Programs and services**
The Literacy Essentials Oakland (LEO) Project is a five-year, $5 million project launched in 2019-20. CTE receives additional resources including career program redesign and initial funding for a mobile classroom (the STEMi) beginning Spring 2020-21; the CTE allocation to LEAs was increased by more than 25% in 2019-20 and that level continues in 2021-22. Technology services are provided to fifteen constituent districts and business office services on a limited basis to four districts under intergovernmental agreements. MiPEER, formed in FY 2012-13 by Oakland Schools and 22 Oakland County districts, is converting members to PowerSchool BusinessPlus in phases between 2015-16 and 2021-22. Illuminate Education has been the countywide assessment vendor since Fall 2016, covering 28 districts and two public school academies, with a 100% subsidy again in 2021-22. A countywide emergency radio communications channel is budgeted at $700,000 within a project estimated at $1.5 million.

**Personnel costs**
Step increases are included; no across-the-board salary increases are budgeted. The Basic/MIP with Health Care Premium Subsidy retirement rate is projected to rise from 28.21% to 28.23% effective October 1, 2021, and Oakland Schools projects a blended rate of 28.23% for 2021-22. Health care hard cap limits, assuming 3.3% medical CPI growth:

| Tier | Plan year beginning after 1/1/21 | Plan year beginning after 1/1/22 (projected) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Family | $19,210.66 | $19,844.61 |
| Individual plus one | $14,730.96 | $15,217.08 |
| Single | $7,043.89 | $7,276.34 |

**PA-18 special education**
Property tax revenue growth of 2.7% is projected. The base distribution of PA-18 funding to local districts is budgeted to increase approximately $3.8 million or 2.8%, with $3.9 million budgeted for other LEA distributions. In FY 2020-21 Oakland Schools distributed additional PA-18 funds totaling $5.6 million above the base distribution.

**Calendar**
Presentation to 28 local district business managers at the Oakland County School Business Officials meeting on April 23, 2021; Designates Meeting April 27 at 6:00 PM; district resolutions due on or before June 1, 2021; Truth in Budgeting hearing and board consideration of the FY 2021-22 budget documents on June 1. Questions to 248.209.2424.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Document and authorship.** Transmittal letter dated April 5, 2021, signed by Dr. Wanda Cook-Robinson, Superintendent of Oakland Schools, addressed to "Dear Board of Education Designate," with a copy line to the District Superintendent and the District Business Manager. It introduces the enclosed proposed Oakland Schools budget for FY 2021-22 and appears in the Troy School District board materials for the meeting of May 18, 2021.

**Statutory submission and voting.** Per the Michigan School Code, Section 380.624(2), the proposed FY 2021-22 General Fund budget is to be submitted to each constituent district's Board of Education for review by May 1. Not later than June 1, the board of each constituent district shall adopt a resolution of support or non-support of the General Fund budget. For transparency purposes Oakland Schools includes the budgets for all of its funds in the enclosed document; however, it is only the General Fund budget upon which constituent districts vote, and the letter twice stresses that LEA Designates vote only on the General Fund budget.

**Property tax revenue and Headlee.** Oakland Schools is primarily funded by property tax dollars. The letter projects a growth factor in Oakland Schools' property tax revenues of 2.7%. Tax revenue projections are described as conservative compared to Oakland County taxable value increase projections because there is concern that a Headlee rollback of the operating millage is probable for FY 2021-22. A rollback occurs when the annual growth on existing property is greater than the rate of inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index. Additional information on taxable values and the millage reduction factor was to be received by June 1.

**COVID-19 response.** The 2020-21 COVID-19 response included subsidies for Illuminate DnA and the Oakland Human Resource Consortium, elimination of ONE Network Fees, reduction in Shared Services IGA fees, carryover of CTE Regional Allocation funding, and payment of 100% of CTE transportation costs. These actions on behalf of the Oakland Schools Board of Education saved constituent districts approximately $1.9 million in 2020-21. Oakland Schools significantly reduced 2020-21 budgets for travel, conference fees, printing and certain other purchased services; those budgets are reinstated in 2021-22 as operations are expected to slowly return to pre-pandemic status, subject to monitoring and the amendment process. Resources developed for districts include guidance to evaluate, measure and assess well-being within school communities; best practices for remote and hybrid teaching and learning; and curriculum, instruction, and assessment toolkits. Oakland Schools is providing an estimated $2 million in 2021-22 for additional learning opportunities for students and professional learning for teachers, including Tutoring, OSTC Supplemental Instruction, the Oakland Youth Innovation Lab, and the Design Studio. Financial support to local districts in 2021-22 includes a full subsidy of Illuminate DnA base costs and allowing districts to carry over the unspent portion of their CTE Regional Allocation from 2020-21 to 2021-22. Unlike local districts, Oakland Schools has not received funding under the Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief Fund (ESSER Fund), the Governor's Emergency Education Relief Fund, or the Coronavirus Relief Fund distributed by MDE, and will not receive funding under ESSER II; its COVID-19 related expenditures are funded with tax revenues and state aid ISD funding.

**Literacy Essentials Oakland (LEO).** The LEO Project is centered on ensuring early literacy success for children in Oakland County. It is a five-year, $5 million project launched during the 2019-20 school year, developed to be deeply rooted in research, to build capacity in districts, to be tailored to the needs of districts, and to focus on job-embedded professional learning.

**Career and Technical Education.** To align with the Michigan Department of Education's Top 10 in 10 Years goals and strategies, additional resources are dedicated to career and technical education. Beyond significant resources for the four technical campuses, the 2021-22 budget adds funds for career program redesign and initial funding for a CTE mobile classroom (the STEMi) intended to bring STEM activities to local districts beginning in Spring 2020-21. In 2019-20 the CTE allocation to LEAs was increased by more than 25%, and that level of funding continues in 2021-22, providing local districts additional resources for local CTE programs from elementary to high school.

**Shared Services.** Oakland Schools provides technology, business office, instruction, and truancy services on a cost recovery basis. Technology services are currently provided to fifteen constituent districts, and business office services are provided on a limited basis to four districts through an intergovernmental agreement (IGA).

**MiPEER Consortium.** In FY 2012-13, Oakland Schools and 22 Oakland County school districts formed the Michigan Partnership for Essential Education Resources (MIPEER) to select a countywide Enterprise Resource Planning system for human resource and financial applications. The consortium standardized the Chart of Accounts and created best practice business processes for finance, human resources, budgeting and procurement. Members are converting to the PowerSchool BusinessPlus software in phases between 2015-16 and 2021-22.

**Illuminate.** Oakland Schools has contracted with Illuminate Education as its countywide student assessment and data analysis tool vendor since the Fall of 2016; all twenty-eight (28) districts and two (2) public school academies are included in the software license and support agreement. Illuminate DnA lets teachers build and administer formative assessments, capture and analyze multiple sources of data, and direct students to learning resources for targeted standards. The Oakland Schools Board of Education agreed to provide a 100% subsidy for the student assessment software and support again in 2021-22; add-ons called "Item Banks" may be purchased through the contract at the districts' cost.

**Subsidies.** Beyond Illuminate DnA, Oakland Schools provides multiple software products at no cost or reduced cost in career and technical education and in curriculum and assessment; a subsidy on the per pupil cost of the PowerSchool BusinessPlus system for MiPEER consortium members; and communication tools such as news services and media monitoring/clipping services at no cost to LEAs. These are exclusive of pass-through grant funds, other district allocations, and the cost of dedicated staff who support student and finance/HR software and applications.

**Countywide Communications Channel.** The 2021-22 General Education Fund budget includes $700,000 for a countywide communications channel, a multi-year project intended to connect constituent districts to first responders via an emergency radio channel. The total cost of the project is estimated at $1.5 million.

**Personnel costs.** Step increases for eligible employees are included in the 2021-22 budget, but no across-the-board salary increases are included due to funding uncertainties at publication. Decisions on salary increases will follow the May Revenue Estimating Conference, final taxable value reports from Oakland County Equalization (generally received in May), and more concrete State budget information; all union salary changes including step adjustments are subject to collective bargaining. On the State-mandated retirement rate, there are 8 rates in effect depending on hire date and retirement benefit choices; the most common choice, Basic/MIP with Health Care Premium Subsidy, is projected to increase from 28.21% to 28.23% beginning October 1, 2021, and Oakland Schools projects an overall blended retirement rate of 28.23% for 2021-22. The "Hard Cap" for employee health care costs remains in effect for all labor groups; limits are adjusted annually based on the medical price index, and Oakland Schools projects growth in the medical price index of 3.3%. Under that assumption the limits move from $19,210.66 to $19,844.61 for Family, from $14,730.96 to $15,217.08 for Individual plus one, and from $7,043.89 to $7,276.34 for Single, comparing plan years beginning after 1/1/21 with projected plan years beginning after 1/1/22.

**PA-18 Special Education Funding.** Oakland Schools receives property tax revenue for support of Special Education programs, with growth in property tax revenue projected at 2.7% for FY 2021-22. The base distribution of PA-18 funding to local school districts is budgeted to increase approximately $3.8 million or 2.8%. Additionally, $3.9 million is budgeted for other LEA distributions covering group home expenditures, reimbursements to districts for educating incarcerated youth, special education program startup, extraordinary expenditures, and capital. In FY 2020-21, Oakland Schools distributed additional PA-18 funds totaling $5.6 million above the base distribution.

**Planning for the future.** Oakland Schools uses a five-year forecast updated with each budget amendment that incorporates Oakland County Equalization taxable value projections, and maintains a five-year capital plan updated annually. The organization pre-funds at least three years and up to five years of the capital plan requirements.

**Schedule.** A presentation of the budget to the 28 local school district business managers was scheduled for the Oakland County School Business Officials meeting on April 23, 2021. The Oakland Schools Board of Education planned a Designates Meeting on April 27 at 6:00 PM so local board designates and district administration could review the General Fund budget before submitting board resolutions to Oakland Schools on or before June 1, 2021. The Oakland Schools Board of Education would hold a Truth in Budgeting hearing on June 1 and consider the FY 2021-22 proposed budget documents for approval during its regular meeting that night. Questions are directed to 248.209.2424.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: The Michigan High School Athletic Association's 2021-22 Handbook Supplement, included in the Troy School District board packet for July 20, 2021, listing substantive regulation changes in place of a printed handbook. The full 2021-22 Handbook (red cover) is available only online to school administrators at MHSAA.com, and the supplement is to be inserted into the 2020-21 Handbook (royal blue cover). Among the changes, the COVID-era adjustments page is declared obsolete, the minimum Previous Academic Credit Record of 66% is again waived for fall 2021-22 sports, and any student born before Sept. 1, 2002 is ineligible for interscholastic scrimmages or contests.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Purpose and distribution**
Because of the COVID-19 pandemic and a small number of regulation changes, the 2021-22 MHSAA Handbook was not printed. The full 2021-22 Handbook (red cover) is available to school administrators logged in at MHSAA.com under School Administrator Services. The supplement contains substantive changes only, is posted online, and is to be inserted into the 2020-21 Handbook (royal blue cover); changes are gray shaded. Copies are designated for the AD and the Principal. MHSAA 2021-22 Membership Resolutions were mailed to superintendents via US Mail on May 11, 2021 and are due back to the MHSAA by Aug. 1, 2021.

**Eligibility changes**
Page 25, the COVID-19 pandemic adjustments page, is obsolete and all references to it are to be disregarded. The MHSAA minimum Previous Academic Credit Record (66%) is again waived for sports played in the fall of 2021-22; the Pre-Participation physical exam returns for 2021-22 and the Health Questionnaire is not in use. Page 31, Regulation I, Section 2(A): a participant must be under nineteen (19) years of age, except that a student whose nineteenth birthday occurs on or after September 1 of a current school year is eligible for the balance of that year; any student born before Sept. 1, 2002 is ineligible. Page 33, Regulation I, Section 4, Interpretation 24 and Interpretation 46 govern students splitting classwork between 8th and 9th grades, with thresholds of 3 of 4, 4 of 5 or 6, 5 of 7, and 6 of 8 high school classes; the 66% allowance applies only to a student in the 8th grade for the first time. Page 47, Regulation I, Section 9, Interpretation 77-b tightens proof of a full residential change. Page 56, Regulation I, Section 12(C) permits a student who has completed a 12th-grade season to play in one high school all-star event held after the MHSAA Final in that sport, with written notice to the MHSAA at least 30 calendar days prior.

**Cooperative programs, coaches and officials**
Page 29, Regulation I, Section 1(E-2) makes permanent the allowance for cooperative agreements in nine sports between public schools of the same district: baseball, bowling, girls competitive cheer, cross country, golf, soccer, girls softball, tennis and wrestling. Page 61, Regulation II, Section 3(B) requires CPR certification attestation for varsity head coaches, extending to JV and 9th-grade head coaches effective Aug. 1, 2022. Page 64, Regulation II, Section 7(A) requires that only MHSAA registered officials who have completed a current year's rules meeting may officiate high school regular season or tournament contests; a rules meeting is not required for middle school contests.

**Competition limits and dates**
Page 67, Regulation II, Section 10(A): in basketball a student may play no more than five quarters in a day, no more than three days of competition in a week Monday through Sunday, and no more than 20 days of competition exclusive of the MHSAA tournament; a team is limited to three games Monday through Sunday, four interscholastic scrimmages and 20 games, and one game per day; overtime counts as an extension of the 4th quarter. Pages 71 and 72 set fall practice at Aug. 9, 2021, spring practice at March 14, 2022, and winter practice dates from Nov. 1 through Nov. 22, 2021 by sport.
