**Instrument**
MHSAA Membership Resolution for the year August 1, 2021 through July 31, 2022, addressed from the Michigan High School Athletic Association, 1661 Ramblewood Drive, East Lansing, MI 48823, (517) 332-5046. The MHSAA is described as a voluntary, nonprofit corporation of public, private and parochial junior high/middle and senior high schools whose boards of education or governing bodies have applied for and received membership. Resolutions that are modified in any way, or supplemented with letters placing additional conditions on membership or tournament participation, are rejected; one signed copy is returned to the MHSAA and one retained.

**Adopting body**
Troy Board of Education, City/Township of Troy, County of Oakland, State of Michigan. Record of adoption shows the resolution adopted on the 20th day of July, 2021 for the Troy schools. Address given as 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, with contact e-mail jholmes@troy.k12.mi.us. Signature lines are provided for the Board Secretary or designee.

**Effect of adoption**
The listed schools are enrolled as members of the Michigan High School Athletic Association, Inc. and are further enrolled to participate in the approved interschool athletic activities it sponsors. The board delegates to the Superintendent or designee the responsibility for supervision and control of those activities, accepts the association's Constitution and By-Laws, and adopts as its own the rules, regulations and interpretations published in the current Handbook as minimum standards, agreeing to primary enforcement. Schools that host or participate in association meets and tournaments must follow and enforce all tournament policies, procedures and schedules. Tournaments are the collective property of the MHSAA, not of any individual member school. Districts are not required to join at the junior high/middle school level or to sponsor athletics for 6th-grade students, but if a listed middle school sponsors a 6th-grade team or lets a 6th-grader play with 7th and 8th graders, all of Regulations III and IV apply to all 6th-graders in all such sports.

**Instrument and issuer.** The 2021-22 Michigan High School Athletic Association Membership Resolution, issued from 1661 Ramblewood Drive, East Lansing, MI 48823, telephone (517) 332-5046, and executed by the Troy Board of Education. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A PowerPoint presentation titled "Strategic Planning 2026 Recommendations: Update on Stakeholder Planning," delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on August 17, 2021. It reviews the district's five-year strategic plan redesign process -- See, Engage, Act -- reports stakeholder feedback from collaborative teams, and presents refreshed statements for the Green, Red, Blue and Gold pillars. The central admission is that accountability was missing from the prior plan, and the answer proposed is an Accountability Plan built on objectives and key results, co-designed with pillar teams and reported back to the Board in the second semester.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Presentation**
Strategic Planning 2026 Recommendations: Update on Stakeholder Planning, August 17, 2021, to the Troy School District Board of Education. Outline: overview of the strategic planning process, current state, future state, and a preview of the accountability plan. The redesign process is framed as See, Engage, Act, aimed at system coherence in a 5-Year Strategic Plan in which research defines world class.

**Stakeholder feedback**
Key wonderings from collaborative teams: accountability is missing, specifically data and collective commitments; continue with clarity and simple understanding of a complex process; coordination and how the pillars interact; define deep learning; Red Pillar understanding; equity and inclusion not specifically called out; the Gold Pillar should include ALL staff, students and families; and the Green Pillar should include a through line to career with a focus on access and exposure to career.

**Research base**
Fullan 2021 is cited for the right drivers for system success: Well-being and Learning, Social Intelligence, Equality Investments, and Systemness. Louis et al., 2010 and the Wallace Foundation study of effective district leadership are cited for the point that district leaders must be crystal clear and repetitive in communicating the agenda for action, but that the best indicator of coherence is when system members experience it -- the ability to "talk the walk." A further quotation notes that most strategic plans are high on aspirations and almost empty on HOW to achieve the goals.

**Pillar refreshes**
Green Pillar, Investing in Early Childhood to Career: continue investing in high-quality early childhood education including advocating for universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds; expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students, broaden access to computer science and CTE, connect underrepresented students to in-demand high-growth sectors, and build partnerships supporting work-based learning, credentials and college credit. Red Pillar, Ensuring a Focus on Equity and Well-Being: safely reopen schools and support students disproportionately impacted by the pandemic; fund whole-child supports including community schools with wraparound services such as afterschool programs and hiring more counselors, social workers and school psychologists; assess and act on facility upgrade needs. Blue Pillar, Deepening Learning for All: create and sustain systems of support that deepen learning and empower student voice; improve technology access for students and families with quality training; pursue global best practices in all content areas. Gold Pillar, Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families: improve educator preparation, strengthen pipelines for underrepresented educators, sustain job-embedded professional learning, and co-design impactful learning experiences for staff, community and students.

**Resource allocation and next steps**
Increased social workers and counseling in all buildings; Red Pillar professional learning on Tuesday, August 24 with Dr. Jean Clinton; Media 2.0 positions; sustained literacy coaching and interventions; expanded job-embedded coaching for literacy and math; ELD support; coordinated instructional support; a Delayed Start Model providing 90 minutes for collaboration through professional learning; and Accountability Plan co-design with a report to the Board in the second semester. Other items include summer professional learning dates, new teacher orientation, an Apple technology refresh in ALL elementary buildings, and shared leadership of pillar teams.

**Accountability plan preview**
System-level implementation considerations: build cohesive leadership teams with systemness including all departments; create clarity by focusing on a FEW things; overcommunicate clarity; identify objectives and key results; establish timelines. A cabinet example sets the objective of sustaining a world class school system with key results of visiting five classrooms per week, aligning vision with facility enhancement through six collaborative meetings with a community team, hosting six meetings for all support staff in CO and Services, and improving internal communication with Cabinet notes twice per month. The closing section commits the leadership team to the OneTroy values of cultivating a collaborative culture, deepening learning, and focusing direction, with the vision of world class for ALL.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Presentation identity.** "Strategic Planning 2026 Recommendations: Update on Stakeholder Planning," a PowerPoint delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on August 17, 2021. The presentation outline covers an overview of the strategic planning process, current state, future state, and a preview of the accountability plan.

**Current state and process.** The current-state section is titled Building on Success. The redesign process is described as See, Engage, Act. System coherence is pursued through a 5-Year Strategic Plan with a VISION (WHAT) element and the premise that research defines world class. A slide on clarifying the foundation is followed by guiding questions posed to stakeholders: for current state, what are we proud of and what are we challenged by; for future state, what is possible over the next five years.

**Stakeholder feedback -- key wonderings from collaborative teams.** Accountability is missing, specifically data and collective commitments. Continue with clarity and simple understanding of a complex process. Coordination and how the pillars interact. Define deep learning. Red Pillar understanding. Equity and Inclusion are not specifically called out. The Gold Pillar should include ALL staff, students and families. The Green Pillar should include a through line to career with a focus on access and exposure to career.

**Research cited.** Under "Latest Research on Key Drivers, Fullan 2021," the right drivers for system success are listed as Well-being and Learning, Social Intelligence, Equality Investments, and Systemness. A slide titled Challenge -- Coherence and Clarity quotes Louis et al., 2010, that district leaders must "be crystal clear and repetitive when communicating the district's agenda for action," then argues that the true test of coherence is not a leader's ability to explain alignment but whether system members experience it, described as the ability of individuals and the group to "talk the walk" -- embedded coherence. Whole-system reform is characterized as coherence making: when systems focus on structural elements such as having meetings and stipulating agendas they end up being just another program, because the reform comes from the mindsets behind them. The slide urges an asset lens that recognizes strengths in people and invests belief in them.

**Future state framing.** A slide asks What's Next, quoting that the world's best school systems ensure all stakeholders understand the purpose, priorities and goals of the system, with leaders clarifying a few very specific non-negotiables that must be honored throughout the system while encouraging autonomy and creativity at all levels to foster ownership and innovation.

**Green Pillar Refresh -- Investing in Early Childhood to Career.** Continue to invest in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for universal preschool for all three and four-year-olds and access for all. Expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students, aiming to provide more students with access to high-quality career and technical education programs that expand access to computer science, connect underrepresented students to careers in in-demand, high-growth industry sectors, and include partnerships with institutions of higher education, employers and other stakeholders that allow students to engage in quality work-based learning opportunities, earn a credential, and/or earn college credit.

**Red Pillar Refresh -- Ensuring a Focus on Equity and Well-Being.** Safely reopen schools and support students, particularly those disproportionately impacted by the pandemic. Fund additional investments to support the needs of the whole child, including community schools that provide wraparound services such as afterschool programs and hiring more counselors, social workers and school psychologists. Assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities.

**Blue Pillar Refresh -- Deepening Learning for All.** Create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice, with access to deep learning described as imperative for all children. Improve technology access for students and families while providing quality training to leverage use of technology to deepen learning. Continue to pursue the global best practices of all content areas.

**Gold Pillar Refresh -- Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families.** Improve educator preparation, strengthen pipelines for underrepresented educators, and support current educators. Continue to provide job-embedded professional learning experiences for all staff. Provide professional learning opportunities for staff, community and students with the goal of co-designing impactful experiences to better the OneTroy community.

**Resource allocation and simple next steps.** Increased social workers and counseling in all buildings. Emphasis on Red Pillar professional learning on Tuesday, August 24, with Dr. Jean Clinton. Media 2.0 positions. Sustained support for literacy coaching and literacy interventions. Expanded job-embedded coaching for literacy and math. ELD support. Coordinated instructional support. A Delayed Start Model to ensure collaboration through professional learning, at 90 minutes. Accountability Plan co-design, with a report out to the Board of Education in the second semester. Other dates and opportunities listed are summer professional learning dates, new teacher orientation, an Apple technology refresh in ALL elementary buildings, and shared leadership of pillar teams.

**Accountability plan preview -- distributing leadership.** The presentation cites the landmark study of effective district leadership supported by the Wallace Foundation, which concluded that district leaders must "be crystal clear and repetitive when communicating the district's agenda for action," and repeats that the best indicator of coherence is when system members experience it. It states that most strategic plans are high on aspirations and almost empty on HOW to achieve the goals, and that when virtually all members of a group articulate the same story in terms of goals, strategies and progress -- knowing what they are doing and WHY -- it is a powerful indicator of widespread ownership and cultural coherence, making improvement efforts far more likely to be sustainable.

**Next steps for system-level implementation.** Key considerations are to build cohesive leadership teams with systemness including all departments; create clarity by focusing on a FEW things; overcommunicate clarity; identify objectives and key results; and establish timelines. The implementation plan slide is headed Meaningful Teams and returns to the Foundation. A Blueprint Preview states that teams will report out to the Board of Education in the second semester, that Project 2026 is in draft, and that objectives and key results will be continually monitored. The Project 2026 Blueprint is organized at District, School and Troy levels.

**Measuring what matters -- cabinet example.** Objective: sustaining a world class school system. Key results: visit five classrooms per week; align vision with facility enhancement through six collaborative meetings with a community team; host six meetings for all support staff in CO and Services; and improve internal communication with Cabinet notes twice per month. A subsequent section outlines the Green Pillar in terms of Overview, Objectives and Key Results.

**Closing accountability statement.** Continuing the world class journey to 2026 is described as the largest and most important challenge the district has undertaken, large in terms of commitment. The leadership team re-commits to carrying out the mission of ensuring learning for ALL, with the vision of world class for ALL described as ambitious and as a challenge to hold the team accountable to newly established goals co-designed with the teams in place. As OneTroy, the district will carry out its values of cultivating a collaborative culture, deepening learning, and focusing direction, with the success of the plan expected to highlight a significant impact on students, and staff told they will play a major role in ensuring a world class learning environment for ALL.

Budgeted revenue was increased by $5.0 million, primarily state and federal, reflecting the 2024 State School Aid Act's full funding of Section 31a At-Risk revenue for hold harmless districts; expenditures were adjusted for 2023-2024 staffing levels and for retirement costs passed through the state under Section 147c. On the budgetary schedule, actual General Fund revenue of $195,623,909 exceeded the $193,048,749 final budget by $2,575,160, and actual expenditures of $191,469,703 came in $778,787 below the $192,248,490 final budget, producing an ending fund balance of $36,774,527 versus a budgeted $33,420,580. Two functions exceeded appropriations: support services-general administration, $2,635,590 actual against $2,424,946 budgeted, and community services, $163,173 against $147,065.

Capital assets and construction. Gross capital assets were $439,700,922 (land $1,861,010; construction in progress $21,750,478; buildings and improvements $358,803,377; furniture and equipment $56,228,659; lease asset-building $530,288; lease assets-equipment $527,110) less accumulated depreciation and amortization of $222,290,537, for net capital assets of $217,410,385, up from $202,522,934 in 2023. Additions totaled $25.4 million for building renovations, site work, furniture, equipment, and technology infrastructure. Depreciation and amortization of $10,501,708 was charged to instruction $4,600,562, support services $5,683,791, community services $106,536, food services $46,356, and athletics $64,463. Remaining contractor commitments totaled $43,106,762: $38,591,768 in the 2023 Capital Projects Fund and $4,514,994 in the Sinking Fund. The projects funded by the 2019 School Building and Site Bonds were considered complete on June 30, 2024, with cumulative construction-period expenditures of $26,703,725; the 2023 Capital Projects Fund is not yet substantially complete and a subsequent-year audit is expected. The district reported compliance with Section 1351a of the Revised School Code for the bonded capital projects funds and Section 1212 for the Sinking Fund.

Debt. General obligation bonds outstanding fell to $252,170,000 from $271,570,000 after $19,400,000 of reductions; with unamortized premium of $23,229,081, total bonds payable was $275,399,081. Outstanding series: the $31,930,000 2015 refunding qualified bond, $6,435,000 remaining at 5.00 percent maturing May 1, 2026; the $40,000,000 2016 qualified bond, $29,150,000 at 2.94-4.50 percent to May 1, 2032; the $7,125,000 2018 unqualified bond, $6,060,000 at 3.00-3.75 percent to May 1, 2040; the $22,630,000 2019 qualified bond, $17,425,000 at 5.00 percent to May 1, 2034; the $6,100,000 2020 unqualified bond, $4,645,000 at 2.00 percent to May 1, 2035; the $33,315,000 2021 refunding qualified bond, $24,505,000 at 0.50-1.56 percent to May 1, 2028; and the $171,370,000 2023 qualified bond, $163,950,000 at 2.75-5.00 percent to May 1, 2052. Remaining debt service to maturity is $401,657,563, comprising $252,170,000 of principal and $149,487,563 of interest, with $32,685,180 due in fiscal 2025. Standard & Poor's affirmed an AA/Stable rating in January 2024. The district's outstanding unqualified general obligation debt of $10.7 million is well below the $1.1 billion statutory limit (15 percent of assessed value); qualified debt totals $241 million. Other long-term liabilities were leases $690,681 (Troy Career Center building and equipment; $763,090 of future payments including $72,409 interest), compensated absences $7,896,313, other termination benefits $165,000, and a newly recorded arbitrage liability of $3,693,631 to be liquidated primarily by the 2023 Capital Projects Fund. Total governmental long-term debt was $287,844,706 with $25,028,546 due within one year.

Deposits and investments. Restricted assets of $189,182,996 comprised unspent bond proceeds and related interest $184,841,180, unspent sinking fund property taxes $1,716,473, and unspent debt service property taxes $2,625,343. The district designated nine financial institutions and used three. Bank deposits of $40,535,431 were uninsured and uncollateralized. Investments carried at amortized cost were the Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Cash Management Money Market Fund $90,570,752 and MILAF MAX Class Money Market $102,724,121, totaling $193,294,873, both AAA-rated by S&P. Unearned revenue of $6,928,277 consisted of student lunch accounts $72,753, tuition and fees in advance $418,825, and grant and categorical aid received before eligibility requirements were met $6,436,699. The district participates in the SET-SEG shared-risk pool for property and general liability.

MPSERS pension and OPEB. The district reported a net pension liability of $288,852,665 (proportion 0.89246 percent, down from 0.90524 percent, a change of (1.41) percent) and a net OPEB asset of $(4,916,519) (proportion 0.86911 percent, down from 0.90842 percent, a change of (4.33) percent), both measured September 30, 2023 from a September 30, 2022 valuation rolled forward. Required and actual pension contributions for the year were $37,379,662, including $17,121,354 of state revenue remitted to fund the MPSERS unfunded actuarial accrued liability stabilization rate; OPEB contributions were $7,817,400. Pension expense was $36,852,268 and the district recognized an OPEB recovery of $8,328,040. Pension deferred outflows totaled $83,291,882 against deferred inflows of $33,483,299; OPEB deferred outflows were $17,884,951 against inflows of $40,841,150. Contribution rates ran 13.90-23.03 percent for pension and 7.06-8.31 percent for OPEB from October 1, 2023 through September 30, 2024. Key assumptions: entry age normal cost method, 6.00 percent investment return and discount rate, salary increases of 2.75-11.55 percent, health care cost trend of 6.25-7.50 percent grading down, PubT-2010 mortality with MP-2021 projection, and a 3.00 percent noncompounded COLA for MIP members. At a 5.00 percent discount rate the net pension liability would be $390,239,103; at 7.00 percent, $204,444,788. Year-end payables to the pension and OPEB plans were $7,976,870 and $1,201,887. Statutorily required contributions were $36,615,148 for pension (41.43 percent of $88,371,160 covered payroll) and $7,260,066 for OPEB (8.22 percent). Plan fiduciary net position reached 65.91 percent of total pension liability and 105.04 percent of total OPEB liability.

Taxes and statistical data. Tax year 2023 taxable value was $6,194,962,650 (residential $4,113,587,760; commercial $1,305,736,060; industrial $411,040,030; personal property $364,598,800) against $4,623,935,940 in tax year 2022, levied at 27.8415 mills with estimated actual value of $12,389,925,300. Direct millage in tax year 2023 was 2.7764 homestead operating, 18.0000 non-homestead, 6.1000 debt, and 0.9651 sinking fund, for 9.8415 total homestead and 25.0651 total non-homestead; overlapping rates included Oakland County 3.9686, community college 1.4891, intermediate school district 3.1658, State Education 6.0000, and City of Troy 9.8966. The FY2024 levy of $76,169,213 was 96.71 percent currently collected, rising to 99.74 percent ($75,972,515) with $2,311,543 of delinquent collections. Principal taxpayers were Somerset Collections ($63,920,120, 1.03 percent), DTE Electric Co. ($50,052,990), Lithia Real Estate Inc ($44,085,040), Troy Apts I-IV LLC ($33,682,460), Zen Troy LLC ($30,730,160), Midtown Place Troy LLC ($28,540,680), Pentrecentre LLC, MK Oakland Mall LLC, CC Troy Associates LLC, and Consumers Energy, together 5.75 percent of taxable value. Industrial facilities tax exemptions under PA 198 of 1974 and brownfield redevelopment agreements reduced property tax revenue by $922,000, of which approximately $662,000 was reimbursed by the State of Michigan. Net general bonded debt was $272,773,738, or 4.40 percent of taxable value and $3,098 per capita; direct and overlapping debt totaled $271,841,016, including City of Troy $10,014,855, Oakland County $9,709,634, and Oakland ISD $2,571,870. The legal debt margin was $918,539,398.

Operations and enrollment. Spring 2024 enrollment was 12,447 across twelve elementary schools, four middle schools, two traditional and one non-traditional high school, and International Academy East, occupying 448.74 acres and 2,185,181 square feet plus 128.30 acres of vacant property. Building enrollments include Troy High School 2,030 (343,207 square feet, built 1992), Athens High School 1,476 (398,426 square feet, 1974), International Academy East 539, Troy College and Career High School 160, Boulan Middle 832, Larson Middle 821, Smith Middle 644, Baker Middle 643, the Preschool/Early 5s building 222, and Troy Center for Transitions 70. Operating expenditures per pupil were $15,383 and operating revenue per pupil $15,666; average teacher salary was $78,145; 17.51 percent of students qualified for free or reduced meals; teaching staff numbered 887 and total FTEs 1,078; the fleet totaled 74 buses. Troy's population was 88,051 with 3.50 percent unemployment; the largest employer was Corewell Health Beaumont Troy Hospital (3,260 employees, 5.43 percent), with Troy School District second at 1,338 out of total employment of 60,058.

Outlook. The 2024-2025 budget, adopted in June 2024, assumes a September 2024 count of 12,297 students, with roughly 66.6 percent of General Fund revenue from the foundation allowance and state sources. The budget was built assuming a $241 per pupil foundation allowance increase, but the enacted state budget provided no foundation allowance increase and instead offsets MPSERS UAAL expenditures, equivalent to $498 per pupil for Troy; the transmittal letter describes the resulting retirement-rate change as worth about $4.7 million and warns the funding is one-time in nature. Voters approved a $555 million bond on November 8, 2022, to be issued in three series over six years with projects planned over 10 to 12 years; the first series was issued in March 2023, and the district expects to exhaust remaining 2013 bond funds in the next fiscal year. Sinking fund millage collections were $4.9 million in 2024. Management notes continued labor-market pressure on custodial, food service, transportation, and special education support staffing, and anticipates difficult decisions to keep the budget balanced. GASB Statements 101 and 102 take effect for the year ending June 30, 2025 and Statement 103 for the year ending June 30, 2026.

Direct millage in tax year 2023 was 2.7764 homestead operating, 18.0000 non-homestead, 6.1000 debt, and 0.9651 sinking fund, for 9.8415 total homestead and 25.0651 total non-homestead; overlapping rates included Oakland County 3.9686, community college 1.4891, intermediate school district 3.1658, State Education 6.0000, and City of Troy 9.8966. The FY2024 levy of $76,169,213 was 96.71 percent currently collected, rising to 99.74 percent ($75,972,515) with $2,311,543 of delinquent collections. Principal taxpayers were Somerset Collections ($63,920,120, 1.03 percent), DTE Electric Co. ($50,052,990), Lithia Real Estate Inc ($44,085,040), Troy Apts I-IV LLC ($33,682,460), Zen Troy LLC ($30,730,160), Midtown Place Troy LLC ($28,540,680), Pentrecentre LLC, MK Oakland Mall LLC, CC Troy Associates LLC, and Consumers Energy, together 5.75 percent of taxable value. Industrial facilities tax exemptions under PA 198 of 1974 and brownfield redevelopment agreements reduced property tax revenue by $922,000, of which approximately $662,000 was reimbursed by the State of Michigan. Net general bonded debt was $272,773,738, or 4.40 percent of taxable value and $3,098 per capita; direct and overlapping debt totaled $271,841,016, including City of Troy $10,014,855, Oakland County $9,709,634, and Oakland ISD $2,571,870. The legal debt margin was $918,539,398.

Operations and enrollment. Spring 2024 enrollment was 12,447 across twelve elementary schools, four middle schools, two traditional and one non-traditional high school, and International Academy East, occupying 448.74 acres and 2,185,181 square feet plus 128.30 acres of vacant property. Building enrollments include Troy High School 2,030 (343,207 square feet, built 1992), Athens High School 1,476 (398,426 square feet, 1974), International Academy East 539, Troy College and Career High School 160, Boulan Middle 832, Larson Middle 821, Smith Middle 644, Baker Middle 643, the Preschool/Early 5s building 222, and Troy Center for Transitions 70. Operating expenditures per pupil were $15,383 and operating revenue per pupil $15,666; average teacher salary was $78,145; 17.51 percent of students qualified for free or reduced meals; teaching staff numbered 887 and total FTEs 1,078; the fleet totaled 74 buses. Troy's population was 88,051 with 3.50 percent unemployment; the largest employer was Corewell Health Beaumont Troy Hospital (3,260 employees, 5.43 percent), with Troy School District second at 1,338 out of total employment of 60,058.

Outlook. The 2024-2025 budget, adopted in June 2024, assumes a September 2024 count of 12,297 students, with roughly 66.6 percent of General Fund revenue from the foundation allowance and state sources. The budget was built assuming a $241 per pupil foundation allowance increase, but the enacted state budget provided no foundation allowance increase and instead offsets MPSERS UAAL expenditures, equivalent to $498 per pupil for Troy; the transmittal letter describes the resulting retirement-rate change as worth about $4.7 million and warns the funding is one-time in nature. Voters approved a $555 million bond on November 8, 2022, to be issued in three series over six years with projects planned over 10 to 12 years; the first series was issued in March 2023, and the district expects to exhaust remaining 2013 bond funds in the next fiscal year. Sinking fund millage collections were $4.9 million in 2024. Management notes continued labor-market pressure on custodial, food service, transportation, and special education support staffing, and anticipates difficult decisions to keep the budget balanced. GASB Statements 101 and 102 take effect for the year ending June 30, 2025 and Statement 103 for the year ending June 30, 2026.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Three bundled memoranda supporting a Troy School District Board of Education policy discussion: a September 15, 2022 memo from Rick West of the Business Office laying out Policy Manual updates recommended by Miller Johnson School Policy Services, the Board Policy Committee, and District Administration; a September 19, 2022 Miller Johnson memo replacing the Open Meetings Act remote-participation language in Policy 1002; and a September 1, 2022 Michigan Department of Education memo on Section 98c learning loss funding. Most consequential is Section 98c of Public Act 144 of 2022 (MCL 388.1698c), appropriating $52,056,000 in federal GEER/ESSER II money, with district applications due November 30, 2022.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Source and authorship**
Memorandum to the Board of Education from Rick West, dated September 15, 2022, subject "Policy Manual Recommended Updates," issued from the Business Office at 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098 (phone 248.823.4022, fax 248.823.4013). Revisions were recommended jointly by Miller Johnson School Policy Services, the Board of Education Policy Committee, and District Administration, and are organized by Policy Manual series.

**Introduction and Bylaws (0000 and 1000 series)**
Policy 0000.03 (The Superintendent of Schools) gains two additions: express authority for the Superintendent to make employment decisions, including hiring and termination, for all non-administrative and non-teaching staff; and authority for the Superintendent to select the School District bargaining team, with the Board approving all team members prior to the start of negotiations and ratifying all negotiated agreements. Administrative Regulations are not effective for one month from the date provided to the Board. Policy 1000.01 renames the sub-policy "Removal from Office" to "Removal from Officer Positions."

**Students (2000 series)**
Policy 2000.01, "Children of Non-Resident Employees," is rewritten to close a loophole allowing a pupil to remain enrolled tuition-free after the parent voluntarily leaves employment; continued attendance is preserved only while the employee remains employed, or where the employee's departure was due to layoff or elimination of the position. "Employee" is defined as an individual with regularly scheduled hours while school is in session, excluding seasonal, coaching, and third-party contracted employees, including substitute teachers. Policy 2000.06 adds personal electronic device rules: use permitted only before and after the regular school day, during the student's scheduled lunch, or as directed by staff for educational purposes; devices otherwise powered off and out of sight; no recording or broadcasting of any student, staff member, or other person without permission, excepting athletic events, arts performances, and similar activities. Policy 2000.07 and 2000.07-AR update Wellness language.

**Curriculum and Instruction (3000 series)**
The entire 3000 section was reviewed given escalating attacks on schools over curriculum. Policy 3000.01 ties curriculum to legally-compliant, research-based standards and states that core academic curriculum changes require Board approval to the extent required by MCL 380.1278. Policy 3000.02 is renamed "Parent and Family Engagement (PFE)" and aligned to Title I. Policy 3000.03 drops an extraneous word. Policy 3000.04 is fully replaced as "Textbooks, Technology, and Other Essential Curricular Materials," citing MCL 380.1421/22 and delegating approval and purchase of non-textbook instructional materials to the Superintendent. Policy 3000.05 is retitled "Selection of Media Center/Library Materials."

**Personnel, Business, General (4000, 5000, 8000 series)**
Policy 4000.03 adds authority to require a medical examination on reasonable suspicion of drug, alcohol, or illegal substance influence, with all costs borne by the School District and reports kept in a separate confidential personnel file. Policy 5000.03 gains a new "Real Property and Structures" acquisition sub-policy; Policy 5000.05's disposition sub-policy is renamed to match. Policy 5000.11 deletes the list of fundraising sites (DonorsChoose.org, Kickstarter.com, GoFundMe.com, CrowdRise.com). No 6000 series changes. Policy 8000.07 is revised for Title IX and designates the Assistant Superintendent of Employees Services and Title IX Coordinator.

**Attached memoranda**
A September 19, 2022 Miller Johnson memo offers Option A and Option B replacements for the Open Meetings Act remote-participation language in Policy 1002. A September 1, 2022 MDE memo from Deputy Superintendent Delsa D. Chapman covers Section 98c learning loss funds of $52,056,000.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Cover memorandum.** Rick West wrote to the Troy School District Board of Education on September 15, 2022, subject "Policy Manual Recommended Updates," on Business Office letterhead showing 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, phone 248.823.4022, fax 248.823.4013. The updates were recommended by Miller Johnson School Policy Services, the Board of Education Policy Committee, and District Administration, and are organized by Policy Manual section.

**Introduction - 0000 Series.** Policy 0000.03, The Superintendent of Schools, gains two additions. The Superintendent, employed in conformity with the Revised School Code as chief administrator, is authorized by the Board to make employment decisions, including hiring and termination, for all non-administrative and non-teaching staff, and develops Administrative Regulations that, except as otherwise agreed by the Board, will not be effective for a period of one month from the date provided to the Board; the Board may but need not formally approve them, and references to the Superintendent include his/her designee. On collective bargaining, the Board is represented in all labor negotiation proceedings by a negotiating team whose members the Board approves prior to the start of negotiations, the Superintendent shall select the bargaining team, and all negotiated agreements are subject to Board ratification.

**Bylaws - 1000 Series.** Policy 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board, renames the sub-policy "Removal from Office" to "Removal from Officer Positions," since it concerns removal of Board officers from officer positions rather than removal from the Board itself.

**Students - 2000 Series.** Policy 2000.01, Admission and Enrollment, sub-policy "Children of Non-Resident Employees," is rewritten consistent with the State Aid Act and the Pupil Accounting Manual to close a loophole under which a person could obtain employment, enroll a child, then voluntarily leave employment while the pupil kept tuition-free enrollment. A child of a non-resident employee may enroll without tuition in the K-12 program and continue through graduation or a certificate of completion while the employee remains employed, or if the employee's departure was due to layoff or elimination of the position; long-term suspension or expulsion under the Student Code of Conduct is not barred. "Employee" means an individual with regularly scheduled hours while school is in session, excluding seasonal, coaching, and third-party contracted employees including substitute teachers, with eligibility starting at the next school term/semester.

Policy 2000.06, Behavior, defines a personal electronic device as a privately owned device used for audio, video, or text communications. Use is permitted only before and after the regular school day, during the student's scheduled lunch time, and as directed by a teacher or other professional staff member for educational purposes; otherwise devices must be powered off and out of sight in backpacks/purses or lockers. Students may not broadcast or record audio, images, or video of any student, staff member, or other person in school or at a school-related activity without permission, except for activities where personal recording is generally permitted such as athletic events and arts performances. Policy 2000.07, Health and Safety, updates Wellness in both policy and administrative regulation 2000.07-AR for compliance with the latest federal regulatory guidance on student wellness and nutrition.

**Curriculum and Instruction - 3000 Series.** Citing the current political environment and escalating attacks on schools and boards over curriculum development and approval, the whole 3000 section was reviewed. Policy 3000.01, Curriculum Development, directs the Superintendent to develop, implement, and evaluate the core academic curriculum, consistent with the Board's policy on Student Learning and Achievement, meeting or exceeding all State of Michigan requirements, standards based on legally-compliant, research-based grade level learning and achievement standards leading to a School District diploma, and addressing career and technical education, students of all abilities and with disabilities, and gifted students; core curriculum changes require Board approval to the extent required by MCL 380.1278. Policy 3000.02 is renamed "Parent and Family Engagement (PFE)," with regulations covering skill development, review of curriculum, textbooks, and teaching materials, observation of instruction other than testing and assessments, and disclosure of student information for sales or marketing, plus Title I duties to inform and train parents and staff, consult regularly, involve families in program design and evaluation, and enable participation by those lacking literacy skills or whose native language is not English, with services in Title I schools comparable to non-Title I schools. Policy 3000.03, Instruction (cited in the memo body as 3003.03), drops an extraneous word, leaving instruction delivered to the maximum extent feasible using research based and peer reviewed instructional methodologies. Policy 3000.04 is comprehensively replaced and retitled "Textbooks, Technology, and Other Essential Curricular Materials" from "Textbooks and Other Instructional Materials"; textbooks are recommended to the Board for approval to the extent required by MCL 380.1421/22, while the Board delegates to the Superintendent authority to approve and purchase other instructional materials, which need no Board approval but must be compatible with the approved core curriculum. Policy 3000.05 is retitled "Selection of Media Center/Library Materials," authorizing the Superintendent to approve purchases for the media center and classroom libraries on recommendations from professional staff members, parents, and students.

**Personnel - 4000 Series.** Policy 4000.03, Conditions of Employment, sub-policy Alcohol and Drug Free Workplace, lets the Superintendent require a medical examination on reasonable suspicion that an employee is under the influence of drugs, alcohol, or illegal substances while performing job duties or on school grounds; employees or volunteers who unlawfully manufacture, distribute, dispense, possess, or use alcohol or any drug in the workplace, or are present under the influence, face discipline up to and including discharge. The Medical Examinations sub-policy lists triggers: required or permitted by federal or state law; required or permitted by the employment contract; information suggesting a health condition may negatively affect performance of essential functions with or without accommodations; information suggesting a direct threat to the employee's safety or that of others; insufficient medical documentation for a health leave after a chance to supplement; and reasonable suspicion of influence. All costs are borne by the School District, the employee signs a release for the physician to report directly to the Superintendent, and the report is kept in a separate confidential personnel file.

**Business - 5000 Series.** A new sub-policy "Real Property and Structures" is added to Policy 5000.03, Purchasing, because baseline policies covered only disposition of land, buildings, facilities, and real estate without matching acquisition authority, and because title agencies routinely require a board resolution and a document authorizing an individual, most commonly the Board President or Superintendent, to execute closing documents; Board approval is required for both the process and the purchase, and the Superintendent may execute all closing documents. Under Policy 5000.05, Surplus Property, the sub-policy "Land, Buildings, Facilities, and Real Estate" is renamed "Real Property and Structures" for sale or disposition, with parallel provisions; the memo notes the two share a title but differ in objective and impact. Policy 5000.11, Online Fundraising, deletes the list of services DonorsChoose.org, Kickstarter.com, GoFundMe.com, and CrowdRise.com; no employee may create, post, or sponsor an online fundraiser without prior written consent from the Superintendent, and property secured becomes District property.

**Facilities and Operations - 6000 Series:** no recommended updates. **School and Community Relations - 7000 Series** is listed without changes.

**General Policies - 8000 Series.** Policy 8000.07, Discrimination and Harassment, and regulation 8000.07-AR are revised for Title IX. The U.S. Department of Education issued new guidelines in 2020, updating the regulations for the first time since 1997, and the 2021-22 school year was the first meaningful opportunity for most districts to live with them in a normal school year. Draft Title IX regulations issued in June 2022 are not final and are not integrated; finalization is not expected until approximately late 2023. The policy bars discrimination or harassment based on race, color, national origin, religion, sex (including sexual orientation and gender identity), marital status, genetic information, disability, age, or any other basis prohibited by law, and designates the Assistant Superintendent of Employees Services and Title IX Coordinator to supervise implementation.

**Miller Johnson Open Meetings Act memo.** Dated September 19, 2022, from MJ School Policy Services to MJ Policy Service Clients, concerning Policy 1002 ("Meetings of the Board of Education"). The July 2022 Electronic Meetings and Remote Participation language is marked OUTDATED AS OF 9/16/22 UPDATE. Both replacement options permit remote participation only for absence due to military leave or reasonable accommodation for a disability; medical condition and local state of emergency/disaster bases were removed because the Open Meetings Act no longer permits them. Attorney General Nessel released an opinion letter earlier in the year holding a board member with a disability must be accommodated, reasoning the Americans with Disabilities Act negates the OMA where compliance would require violating the ADA. The memo weighs MCL 15.263a(1), allowing electronic meetings, against MCL 15.263a(8), limiting electronic participation to members absent on military duty, and argues members may still contribute remotely if not counted toward a quorum and not a deciding vote. Option A requires physical presence to participate except as otherwise permitted by the OMA; Option B requires physical presence only to be counted toward a quorum or to vote. Conditions for military-duty or disability remote attendance: advance notice consistent with MCL 15.263a(4) and agenda posting consistent with MCL 15.263a(5); the Board Secretary recording each remote member's name in the minutes plus an opening announcement that, except for military duty, identifies the member's location by state and city, township, county, or village; 2-way communication; notice to the Board President at least one business day before the meeting; and steps such as roll call voting. Questions go to Policy@MillerJohnson.com.

**Michigan Department of Education Section 98c memo.** Dated September 1, 2022, to Local and Intermediate School District Superintendents and Public School Academy Directors, from Delsa D. Chapman, Ed.D., Deputy Superintendent, Division of Educator, Student, and School Supports, subject "Public Act 144 of 2022 - Section 98c - Learning Loss." MDE opened the application window September 15, 2022 for LEAs, both traditional districts and public school academies. PA 144 of 2022 (MCL 388.1698c) was signed July 14, 2022 by Governor Gretchen Whitmer and appropriates $52,056,000 in federal funding under the Governor's Emergency Education Relief (GEER) Fund and the federal Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) II Fund. Applications were due no later than November 30, 2022 and required an assurance that by not later than October 30, 2022 a presentation on use of the funds would be given at a public meeting of the LEA board, a link to the learning loss plan posted on the LEA website with an assurance to post updates, and a brief description of district metrics. Recipients must report to MDE by July 14, 2023 on funds spent, services provided, students reached, metrics, and impact, feeding a single legislative report due August 15, 2023; funds are recaptured if a district misses the deadline. ESSER II targets low-income students, children with disabilities, English learners, racial and ethnic minorities, students experiencing homelessness, and children and youth in foster care via reliable assessments, evidence-based activities, parent and family assistance, and tracking of engagement in distance learning. Funding is distributed to each LEA in an equal amount per pupil in membership, calculated after the November 30 close, with disbursement anticipated in the early winter state school aid payments. The application link is https://mdoe.state.mi.us/gems/public/QuestionnaireHome.aspx?code=i4d1tcbt; technical assistance meetings were set for 2:30 p.m. EST on September 19, 2022 and 11:00 a.m. EST on November 4, 2022; application questions go to mde-gems@michigan.gov and learning loss questions to Ruth Anne Hodges at hodgesr3@michigan.gov, with copies to the Michigan Education Alliance and the Confederation of Michigan Tribal Education Departments. The letterhead lists State Board of Education members Casandra E. Ulbrich (President), Pamela Pugh (Vice President), Tiffany D. Tilley (Secretary), Tom McMillin (Treasurer), Judith Pritchett (NASBE Delegate), Ellen Cogen Lipton, and Nikki Snyder, State Superintendent Michael F. Rice, Ph.D., Governor Gretchen Whitmer, and 608 West Allegan Street, P.O. Box 30008, Lansing, Michigan 48909, telephone 833-633-5788.

**Instrument and setting**
Resolution Authorizing 2023 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, drafted for a regular Board of Education meeting held December 13, 2022 at 7:00 p.m. local time. The circulated copy has blanks for members present and absent, for the mover and supporter, and for the AYES and NAYS roll, and is certified by Gary Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education, with a recital of compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of 1976.

**Voter authorization**
At the General School Election held November 8, 2022, qualified electors approved bonds issuable in one or more series in an amount not to exceed $555,000,000 (the 2022 Bond Proposal) for remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields, playgrounds and other facilities; erecting and completing, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom additions and other additions; acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment; acquiring, preparing, developing and improving sites; and the purchase of school buses.

**Bond parameters**

| Term | Provision |
|---|---|
| First series maximum | not to exceed $190,000,000 |
| Denomination | $5,000 or integral multiples |
| Maturity dates | May 1 or November 1, as determined at sale |
| Final maturity | not later than 30 years from date of issue |
| Maximum true interest cost | 6.50% per annum |
| Interest payment dates | semi-annually, May 1 and November 1 |
| Underwriter's discount cap | 0.50% of principal amount |
| Record date | fifteenth day of the month prior to payment |

Bonds may be issued in book-entry-only form through The Depository Trust Company in New York, New York, as serial or term bonds, subject to optional or mandatory redemption as determined at sale.

**Funds and tax pledge**

Commencing with the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2023, the District must levy annually a tax sufficient to pay principal and interest, without limitation as to rate or amount under Article IX, Sections 6 and 16 of the Michigan Constitution of 1963.

**Professionals and process**
Stifel, Nicolaus & Company, Incorporated is appointed senior managing underwriter; Miller, Canfield, Paddock and Stone, P.L.C. is appointed bond counsel, with disclosure of its periodic unrelated representation of Stifel; PFM Financial Advisors LLC is appointed Municipal Advisor. The Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, either acting individually, serve as Authorized Officer with power to negotiate and execute the bond purchase agreement, execute a sale order, seek ratings and bond insurance, and approve official statements. **Exhibits**
Exhibit A is the bond form naming Cede & Co. as registered owner, citing Act 451, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, interest on a 360-day year of twelve 30-day months, and redemption notice 30 to 60 days in advance. Exhibit B is the Continuing Disclosure Undertaking under SEC Rule 15c2-12, requiring annual filing through MSRB EMMA by the last day of the sixth month after fiscal year end, commencing with the fiscal year ending June 30, 2023. Exhibit C is the Application for Final Qualification of Bonds. Identifier 39939819.

**Caption and posture.** Captioned TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT, COUNTY OF OAKLAND, State of MICHIGAN, RESOLUTION AUTHORIZING 2023 School Building and Site Bonds (UNLIMITED TAX GENERAL OBLIGATION). It recites that it was offered at a regular meeting of the Board of Education of the Troy School District held in the School District on December 13, 2022, at 7:00 p.m., local time. The packet copy leaves the PRESENT and ABSENT member lists blank, leaves blank the members offering and supporting the resolution, and leaves the AYES and NAYS lines blank; Gary Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education, signs twice, once beneath "RESOLUTION DECLARED ADOPTED" and once certifying the document as a true and complete copy of a resolution adopted at a regular meeting held December 13, 2022, conducted with public notice given in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of 1976, as amended.

**Recitals.** At the General School Election held in the School District on November 8, 2022, qualified electors approved the issuance of bonds, in one or more series, in an amount not to exceed $555,000,000, the 2022 Bond Proposal. Approved purposes are remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields, playgrounds and other facilities; erecting and completing, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom additions and other additions to existing school buildings and other facilities; acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment; and acquiring sites, preparing, developing and improving sites at school buildings and other facilities and the purchase of school buses, collectively the Projects. Under Section 6, Article IX and Section 16, Article IX of the Michigan Constitution of 1963, tax levies for these bonds are without limitation as to rate or amount. The Board authorizes a first series not to exceed $190,000,000 to pay Project and issuance costs, and designates the Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, either one acting individually, as the Authorized Officer empowered to accept an underwriter's offer, negotiate, approve and execute a bond purchase agreement, and approve other terms and documents. The School District must either be granted qualified status within the meaning of Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended, or receive prior approval from the Michigan Department of Treasury.

**Bond details.** The Bonds are designated 2023 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), issuable in one or more series with name, designation or suffix changes as appropriate, in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $190,000,000 or such lesser amount as the Authorized Officer determines upon sale. They are registered as to principal and interest in the denomination of $5,000 or integral multiples, dated as of the date of delivery or another date set by the Authorized Officer, and numbered as determined by the Transfer Agent. Bonds mature on May 1 or November 1 in years and amounts set at sale, with final maturity not later than thirty (30) years from the date of issue. Interest is set upon negotiated sale at a rate or rates not exceeding a true interest cost of six and one-half percent (6.50%) per annum, payable semi-annually on May 1 and November 1. The underwriter's discount shall not exceed 0.50% of the principal amount. Principal is payable at a bank or trust company selected by the Authorized Officer serving as registrar and transfer agent. Interest is paid by check drawn on the Transfer Agent and mailed to the registered owner of record as of the fifteenth day of the month prior to each payment date, a date the District may change to conform to market practice. Bonds may be issued in book-entry-only form through The Depository Trust Company in New York, New York, as serial or term bonds or both, subject to optional or mandatory redemption at times, in the manner and at prices determined by the Authorized Officer. Official notice of redemption must state at minimum the original issue date, maturity dates, interest rates, CUSIP numbers if any, certificate numbers and called amounts for partial redemptions, the redemption date, the redemption price, the surrender location, and that interest ceases to accrue after the redemption date.

**Execution and funds.** Bonds follow the form in Exhibit A, signed by manual or facsimile signatures of the President and Secretary of the Board, and are invalid until authenticated by the Transfer Agent, which delivers them to the purchaser on instructions from the Treasurer of the Board upon payment. Unless a Common Debt Retirement Fund is established, the Treasurer shall open a special depositary account designated the 2023 School Building and Site Bonds Debt Retirement Fund, into which all tax proceeds levied for principal, interest and redemption price, plus any accrued interest received on delivery, are deposited and used solely for those payments. The Treasurer shall also establish the 2023 School Building and Site Bonds Projects Fund, holding amounts specified by the Authorized Officer from net sale proceeds and any net original issue premium, used only for Project costs and issuance costs and, as necessary, to rebate arbitrage earnings to the United States Department of Treasury under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended. Net original issue premium may be used for capitalized interest or to reduce the principal amount issued and shall be counted against the 2022 Bond Proposal. Remaining moneys after Project completion may be used first for any purpose permitted by the 2022 Bond Proposal, second for any purpose permitted by law, and then transferred to the Debt Retirement Fund.

**Unlimited tax pledge.** Commencing with the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2023, the School District has a duty to levy annually a tax sufficient so that estimated collections will promptly pay principal and interest when due, without limitation as to rate or amount.

**Sale method and professionals.** Having considered competitive and negotiated sale, and on the advice of the Municipal Advisor, the District determined a negotiated sale provides greater flexibility in structuring maturities and timing and will enable better marketing to the advantage of the School District and its taxpayers. Stifel, Nicolaus & Company, Incorporated is appointed senior managing underwriter; the Authorized Officer may appoint co-managing underwriters if recommended by the Municipal Advisor, may award the sale within the resolution's parameters, and may execute the bond purchase agreement and a sale order without further Board approval. Miller, Canfield, Paddock and Stone, P.L.C. is appointed bond counsel, with the Board approving that representation notwithstanding Miller Canfield's periodic representation in unrelated matters of Stifel, Nicolaus & Company, Incorporated and other potential parties. PFM Financial Advisors LLC is appointed financial advisor, the Municipal Advisor. The Authorized Officer may apply for bond ratings and purchase municipal bond insurance if deemed appropriate by the Municipal Advisor and Bond Counsel. The President of the Board and the Authorized Officer may each approve preliminary and final official statements and execute and deliver the final Official Statement and any amendments, ensuring the statements contain no untrue statement of material fact and omit no material fact necessary to make them not misleading.

**Disclosure, tax and Treasury.** The District covenants under SEC Rule 15c2-12 to provide the Exhibit B information, and covenants to take all actions within its control to maintain the exclusion of interest on the Bonds from adjusted gross income for federal income tax purposes under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, including arbitrage rebate and the expenditure and investment of bond proceeds. The Authorized Officer may apply to Treasury for prior approval or file a qualifying statement, request waivers including rating waivers, and file a Security Report pursuant to the Act. District officers may seek interim approval and qualification under the School Bond Qualification, Approval, and Loan Act, Act 92, Public Acts of Michigan, 2005, as amended; the Authorized Officer may approve the Application for Final Qualification substantially in the form of Exhibit C and sign loan agreements, and the Secretary of the Board is directed to execute and submit the completed Application to Treasury. Officers, administrators, agents and attorneys may pay costs of issuance including Bond Counsel fees, Municipal Advisor fees, rating agency fees, Transfer Agent fees, and costs of printing the preliminary and official statements. All conflicting resolutions are rescinded.

**Exhibit A, Bond Form.** Names Cede & Co. as Registered Owner, with blanks for Interest Rate, Maturity Date of May 1, 20__, Date of Original Issue, and CUSIP. Interest is computed on a 360-day year consisting of twelve 30-day months. The bond recites issuance under Act 451, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, as amended, and Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended, pursuant to the resolution adopted December 13, 2022, as the first series authorized by majority vote of electors at the General School Election held November 8, 2022. The full faith and credit of the School District is irrevocably pledged and the District must levy annually sufficient taxes without limitation as to rate or amount. Redemption notice is mailed at least 30 days and not more than 60 days prior to the redemption date; bonds are called in multiples of $5,000, with no further interest accruing after the redemption date if funds are on hand. The Transfer Agent need not register a transfer during the 15 days before mailing a redemption notice. Signature blocks provide for the President and countersigning Secretary and a Transfer Agent Certificate of Authentication dated in 2023.

**Exhibit B, Continuing Disclosure Undertaking.** Defines Audited Financial Statements prepared as required by Act 2, Public Acts of Michigan, 1968, as amended, along with Bondholders, EMMA (the MSRB's Electronic Municipal Market Access system), Financial Obligation, MSRB, Rule, and SEC. The District must file through EMMA on or before the last day of the sixth month after its fiscal year end, commencing with the fiscal year ending June 30, 2023, annual financial information and operating data matching Official Statement tables on Enrollment - Historical Enrollment; State Aid Payments; Property Valuations - History of Valuations; Major Taxpayers; School District Tax Rates (per $1,000 of Valuation); Tax Levies and Collections; Retirement Plan - Contribution to MPSERS; Debt Statement - Direct Debt; School Loan Revolving Fund (SLRF) Program; and General Fund Budget Summary in Appendix C, together with the Audited Financial Statements, with unaudited statements filed if the audit is not ready. Failure to disclose must be noticed timely. Sixteen enumerated events require notice within ten business days, including payment delinquencies, material non-payment defaults, unscheduled draws on debt service reserves or credit enhancements, adverse tax opinions and IRS determinations including Notices of Proposed Issue (IRS Form 5701-TEB), material bond calls and tender offers, defeasances, rating changes, bankruptcy or receivership, material mergers or asset sales, and material incurrence of or default under a Financial Obligation. Materiality is determined under federal securities laws; the obligation terminates when the District is no longer an obligated person, including upon legal defeasance; enforcement is limited to specific performance and non-compliance is not an event of default on the Bonds.

**Exhibit C.** Form of Application for Final Qualification of Bonds. The document carries the internal identifier 39939819.

**Origin**
Memorandum of March 2, 2022 from Rick West, Business Office, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098 (phone 248.823.4022, fax 248.823.4013), to the Troy School District Board of Education. Recommendations come from Miller Johnson School Policy Services, the Board of Education Policy Committee and District Administration, broken down by Policy Manual section.

**Bylaws**
Policy 1000.02 Meeting of the Board of Education: quorum language modified and the Electronic Meetings and Remote Participation section removed, because Michigan Open Meetings Act revisions took effect January 1, 2022. A majority of serving members constitutes a quorum; a member not physically present may participate remotely if all attendees can hear and interact with that member, with 24 hours advance notice to the presiding chair. The deleted section had required one business day notice to the Board President, naming remote attendees in the minutes, and roll call voting.

**Students**
- 2000.01 Admission and Enrollment: children of non-resident employees may enroll tuition-free only if enrolling in the K-12 program; enrollment continues through graduation or certificate of completion, subject to long-term suspension or expulsion.
- 2000.02 Learning Environment: adds Child Find under IDEA and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, with notices naming Jessica Carrier as both Section 504 Coordinator and Director of Special Education, 248-823-5002, jcarrier@troy.k12.mi.us.
- 2000.06 Attendance and Truancy: expanded language referencing MCL 380.1561 and referral to Child Protective Services, police or prosecutor.
- 2000.06 Student Code of Conduct: additions for House Bills 5330-5332 covering criminal sexual conduct and cyberbullying committed off campus.
- 2000.06 Student Bullying: most granular language moves to the Administrative Regulation Manual, consistent with MCL 380.1310b.

**Curriculum and Instruction**
- 3000.01 Virtual Courses Allowance, added for the 2020-2021 school year, is recommended for removal.
- 3000.02 Parental Involvement: terminology discussion concluding the terms are interchangeable.
- 3000.09 Limited English Proficiency: rewritten around emergent multilingual students and the Michigan Department of Education Entrance and Exit Protocols.

**Personnel**
- 4000.02 Discrimination and Harassment and Nepotism, the latter expanding "relative" to in-laws, step- and half-relations and co-residents.
- 4000.05 Outside Activities and a new Illegal Conflicts of Interest provision citing MCL 380.1203 and MCL 15.321 et seq.

**Business**
- 5000.03 Purchasing rewritten; Federal Procurement Standards added referencing EDGAR and 2 CFR Part 200, delegated to the Assistant Superintendent for Business Services.
- 5000.05 Surplus Property broadened to facilities, real estate and other personal property.
- New 5000.11 Online Fundraising requires prior written Superintendent consent, naming DonorsChoose.org, Kickstarter.com, GoFundMe.com and CrowdRise.com.

**Facilities and Operations / General**
6000.02 Firearms and Other Weapons; new 6000.07 Private Transportation with IRS-rate mileage reimbursement; new 6000.09 Stormwater Discharge under the NPDES rules; 8000.07 Discrimination and Harassment naming Jordan Harris as Compliance Officer and Title IX Coordinator; and 8000.10 Animals on District Property.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum dated March 2, 2022, sent from Rick West of the Troy School District Business Office at 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098 (phone 248.823.4022, fax 248.823.4013) to the Board of Education, outlines proposed updates to the District's Policy Manual as recommended by Miller Johnson School Policy Services, the Board of Education Policy Committee and District Administration, with the rationale for each change and revisions grouped by manual section. No recommended updates are offered for the Introduction section or for School and Community Relations.

BYLAWS. Policy 1000.02, Meeting of the Board of Education, is modified in its quorum provision and the Electronic Meetings and Remote Participation section is removed. The memorandum explains that the Michigan Open Meetings Act has undergone significant revision since the onset of the pandemic; after initially allowing broad latitude for online meetings and remote participation, those options were significantly scaled back in OMA revisions that took effect on January 1, 2022. Removal still permits remote participation in limited situations as provided in the OMA. The retained quorum language provides that, unless otherwise required or permitted by law, a majority of the serving members constitutes a quorum; a member not physically present at a duly held meeting where a quorum is already present may participate by telephone, teleconference, video conference or other electronic means so long as any attendee can hear and interact with that member, and the absent member must notify the presiding chair 24 hours in advance to participate remotely and may vote to the extent allowed by Michigan law. The deleted section required the Board Secretary to name each remotely attending member in the minutes, required the remote member to hear and be heard, required notice to the Board President at least one business day before the meeting so the public could be told how to contact the member, and required the Board President to ensure the public knew how any remote member voted, such as by requiring roll call voting.

STUDENTS. Policy 2000.01, Admission and Enrollment, revises the Children of Non-resident Employees provision so a child of a non-resident district employee may enroll without tuition only if enrolling in the K-12 program and not some other district offering; once enrolled the student may continue through graduation or receipt of a certificate of completion, without barring long-term suspension or expulsion for violating the Student Code of Conduct. Policy 2000.02, Learning Environment, adds Child Find language committing the district to identify and locate every student residing in the district who may be a student with a disability under the Individuals with Disabilities in Education Act and/or Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, regardless of whether they currently receive a public education, using advertising, posted notices, district publications including its website, and direct contact with parents. The notices must be easily understandable to a parent and must list the Section 504 Coordinator and Director of Special Education, both identified as Jessica Carrier, 248-823-5002, jcarrier@troy.k12.mi.us.

Policy 2000.06, Behavior, receives three sets of changes. Attendance and Truancy is expanded to require attendance every day school is in session except when excused, to direct the Superintendent to develop implementing regulations, and to allow referral to Child Protective Services or the appropriate police agency or prosecutor's office where a parent fails to comply with Michigan's compulsory school attendance law, MCL 380.1561. The Student Code of Conduct provision is amended because the Michigan Legislature recently passed House Bills 5330-5332, which require districts to expel, suspend and/or transfer students who commit criminal sexual conduct on school grounds or against another student at the same school; the code is stated to apply on school premises, en route to and from school, at district-related events and to off-campus behavior that substantially disrupts district activities or that the district is legally required to consider, such as criminal sexual conduct and cyberbullying. The Student Bullying policy is streamlined, with most granular language moved into the Administrative Regulation Manual in compliance with MCL 380.1310b while retaining the prohibition on bullying "at school" and on off-campus conduct likely to cause material or substantial disruption, protection against retaliation and false accusations, confidentiality for reporters, building principals as responsible school officials, annual Superintendent reporting to the Board of all verified incidents and consequences imposed, and definitions of "bullying," "at school" and "cyberbullying," including the off-premises use of a telecommunications access device or service provider owned or controlled by the district.

CURRICULUM AND INSTRUCTION. Policy 3000.01, Curriculum Development, is recommended for removal of the Virtual Courses Allowance added at the outset of the pandemic for the 2020-2021 school year under the Michigan Department of Education Pupil Accounting Manual. Policy 3000.02, Parental Involvement, is addressed only in commentary: some clients argue for "parental and family engagement," federal law since December 2015 uses "community and family engagement," prior federal law and the Revised School Code use "parental involvement," and the terms are treated as interchangeable. Policy 3000.09, Limited English Proficiency, is revised in its entirety, replacing "English language deficiency" language with a commitment to equitable opportunities for emergent multilingual students and English learners, identification under the Michigan Department of Education's Entrance Protocol for English Language Development Programs, and annual assessment measured against the MDE Exit Protocol.

PERSONNEL. Policy 4000.02, Employment Considerations, clarifies Discrimination and Harassment protections covering race, color, national origin, religion, sex, marital status, genetic information, disability, age or any other illegal grounds, cross-referencing Policy 8000.07. The Nepotism provision expands "related" and "relative" to father, mother, son, daughter, brother, sister, spouse, father-in-law, mother-in-law, brother-in-law, sister-in-law, son-in-law, daughter-in-law, step-father, step-mother, step-son, step-daughter, step- or half-brother, step- or half-sister, and any other persons residing at the same location. Policy 4000.05, Other Matters of Employment, adds to Outside Activities restrictions on paid tutoring of currently assigned students, tutoring during the school day or on district property, political campaigning on district premises or during work hours, use of district resources for political activity, and employee sales to students; and adds a new Illegal Conflicts of Interest provision citing MCL 380.1203 and Contracts of Public Servants with Public Entities, MCL 15.321 et seq., recommended after auditor feedback in other districts.

BUSINESS. Policy 5000.03, Purchasing, replaces the prior competitive-purchasing language with authority for the Superintendent to purchase or supervise purchases, to seek maximum value, to promulgate administrative regulations, to use competitive bidding when and as required by law, and to use competitive bidding or cooperative pricing otherwise at his or her discretion. A Federal Procurement Standards subsection is added acknowledging the Education Department General Administrative Regulations (EDGAR) and their gradual transfer to 2 CFR Part 200, the Federal Uniform Guidance, with responsibility delegated to the Assistant Superintendent for Business Services. Policy 5000.05, Surplus Property, is broadened from land and buildings to land, buildings, facilities and real estate, and from equipment and supplies to equipment, supplies and other personal property including identified surplus personal property. A new Policy 5000.11, Online Fundraising, bars any employee from creating, posting or sponsoring an online fundraiser using the District's name, logo or likeness without prior written Superintendent consent, and vests any property so obtained in the District rather than the employee, naming DonorsChoose.org, Kickstarter.com, GoFundMe.com and CrowdRise.com as examples.

FACILITIES AND OPERATIONS. Policy 6000.02, Safety and Security, adds language to Firearms and Other Weapons permitting law enforcement officers and security resource officers to carry firearms on school property, while employees and students who violate the policy face discipline including permanent expulsion or discharge and others may be banned from district premises and functions. Policy 6000.07, Transportation, adds a stand-alone Private Transportation policy allowing parents or guardians to request permission for a student to self-transport to and from a district site or program, prompted by a rise in lawsuits and insurance claims from students injured in privately owned vehicles driven by district employees, and authorizing employee travel reimbursement at the Internal Revenue Service rate. Policy 6000.09 adds Stormwater Discharge, responding to Clean Water Act amendments and the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System regulation of Non-Point Sources by the United States Environmental Protection Agency, and directing the Superintendent to promulgate administrative regulations.

GENERAL POLICIES. Policy 8000.07, Discrimination and Harassment, is aligned with the new Title IX regulations issued by the U.S. Department of Education and designates Jordan Harris, Compliance Officer and Title IX Coordinator, to investigate and resolve complaints and supervise implementation. Policy 8000.10, Animals on District Property, recognizes animals used in classroom presentations and housed on campus and the presence of service or therapy animals accompanying employees, students, parents, vendors and members of the public under federal and state law, applying to all animals including service animals, with administrative regulations to follow.
