**Presentation**
Overview of Fiscal Year 2022-23 Oakland Schools Proposed Budgets, presented by Michelle Saunders on April 22, 2022, covering an enterprise-wide overview, the General Education Fund, the Special Education Fund, the Career Focused Education Fund and other funds.

**Budget timeline**
Nov 2021 develop budget assumptions; Jan 2022 first draft of FY23 budgets to OS Administration; Feb 2022 Oakland County Equalization presentation of taxable value estimates; March 2022 budgets submitted to LEAs; April 2022 meetings with OCSBO and LEA Board Designates; June 1, 2022 L-4028IC received from the County with the millage reduction fraction, rollback determined and LEA budget resolutions received; June 6, 2022 Truth in Budgeting Hearing and FY23 budget approved by the Board.

**Assumptions for the three major operating funds**
Revenue: property tax increase of 4% including the probability of a Headlee rollback; state aid held flat except Sec. 81 ISD Operations up 2%, Sec. 147c UAAL increasing and Sec. 61a Vocational Education reverting to FY21 levels. Expenditures: salary increase of 2% for all staff plus steps (approximately .98% union, 1.28% non-union), blended MPSERS rate of 28.26%, health care cap increase of 3.7%, and dental/vision reductions from a move to a premium-based program. Fund balance targets are 7.5% to 12.5% of expenditures for GEF and CFEF and 5% to 10% for SEF, net of LEA distributions.

**Enterprise-wide FY23**
Revenue $391.2 million; expenditures $393.2 million, all funds except the Internal Service Fund. Expected FY23 levy $216.6 million.

**Fund summaries**

| Fund | FY23 revenues | Property tax share | Key expenditure |
|---|---|---|---|
| General Education | $22.9M | $12.9M (56.3%) | Expenditures $23.5M |
| Special Education | $171.9M | $163.7M (95.2%) | PA-18 base distribution $148.3M (86.3%) |
| Career Focused Education | $46.3M | $40.0M (86.4%) | Campus & other program operations $27.3M (59.0%) |

**Distributions to districts**
Subsidies total $1,211,750: Illuminate DnA $363,800, Career cruising software $302,700, Atlas Rubicon $184,500, Nepris $155,000, Discovery Education Streaming $149,500, communications media monitoring $23,850, MiPEER $17,400, CDX automotive software $15,000. Other distributions and program subsidies total $167,285,400: PA-18 base distribution $148,300,000, Medicaid distributions $11,397,400, CTE career readiness $3,088,000, other special education subsidies $2,700,000 and CTE transportation reimbursement $1,800,000.

**Staffing as of 3.8.22**
Business & Operations subtotal moves from 69.82 to 72.82 FTE; Programs & Services from 421.29 to 423.39; Other Programs & Services steady at 169.20; total across all departments 665.41 for 2022-23, a change of 5.10.

**Other funds**
Three grant funds with $84.2M in new awards and $22.8M carryover, including direct transfers to districts of $81.6M; five special revenue funds, three debt service funds, three capital projects funds and two proprietary funds. Under Revised School Code 380.624, constituent districts must review the proposed ISD General Fund budget and adopt a resolution of support or disapproval by June 1.

An Oakland Schools slide deck titled Overview of Fiscal Year 2022-23 Oakland Schools Proposed Budgets, presented by Michelle Saunders on April 22, 2022, walks the Oakland County School Business Officials through the intermediate district's FY23 budget: an enterprise-wide overview, the General Education Fund, Special Education Fund, Career Focused Education Fund, other funds and budget timelines.

TIMELINE. November 2021, develop budget assumptions. January 2022, first draft of FY23 budgets to OS Administration. February 2022, Oakland County Equalization presentation of taxable value estimates. March 2022, budgets submitted to LEAs. April 2022, meetings with OCSBO and LEA Board Designates. June 1, 2022, L-4028IC received from the County with the millage reduction fraction, rollback determined and LEA budget resolutions received. June 6, 2022, Truth in Budgeting Hearing and FY23 budget approved by the Board.

FUND DEFINITIONS. The General Education Fund is the district's general fund, supported by a property tax millage, state aid section 81 and other local revenue such as workshop revenue and technology licensing revenue. The Special Education Fund is supported primarily by a property tax millage and is the source of the PA-18 distribution to local districts. The Career Focused Education Fund is the vocational education fund, supported primarily by a property tax millage and state aid section 61, and supports the four Oakland Schools Technical Campuses (OSTC).

PROPERTY TAX AND MEMBERSHIP. The FY23 expected levy is $216.6 million. Countywide LEA membership is charted for 2013 through 2022 with Blended Public School Membership of 182,575; 179,491; 177,037; 176,196; 176,350; 177,024; 175,199; 173,898; 172,041; and 165,013, and Blended PSA Membership of 9,654; 10,980; 11,452; 11,700; 12,554; 11,965; 11,733; 14,537; 14,913; and 15,904, with combined column labels of 192,229; 190,471; 188,489; 187,896; 188,904; 188,989; 186,932; 188,435; 186,954; and 180,917.

FY23 ASSUMPTIONS FOR THE THREE MAJOR OPERATING FUNDS. On revenue, a property tax increase of 4% including the probability of a Headlee rollback; state aid revenue held flat except for Sec. 81 ISD Operations at a 2% increase, Sec. 147c UAAL increasing, and Sec. 61a Vocational Education reverting to FY21 levels; fee-based revenues stable except subsidized programs that have returned to pre-pandemic levels; and workshop revenues increasing as onsite professional learning increases. On expenditures, a salary increase of 2% for all staff based on the union bargaining agreement plus steps (approximately .98% union and 1.28% non-union); a blended MPSERS rate of 28.26%; a health care cap increase of 3.7% to be adjusted in future budget amendments; and dental/vision budget reductions from the change to a premium-based program. The fund balance protocol sets a target of 7.5% to 12.5% of expenditures for the General Education and Career Focused Education funds and 5% to 10% of expenditures net of LEA distributions for the Special Education Fund, considering known economic liabilities or designated reserves, the State of Michigan's economic environment and the financial condition of LEAs.

ENTERPRISE-WIDE. Fiscal Year 2023 revenue is $391.2 million and expenditures are $393.2 million, in both cases for all funds except the Internal Service Fund.

SUBSIDIES AND LEA DISTRIBUTIONS. Subsidies comprise the Illuminate DnA student assessment tool at $363,800, Discovery Education Streaming at $149,500, the Atlas Rubicon curriculum management system at $184,500, the Nepris industry connections platform at $155,000, Career cruising software at $302,700, CDX automotive software at $15,000, communications media monitoring/clipping services at $23,850 and MiPEER at $17,400, for total subsidies of $1,211,750. Other distributions and program subsidies comprise CTE transportation reimbursement of $1,800,000, CTE career readiness distribution of $3,088,000, the PA-18 base distribution of $148,300,000, other special education subsidies of $2,700,000 and Medicaid distributions of $11,397,400, for a total of $167,285,400.

COLLABORATIVE EFFORTS. Social-emotional wellbeing and mental health support adds 2 Mental Health Consultants by shifting existing funding and increases professional learning in Youth Mental Health First Aid and Trauma-Informed Instruction along with PREPaRE (Prevent, Reaffirm, Evaluate, Provide and Respond, Examine) workshops. Cybersecurity investments include identifying security weaknesses across all Oakland-supported applications and devices, increasing multi-factor authentication, implementing an EDR endpoint detection and response platform, and partnering with local districts on penetration testing, a SIEM solution, field services phishing simulations and cybersecurity awareness. Other efforts include STEMi, a mobile STEM classroom; a Countywide Communication Channel; Literacy Essentials Oakland (LEO); the Michigan Collaboration Hub (MiCH); MiPEER; and COVID response.

**What it is**
Draft "Report to the Board of Education" from Plante & Moran, PLLC accompanying the audit of Troy School District's basic financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2023. Dated October 3, 2023; signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager. Sections: Results of the Audit (pp. 3-6), Other Recommendations and Observations (pp. 7-8), Informational Items (pp. 9-19). The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the business office.

**Audit results**
Engagement letter dated May 31, 2023; planning matters discussed at an August 4, 2023 meeting; audit report and management representation letter both dated October 3, 2023; a separate October 3, 2023 letter covers internal control over financial reporting and compliance testing under Government Auditing Standards. No new accounting policies were adopted in 2023. No difficulties, no disagreements with management, no consultations with other independent accountants; management corrected all accumulated misstatements. Most sensitive estimates were the district's shares of MPSERS net liabilities per GASB 68 and GASB 75.

| Estimate at June 30, 2023 | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| MPSERS net pension liability share | $340,447,659 |
| MPSERS net OPEB liability share | $19,240,985 |

**Other recommendations and observations**
- GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1: group purchases individually below the capitalization threshold but above it in aggregate must be capitalized; effective for the year ending June 30, 2024.
- Food Service Fund balance continues to exceed the USDA maximum of three months' operating expenditures; the district should continue its spenddown plan with the Michigan Department of Education.
- Troy Career Center (MiWorks): the program director tracks expenditures manually in an Excel template serving as the subsidiary ledger, including the WIOA program tested in the single audit; automation or more frequent reconciliation recommended.
- Inflation Reduction Act (signed August 16, 2022; $369 billion over 10 years toward roughly 40 percent emissions reduction by 2030) offers tax-exempt entities a direct-payment option on qualifying capital projects such as electric vehicles and solar.

**Fund balance**
General Fund expenditures exceeded revenue by approximately $361,000 in 2022/2023, reducing fund balance to approximately $32,620,000 at June 30, 2023 — 17.2 percent of expenditures, about 8.9 weeks of operation. The statewide average at June 30, 2022 was approximately 20.30 percent, roughly 10 weeks.

**State funding landscape**
The 2023/2024 target foundation allowance rose 5 percent, or $458 per pupil, to $9,608; 2022/2023 was $9,150 after a $450 increase. Cyber schools remain at $9,150. Pupil count stays 90 percent October 2023 / 10 percent February 2023, with a Section 29 two-year blend for declining-enrollment districts. State special education funding moved fully to Section 51 from Section 20, completing the Headlee Amendment funding shift. Other changes: a Section 31a At-Risk opportunity index, Section 31d universal free breakfast and lunch, GSRP eligibility raised to 300 percent of poverty, a riders-per-square-mile transportation formula, one-time mental health, school safety, and student loan repayment funding, and a 5 percent ISD operations increase. Federal pandemic education aid concludes September 30, 2024.

**MPSERS plan-level status (September 30, 2022)**
Net pension liability approximately $37.9 billion, up about 57 percent from $24.2 billion a year earlier; net OPEB liability approximately $2.1 billion, up about 40 percent from $1.5 billion. Driver: a 27.2 percent return for the year ended September 30, 2021 versus a 4.8 percent investment loss for the year ended September 30, 2022.

**Other informational items**
GASB financial reporting model project (exposure draft June 2020, final standards targeted March 2024, governmental funds tentatively removed from scope in June 2023); a Revenue and Expense Recognition standard anticipated 2027; GASB 101 Compensated Absences effective for the year ending June 30, 2025; sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023 permitting transportation uses for millages approved after May 7, 2023, with separate accounting by authorization date; Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1 superseding Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4 for June 30, 2024 audits; arbitrage compliance at the five-year bond anniversary; cybersecurity risk and the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021; and real estate options via Plante Moran Cresa.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Document identity and engagement terms**
A draft communication titled "Troy School District — Report to the Board of Education, June 30, 2023," issued by Plante & Moran, PLLC and dated October 3, 2023. Every page is watermarked DRAFT and footed "Ver. 02/2023." The firm audited the basic financial statements of Troy School District (the "School District") as of and for the year ended June 30, 2023 and issued its audit report thereon dated October 3, 2023. The transmittal letter directs the Board to three sections: Results of the Audit (pages 3-6), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 7-8), and Informational Items (pages 9-19). It thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness, is signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager, and states it is intended solely for the Board of Education and management.

Responsibilities were established in an engagement letter dated May 31, 2023, and the audit followed the scope and timing communicated at a planning meeting on August 4, 2023. Beyond U.S. generally accepted auditing standards, the audit was conducted under Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, which obligates the firm to communicate matters including compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements; error or fraud; illegal acts; and significant internal control deficiencies. A separate letter dated October 3, 2023 addressed internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance.

**Significant audit findings**
No new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies did not change during 2023; significant policies are described in Note 2 to the financial statements. No transactions were entered into for which authoritative guidance or consensus is lacking, and no significant transactions were recognized in a period other than when they occurred. The most sensitive accounting estimates were the School District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75. As of June 30, 2023 those estimates were $340,447,659 (pension) and $19,240,985 (OPEB), based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services; the firm evaluated key factors and assumptions and found them reasonable relative to the financial statements as a whole. Disclosures were described as neutral, consistent, and clear. No significant difficulties were encountered in performing or completing the audit; no disagreements with management arose; management corrected all accumulated known and likely misstatements other than trivial ones; there were no consultations with other independent accountants; and a management representation letter dated October 3, 2023 was obtained. The firm read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to its attention suggesting that other information was materially misstated or materially inconsistent with the financial statements.

**Other recommendations and observations**
GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1 clarifies that items purchased in a group that are individually below a district's capitalization threshold but exceed it in the aggregate should be reported in fixed asset records; the clarified guidance takes effect for the year ending June 30, 2024, and the district should align practices and written policies.

Food Service Fund fund balance continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures; the School District should continue to monitor the spenddown plan it entered into with the Michigan Department of Education.

Troy Career Center (MiWorks) expenditure reporting is tracked manually: the program director enters all Troy Career Center federal and state expenditures into an Excel template that serves as the subsidiary ledger by program — including the WIOA program tested in the single audit — and shares it with the business office. The auditors encourage evaluating a more automated tracking process or, alternatively, more frequent reconciliation to reduce allocation errors.

The Inflation Reduction Act, signed into law August 16, 2022, allocated $369 billion over ten years for energy and climate projects aimed at reducing emissions approximately 40 percent by 2030. Its direct-payment option, in lieu of a nonrefundable tax credit, is available to tax-exempt entities including governmental entities, reimbursing part of the cost of qualifying capital improvements such as certain electric vehicles and renewable energy equipment (for example solar panels).

**Fund balance**
During the 2022/2023 school year, General Fund expenditures exceeded revenue by approximately $361,000, reducing the General Fund fund balance to approximately $32,620,000 at June 30, 2023. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2022 was approximately 20.30 percent of expenditures and outgoing transfers, which would equate to roughly 10 weeks of average operating costs. Troy's fund balance percentage is 17.2 percent, equal to approximately 8.9 weeks of operation.

**School funding — new initiatives and state aid**
The May 2023 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference predicted sufficient resources for current programs plus substantial resources for new initiatives; the School Aid Bill for 2023/2024 was completed and signed into law. In 2022/2023 schools saw the largest per-pupil increase since the start of Proposal A (1994/1995), with all districts except a few hold harmless districts funded at the $9,150 target foundation allowance and all districts receiving a $450 per-pupil increase. For 2023/2024 the target foundation allowance rose 5 percent, or $458 per pupil, to $9,608; hold harmless districts also receive the $458 increase, while cyber schools received no increase and remain at $9,150.

Other 2023/2024 provisions described: new funding for declining enrollment districts to smooth revenue decline; continuation of the blended pupil count at 90 percent October 2023 and 10 percent February 2023, with a two-year blend available to districts whose 2023 final membership count is lower than 2022, funded through Section 29 (calculated as the foundation allowance times the difference between a 50/50 blend of the 2022 and 2023 blended counts and the blended 2023 count); completion of the shift of state special education funding to Section 51 of the State Aid Act from Section 20, so that the Headlee Amendment obligation is met from the special education categorical rather than the foundation allowance; increased Great Start Readiness Program reimbursement at the target foundation allowance level with income eligibility raised to 300 percent of poverty; increased Section 31a At-Risk funding using an opportunity index; revised Section 31d providing universal free breakfast and lunch, state funded and supplemental to the federal Child Nutrition Cluster; additional transportation funding using a riders-per-square-mile formula; one-time funding for student mental health and school safety; a one-time student loan repayment program for employees working directly with students; increased retirement system contributions to reduce long-term cost even after discontinuation of the one-time $1 billion contribution made in 2022/2023; and a 5 percent increase in the intermediate school district (ISD) operations allocation.

Looking forward, the May 2023 conference projected 2024, 2025, and 2026: a substantial 2023 surplus carries into 2024 but is significantly reduced by one-time payments, with 2025 projected to return to significant surplus. Risks flagged are inflation and a potential recession. Federal education-focused pandemic aid concludes September 30, 2024 — the "federal funding cliff." Planning factors listed include use of the ESSER III/11t allocation, staff retention and recruitment, student attraction and retention, pupil count trends, learning loss programming after pandemic funding ends, expanded GSRP preschool, food service redesign under the state free meal program, staffing and inflationary operating cost increases, technology costs, and school security and mental health staffing and costs. The next Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference was scheduled for January 2024.

**Michigan School Meals**
Beginning in 2023/2024, free breakfast and lunch are available to all Michigan students under amendments to the State Aid Act, state funded for students who do not qualify under the National School Lunch and National School Breakfast programs. Participation is not automatic: districts must apply using the 2024 Coordinated Application in the State's NexSys system. Eligibility requires being a public school, charter school, or ISD; participating in the National School Lunch Program; serving breakfast and lunch at no cost to pre-K through 12th grade students; adopting the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP) where the district qualifies; collecting family income information; and writing off all outstanding student negative balances. The Food Service Fund may not absorb that write-off, which requires funding from outside the fund under MDE guidance. Districts must track and claim meals as for federal programs and plan for higher participation across staffing, meal timing, cafeteria seating, menu planning, food orders, and family communications.

**MPSERS plan-level net liabilities**
The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2022 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $37.9 billion, an increase of approximately 57 percent from $24.2 billion at September 30, 2021. The retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB liability of approximately $2.1 billion at September 30, 2022, up approximately 40 percent from $1.5 billion at September 30, 2021. The primary driver in both cases was investment performance: a 27.2 percent annual return for the year ended September 30, 2021 versus a 4.8 percent investment loss for the year ended September 30, 2022.

**Accounting and reporting changes ahead**
The GASB financial reporting model project began in August 2013; an exposure draft titled "Financial Reporting Model Improvements" was issued in June 2020 with a comment period ending February 2021, and Plante & Moran, PLLC submitted comments. The GASB's goal was final standards by March 2024. At its June 2023 meeting the GASB tentatively decided to remove all issues related to governmental fund reporting from the proposed statement's scope, which would significantly reduce its impact. Proposed changes had included additional MD&A information and a variance column in the budget-to-actual statement. A related project, the June 2020 preliminary views on "Revenue and Expense Recognition," could change the timing of revenue and expense recognition; the GASB work plan anticipates issuance during 2027.

GASB Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences, requires recording a liability in the full accrual statements for leave attributable to services already rendered, that accumulates, and that is more likely than not to be used or paid, measured at each employee's pay rate at the financial statement date. It removes the requirement to disclose gross additions and reductions (net change may be disclosed instead) and the requirement to disclose which funds liquidate the liability. It is effective for the School District's year ending June 30, 2025.

**Sinking fund and bond reporting**
Legislation effective August 6, 2023 allows a sinking fund millage approved by voters after May 7, 2023 to be used for acquisition of student transportation vehicles and related parts, supplies, and maintenance equipment, and for trucks and vans registered under the Michigan vehicle code, 1949 PA 300, MCL 257.1 to 257.923, used to carry parts, equipment, and personnel for maintenance of school buildings. Sinking funds authorized (1) prior to March 29, 2017, (2) between March 29, 2017 and May 7, 2023, and (3) after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for separately, each with its own balance sheet and statement of revenue, expenditures, and changes in fund balance. Prior allowable uses — real estate, buildings, building improvements, and technology — were not amended. A district levying a sinking fund must have an annual independent audit of the fund including review of its uses.

During fiscal 2023/2024 the Michigan Department of Treasury will release Numbered Letter 2023-1, superseding Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4, effective for sinking fund and bond compliance audits required for the June 30, 2024 reporting period. Changes: districts will no longer submit financial information to Treasury upon bond closeout (Treasury will use audited statements already filed with the Department of Education) but must submit an annual transmittal letter reporting the status of the bond-funded Capital Projects Fund; the completion date is simplified to the June 30 immediately following the later of the certificate of substantial completion or 95 percent of bond proceeds being spent; multi-series bonds approved by electors at the same time may have closeout reporting at the end of the final issue without Treasury approval; and sinking fund levies renewed after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for in a capital projects fund separate from remaining balances from pre-May 7, 2023 levies, potentially requiring a new separate fund.

**Arbitrage, cybersecurity, and real estate**
Arbitrage — the difference between interest paid by the bond issuer and earnings on invested bond proceeds — has drawn attention amid rising interest rates. As a tax-exempt entity the district is subject to federal arbitrage rules limiting retained earnings, should work with its bond advisor on recurring computations, generally performs a computation at the five-year anniversary of the original bond sale to report excess earnings to the Internal Revenue Service, and uses the annual calculations to determine whether to report an arbitrage liability at June 30 in the full accrual statements.

On data security, the letter notes education remains a top ransomware target and cites the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021, signed into law in October 2021. It observes that the human element is the weakest link (passwords such as "August2023" are easily guessed) and asks whether staff are aware of phishing, whether data with personally identifiable information or FERPA-covered data sits on file-sharing sites, flash drives, or personal email accounts, and how secure data is with remote work; an external vulnerability assessment is suggested.

Understanding that the School District is considering how to leverage or better utilize real estate assets, the firm recommends evaluating options — demolishing and rebuilding, redeveloping for alternative purposes, leasing the building or land, or selling — and offers an introduction to its affiliated real estate consulting entity, Plante Moran Cresa.

**Document.** Transmittal letter dated March 28, 2022 from Dr. Wanda Cook-Robinson, Superintendent, Oakland Schools, addressed "Dear Board of Education Designate," forwarding the proposed Oakland Schools budget for FY 2022-23. Copies to District Superintendent and District Business Manager.

**Statutory basis and vote.** Per the Michigan School Code, Section 380.624(2), the proposed FY 2022-23 General Fund budget goes to constituent districts' Boards of Education for review by May 1, and not later than June 1 each constituent board shall adopt a resolution of support or non-support. Budgets for all funds were included for transparency, but LEA Designates vote only on the General Fund budget.

**Revenue outlook.** Oakland Schools is primarily funded by property tax dollars; the budget projects a growth factor in property tax revenues of 4.0%. Projections are called conservative against Oakland County taxable value increase projections because a Headlee rollback of the operating millage is considered probable for FY 2022-23 -- triggered when annual growth on existing property exceeds inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index. Taxable values and the millage reduction factor arrive by June 1.

**Major budget features.**
- Mental health: two mental health consultants added, broadening support of mental health workers in schools under Section 31n of the Revised School Aid Act, plus Youth Mental Health First Aid and Trauma-Informed Instruction.
- Career and Technical Education: aligned to the Michigan Department of Education's Top 10 in 10 Years goals; four technical campuses, career program redesign, and operational funding for the CTE mobile classroom (the STEMi), operational in spring 2021. The CTE allocation to LEAs rose more than 25% in 2019-20 and that level continues in 2022-23.
- Cybersecurity: multi-factor authentication, an endpoint detection and response platform for local districts, and phishing simulation exercises.
- Shared services on a cost recovery basis: technology to sixteen constituent districts, business office services to four districts through an intergovernmental agreement (IGA), plus instruction and truancy services.
- MiPEER: formed in FY 2012-13 by Oakland Schools and 22 Oakland County school districts as the Michigan Partnership for Essential Education Resources; members convert to PowerSchool BusinessPlus in phases between 2015-16 and 2022-23.
- Illuminate Education has been the countywide student assessment vendor since Fall 2016, covering twenty-eight (28) districts and two (2) public school academies; the Board agreed to a 50% subsidy for 2022-23, with "Item Banks" add-ons at districts' cost.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Oakland Schools Superintendent Dr. Wanda Cook-Robinson issued this transmittal letter on March 28, 2022, addressed "Dear Board of Education Designate," inviting constituent district boards to review the enclosed proposed Oakland Schools budget for FY 2022-23. The Oakland Schools Board of Education and the Superintendent jointly extend the invitation. The letter closes with copies to the District Superintendent and the District Business Manager, and directs budget questions to the Superintendent's office at 248.209.2424, promising prompt replies. Page markers ii, iii and iv appear in the extracted text.

STATUTORY FRAMEWORK AND THE CONSTITUENT VOTE. Per the Michigan School Code, Section 380.624(2), the proposed FY 2022-23 General Fund budget is to be submitted to its constituent districts' Boards of Education for review by May 1. Not later than June 1, the board of each constituent district shall adopt a resolution of support or non-support of the General Fund budget. For transparency purposes, Oakland Schools included the budgets for all of its funds in the enclosed document; however, it is only the General Fund budget upon which constituent districts vote, and the letter repeats that while Oakland Schools provides all of its fund budgets for review, LEA Designates are only voting on the General Fund budget.

PROPERTY TAX REVENUE AND HEADLEE. Oakland Schools is primarily funded by property tax dollars. The budget projects a growth factor in Oakland Schools' property tax revenues of 4.0%. Tax revenue projections are characterized as conservative compared to Oakland County taxable value increase projections because there is concern that a Headlee rollback of the operating millage is probable for FY 2022-23. The letter explains the mechanism: a rollback occurs when the annual growth on existing property is greater than the rate of inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index. Additional information regarding taxable values and the millage reduction factor will be received by June 1.

SOCIAL-EMOTIONAL WELLBEING AND MENTAL HEALTH SUPPORT. Oakland Schools has always provided resources in the areas of social-emotional wellbeing and mental health support, and the pandemic increased the need for these services substantially. To meet those needs, resources were shifted toward mental health support by adding two mental health consultants. These positions will broaden the support of mental health workers in schools under Section 31n of the Revised School Aid Act. Support for professional learning will deepen in programs such as Youth Mental Health First Aid and Trauma-Informed Instruction.

CAREER AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION. To align with the Michigan Department of Education's Top 10 in 10 Years goals and strategies, additional resources are dedicated to career and technical education. Beyond significant resources for the four technical campuses, the 2022-23 budget includes additional funds for career program redesign and operational funding for the CTE mobile classroom -- the STEMi -- which was operational in spring 2021, bringing STEM activities to local districts. In 2019-20 the CTE allocation to LEAs was increased by more than 25%, and that level of funding continues in 2022-23, providing local districts additional resources for local CTE programs from elementary to high school.

FOCUS ON CYBERSECURITY. To maintain the safety, security and integrity of applications and data managed by Oakland Schools, significant investments are being made in cybersecurity. Activities include increasing the use of multi-factor authentication, implementing an endpoint detection and response platform for local districts to detect and thwart security threats, and conducting cybersecurity awareness and phishing simulation exercises. Significant supports are available to constituent districts for cybersecurity awareness and evaluation.

SHARED SERVICES. Oakland Schools provides services to Oakland County districts above and beyond its normal service model, including technology, business office, instruction and truancy services provided on a cost recovery basis. Technology services are currently provided to sixteen constituent districts, and business office services are currently provided on a limited basis to four districts through an intergovernmental agreement (IGA) with Oakland Schools.

MiPEER CONSORTIUM. In FY 2012-13, Oakland Schools and 22 Oakland County school districts formed the Michigan Partnership for Essential Education Resources (MIPEER) to select a countywide Enterprise Resource Planning system for human resource and financial applications. Since then the Consortium has standardized the Chart of Accounts and created many best practice business processes for each function -- finance, human resources, budgeting and procurement. Consortium members are converting to the PowerSchool BusinessPlus software in phases between 2015-16 and 2022-23.

ILLUMINATE. Oakland Schools has contracted with Illuminate Education as its countywide student assessment and data analysis tool vendor since the Fall of 2016, and all twenty-eight (28) districts and two (2) public school academies are included in the software license and support agreement. Illuminate DnA provides teachers with one place to build and administer formative assessments, capture and analyze multiple sources of data to inform instruction, and direct students to learning resources supporting specific, targeted standards. The Oakland Schools Board of Education agreed to provide a 50% subsidy for the student assessment software and support in 2022-23; additional add-ons called "Item Banks" can be purchased through the contract at the districts' cost.

SUBSIDIES. The Illuminate DnA subsidy is one of several. Oakland Schools provides multiple software products at no cost or reduced cost to constituent districts in the areas of Career and Technical Education and curriculum and assessment. A subsidy is provided on the per pupil cost of the PowerSchool BusinessPlus system for districts that are members of the MiPEER consortium. Communication tools such as news services and media monitoring/clipping services are provided to LEAs at no cost. These subsidies in the 2022-23 budget are exclusive of pass-through grant funds, other district allocations, and the cost of dedicated staff who support student and finance/HR software and applications.

COUNTYWIDE COMMUNICATIONS CHANNEL. The 2022-23 General Education Fund budget includes costs for a countywide communications channel in the amount of $700,000. The project is intended to connect constituent districts to first responders via an emergency radio channel.

PERSONNEL COSTS. Step increases for eligible employees are included in the 2022-23 budget along with a 2% across-the-board salary increase. All union salary changes including step adjustments are subject to collective bargaining, and the increase is in accordance with the current bargaining agreement. Regarding the State-mandated retirement rate, there are 8 rates in effect depending on the hire date of employees and their choices for eventual retirement benefits. The most common employee choice is Basic/MIP with Health Care Premium Subsidy, and that rate is projected to remain at 28.23% for 2022-23. Oakland Schools analyzed its own employee choices and projected an overall blended retirement rate of 28.26% for 2022-23.

HEALTH CARE HARD CAP. The "Hard Cap" for employee health care costs remains in effect for all labor groups. The hard cap dollar limits that employers may pay are subject to annual adjustment based on the medical price index, over which the school district has no jurisdiction. Oakland Schools projected growth in the medical price index of 3.7%. The stated limits are:

| Tier | Plan year beginning after 1/1/22 | Plan year beginning after 1/1/23* |
|---|---|---|
| Family | $19,921.45 | $20,658.54 |
| Individual plus one | $15,276.01 | $15,841.22 |
| Single | $7,304.51 | $7,574.78 |

*projected, assuming growth in the Medical CPI of 3.7%

PA-18 SPECIAL EDUCATION FUNDING. Oakland Schools receives property tax revenue for support of Special Education programs. In FY 2022-23 there is growth projected in property tax revenue of 4.0%. The base distribution of PA-18 funding to local school districts is budgeted to increase approximately $7.9 million or 5.6%. Additionally, $2.7 million is budgeted for other LEA distributions for group home expenditures, reimbursements to districts for educating incarcerated youth, special education program startup and extraordinary expenditures, and capital. In FY 2021-22, Oakland Schools distributed additional PA-18 funds totaling $5.4 million above the base distribution.

PLANNING FOR THE FUTURE. Oakland Schools states it is dedicated to sound financial planning and preparing for future economic uncertainties. It utilizes a five-year forecast that is updated with each budget amendment and incorporates projections from Oakland County Equalization for taxable values. It also maintains a five-year capital plan updated annually to prepare for necessary improvements and upgrades to facilities and equipment, and the organization pre-funds at least three years and up to five years of the capital plan requirements. The letter pledges continued work to ensure the budget reflects commitment to increasing student achievement, using economies of scale to decrease operating costs for local districts, customizing and regionalizing programs and services for diverse constituent district needs, and assisting schools and districts in meeting state and federal mandates.

APPROVAL CALENDAR. A presentation of the budget to the 28 local school district business managers was scheduled at their meeting of the Oakland County School Business Officials on April 22, 2022. The Oakland Schools Board of Education would then hold a Designates Meeting on April 25 at 6:00 PM in Conference Room C, giving local board designates and district administration an opportunity to review the General Fund budget before submitting their board's resolution to Oakland Schools on or before June 1, 2022. The Oakland Schools Board of Education will hold a Truth in Budgeting hearing on June 7 and will consider the FY 2022-23 proposed budget documents for approval during its regular meeting that night.

OVERALL EFFECT. The amendment slightly raises General Fund revenue while raising appropriations more, deepening the budgeted General Fund deficit and lowering the projected June 30 fund balance. Among the ancillary funds, Food Service, Community Service, Preschool, Capital Maintenance and the 2019 Capital Projects Fund all end the year with higher projected balances than originally budgeted, while the Facility Rentals Fund is drawn to zero and the Sinking Fund's projected balance is modestly reduced. Every clause of the resolution recites the fiscal year 2021-22 except the Capital Maintenance Fund clause, which recites 2020-21.
